177	## Tensions and contradictions
178	
179	1. **The task's own premise doesn't fully hold.** Both class transcripts (Class 1 and Class 3) are diarized entirely under a single Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line — including Class 3, which the Spring 2026 teaching schedule assigns solo to Rash (`spring-2026-teaching.md`: "Feb. 5 | Conditioning - Alactic-Aerobic | Rash"). Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name instead of doing real per-speaker diarization. This means roughly 30,000 words of the richest, most first-person material in this corpus cannot be confidently attributed to Rash specifically versus Ruf or Wenger. Every transcript-sourced bullet above is marked Inferred for this reason, even where the underlying statement is a confident, first-person claim.
180	
181	2. **Department reporting model is not internally consistent.** The Playbook (p.6) frames Applied Performance as a peer discipline inside Health & Wellness that "enables" Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Nutrition, and Mental Health to answer their own questions. But Week 1 course material lists "Applied Performance" as one of many training sub-categories nested under Athletic Performance itself (p.11), and the same transcript narration describes Rash's role as "helping program and plan the training" — a support-staff framing, not a peer-department framing. Which model actually governs day-to-day authority is not reconciled anywhere in these documents.
182	
183	3. **Coach's-eye-first versus objective-first is argued both ways.** The course material repeatedly argues that "you don't need a fancy test... you have to have a good coach's eye" and criticizes the GPS/load-monitoring era for breeding a fear-driven under-training culture. Eric's own SportSmith writing moves the opposite direction on daily monitoring specifically: he replaced subjective wellness surveys with objective force-plate mRSI because subjective self-report couldn't be trusted. Both share a skepticism of trendy or convenient data, but they land on opposite defaults (trust the trained eye vs. require an objective number) for the daily-monitoring question specifically.
184	
185	4. **The Assessment Manual (V12) reads as an older document than the current technology stack.** It builds its 1RM-estimation protocol around GymAware, and its CMJ description references a "contact mat" for jump height. The current Playbook technology stack and the Development Plan both center velocity-based training on Perch, not GymAware, and the current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol runs all CMJ variants exclusively on ForceDecks force plates, with no contact mat mentioned. This suggests the Assessment Manual predates the current VALD/Perch-centered stack and may be a legacy document rather than the currently operative protocol — worth confirming directly with Eric before treating any of its specifics as current practice.
186	
187	5. **Testing cueing instructions conflict across two protocol documents for the same test.** The Assessment Manual's CMJ instructions say explicitly: "Do not coach the strategy of jumping." The current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol gives testers specific verbal cues to give athletes during CMJ, squat-jump, and hop-test administration ("keep chest up," "land softly," "land stiff-legged on only the toes"). These may be reconcilable (safety/technique cues vs. jump-strategy cues are different things), but the two documents read differently on how much a tester should say out loud.
188	
189	6. **Two different anaerobic-threshold heart-rate methods appear back to back in the same slide deck without being reconciled.** One slide gives an age-based formula (max HR = 220-age for men, 226-age for women, threshold at ~85% of that), and the very next slides give a body-size-based table (big/medium/small athlete, ~165/170/175 bpm threshold) as the operational standard used elsewhere throughout the conditioning material. Which one is actually used day to day is not stated. [class-4-2026.md pp.27-29]
190	
191	7. **The Development Plan's own critique cuts against the corpus it's part of.** It states the current Baylor Playbook "has no educational component whatsoever" and reads "like a vendor product reference manual," even though Eric personally co-teaches a full graduate-level course covering much of the same material the Playbook is missing. The department's teaching capacity clearly exists; it just hasn't been captured back into the Playbook or a formal intern curriculum yet.
192	
193	8. **The Playbook's NordBord documentation has not caught up with practice.** The Playbook's Technology Overview and Workflows still document a full, unqualified, roster-style NordBord data-collection SOP. The SportSmith piece describes explicitly retiring roster-wide NordBord testing for football starting after January 2023, keeping it only for small, targeted return-to-play groups. The written SOP has not been updated to reflect that decision.
194	
195	9. **A personally-stated periodization preference is stated inside an unreliable-speaker transcript.** "For me personally, this is a more preferential model to use" (about undulating over linear periodization) is a strong, direct, first-person preference claim — but it comes from the same unreliably-diarized Class 1 transcript described in Tension 1, so it cannot be confirmed as Eric's own stated preference without his direct confirmation.
196	
197	10. **Older vs. current unit-goal templates show almost no adopted content.** The Geyer and Skodinski Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are staff-authored templates for individual sport programming philosophy; Geyer's is mostly filled in (periodization model, weekly split, KPI tests for softball), Skodinski's is nearly blank (just the section headers). Neither is attributed to Eric, and there's no equivalent document in this corpus showing Eric's own answers to the same template questions — a real gap if Flint wants Eric's own unit-goal-style programming philosophy in his own words.

# Eric's method baseline (draft for Eric's review)

Purpose: this is the step-1 baseline for Flint. It pulls every position, practice, and decision rule out of Eric's own 23-document corpus (Baylor Applied Performance playbook, protocols, assessment manual, professional writing, and HHPR 5355 graduate-course material) so that every future synthesis note comparing an outside source (Landon Evans, TB's Training Info, Old Bull, Harries RTP, SCN/Moyer, etc.) has something of Eric's own to compare against. Date: 2026-09-26.

## Provenance note (read this before the bullets)

Not all 23 documents are Eric's own words, and the two richest sources (the class transcripts) have a diarization problem. Read this once, then use these tags:

- **Eric-authored, high confidence**: the two SportSmith articles, the Performance Playbook Development Plan, the Force Plate Testing V3 and Iso Seated Calf protocols, the Applied Performance Playbook (departmental document under his unit), and the HD ODSF metrics note (adopted practice, though the framework itself is Hawkin Dynamics' own).
- **Course slide decks (Week 1, Week 3, Class 4)**: co-branded to Ruf/Rash/Wenger on every title slide. Per `spring-2026-teaching.md`, Eric was the assigned instructor for the Feb. 5 and Feb. 12 sessions (Week 3 Lecture and Class 4 2026 respectively), so bullets from those two decks are marked **Explicit**. Week 1 (Jan. 22, "All") and Class 8/Lesson 8 (Mar. 19, Wenger's session) are marked **Inferred** — shared team material, not confirmed as Eric's individual position.
- **Both class transcripts (Class 1, Class 3) are diarized entirely under one Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line, across 100+ minutes combined.** This is true even for Class 3 (Feb. 5), which the syllabus assigns solo to Rash. Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name rather than doing real per-speaker diarization. That means specific sentences in these transcripts cannot be confidently attributed to Rash vs. Ruf vs. Wenger. Bullets drawn from the transcripts are marked **Inferred**, with a citation note, even where the statement itself is a direct, confident, first-person claim in the text. Flint should treat these as "the HHPR 5355 teaching team's shared position, individual speaker unconfirmed" until Eric ratifies them.
  - **Confirmed by Eric, 2026-09-26:** HHPR 5355 is taught each spring by Chris Ruf, Eric and Mike Wenger. The lecture material is split among the three of them. This confirms the course is partly Eric's, but it cannot say who spoke a given transcript line. So transcript bullets stay tagged Inferred and read as **course team positions**. Each one becomes Eric's own only when he claims it, in review or in the interview.
- **Reference material, not Eric's position**: `intencurriculumn.md` is Jason Avedesian's (Clemson) authored curriculum end to end, used by the Development Plan as a benchmark, not as something Eric wrote or necessarily agrees with. The two Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are explicitly staff templates filled in (thinly) by Geyer and Skodinski, not Eric. The AP Assessment Manual V12 and the TechnologyTemplateSOP (TMG) have uncertain/likely-legacy authorship (see Tensions below) and are marked accordingly.

Sections below use **Explicit** (the source states Eric holds this position, with confidence in authorship per the tiers above) and **Inferred** (implied by protocol design, shared course material, or transcript content with unconfirmed speaker attribution).

---

## Philosophy and decision principles

- Applied Performance's stated mission is to "drive elite performance ... by leveraging science and technology through education and relationships," enabling the high-performance team to answer questions, ask better questions, and discover new ones — not to hand down answers unilaterally. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
- The department's four operating principles are Athlete Monitoring and Analysis, Athlete Evaluation and Return-to-Performance, Performance Team Collaboration, and Research and Development. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
- Institutional framing: "Prepare Champions for Life" across four pillars (academic, athletic, social, spiritual), operationalized through six "One Standard, One Accord" principles. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.3-4]
- Data collection is judged on cost versus insight: "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention. When the insight stops justifying that cost, it's time to stop collecting." **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- A test can be scientifically valid and still be the wrong choice operationally: "The lesson wasn't about the test. It was about the infrastructure required to make a test useful ... even a valid test stops being valuable" without staff ownership and consistent collection. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]
- "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" — a test's validity doesn't rescue it if it can't be collected consistently at scale. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]
- Reject ownership language ("my team," "my athletes"): the athlete's development is shared across every department that touches them, not owned by any one coach. **Inferred (transcript, speaker unconfirmed)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5, "we got to get away from like the me and my"]
- Injury risk can be reduced, not eliminated, through sound programming, progression, and collaboration with Athletic Medicine — an explicit refusal to promise injury prevention. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.4]
- Be skeptical of social-media-driven training trends: a viral clip is "just a brief snapshot," stripped of the context that would tell you whether it's sound. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.3]
- Recovery has to be earned by training hard first; a culture of fear grew out of early GPS/load-monitoring work that pushed teams toward under-training in the name of "recovery." **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10]
- "Knowledge from experience" as a stated operating value: safety first, keep things simple, teach basic movement skills and basic lifts before anything advanced, treat strength as the base, and require bodyweight competency before loaded work. **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5; week1-lecture.md p.12]

## Department model and roles

- Applied Performance operates inside the Baylor Athletics Health & Wellness department, alongside (not above or below) Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, and Mental Health Services. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.5-6]
- The athlete is described as the hub of a wheel, with every support function (academics, Athletic Medicine, nutrition, mental health, Applied Performance) as a spoke — no single discipline owns the athlete's development. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5]
- An Athletic Performance coach is framed in explicit contrast to a narrower "Strength Coach" identity: "we/our" and holistic mind-body-spirit development versus "me/my" and just lifting/running. **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5; week1-lecture.md p.13]
- The current Baylor Applied Performance Operations Guide is judged, by Eric's own gap analysis, as missing: an intern/GA curriculum, sport-specific data dictionaries, daily operational checklists, Baylor-specific (not generic-template) technology workflows, and a guiding-principles/policy framework for staff and interns. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 1, 3.2]
- A three-phase roadmap (Foundation, weeks 1-4; Operational Depth, weeks 5-10; Education and Culture, weeks 11-16+) is the stated plan to close those gaps, ending with an annual Playbook review cycle each May. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4]
- Some assessments coaches already run inside practice should not be duplicated; use that existing data to triangulate rather than re-testing, and set objective criteria for coach-mandated tests when none exist. **Inferred (author uncertain — see Testing tensions)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md, "Team Cultures and Assessments"]

## Testing and assessment

- Assessment is continuous, not a single test day: start with movement quality, injury history, and training background, then observe daily via warm-ups and practice. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5]
- Testing protocol has to be exactly repeatable over time ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April") or the resulting data cannot be trusted for comparison. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.6]
- Favor a small number of valid, reliable tests mapped to clear KPI categories over an exhaustive battery — illustrated with a simple baseball profile (bodyweight, 60-yard dash, vertical jump, broad jump, back squat, push-up max). **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.6; week1-lecture.md p.16]
- Weekly tracking is preferred over infrequent (e.g., once-a-phase) testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early enough to adjust programming. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7]
- Preparedness (the athlete's underlying physical capability, built over a long period) is explicitly distinguished from readiness (day-to-day fluctuation) — both are tracked, but they answer different questions. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7]
- Reassessment timing is governed by three factors: proximity to competition, the expected magnitude of change for that training phase and athlete level, and current recovery status — "do not reassess an athlete if there is known fatigue." **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md, "Reassessment"]
- 1RM testing is reserved for intermediate/advanced athletes with real exposure to near-maximal loads; novices and most women's-sport testing default to repetition-max protocols, which are described as better tolerated neurologically, psychologically, and physically for smaller-framed lifters. **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.18; week1-lecture.md p.39]
- Velocity-based 1RM estimation (linear-displacement transducer, ~10% load increments to 85-90% or a target mean velocity) is preferred over live 1RM attempts to avoid the fatigue and injury risk of true maxing, with published target mean velocities at 1RM (squat 0.3 m/s, bench 0.2 m/s, power hang snatch 1.0 m/s, power hang clean 0.8 m/s). **Inferred (author uncertain — legacy protocol, see Tensions)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
- The Baylor Sport Assessment Table (V4) assigns a specific battery per sport (movement screen, anthropometrics, CMJ, broad jump, weighted throw, upper/lower strength estimation, strength endurance, aerobic fitness, repeat sprint ability, linear sprint, change of direction) rather than testing every sport the same way. **Inferred** [update-baylor-sport-assessment-table-v4.md]
- The current data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar), not by sport, which Eric's own gap analysis flags as a real usability problem for staff and a priority to fix with sport-specific, threshold-contextualized dictionaries. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]

## Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring

- Force plates (CMJ testing) were already the department's longitudinal performance-tracking tool well before the 2022-23 wellness-survey experiment, and remained in place after that experiment ended. **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were." **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- The standard CMJ family run on ForceDecks: hands-free squat, squat jump (quarter-squat start, 3s hold), countermovement jump (x3), hop test / repeated CMJ (10 reps total, n=5 pairs), and single-leg CMJ (x3 per leg) — each with a scripted weigh-in, stabilization, and rep protocol. **Inferred (protocol; author uncertain)** [revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md]
- The isometric seated calf raise is run on the ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting: 90-degree ankle/knee position, belt pre-tensioned to a fingertip's gap, 3 maximal 6-second contractions with 15 seconds' rest between reps. **Inferred (protocol)** [protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md; revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md]
- Metric selection for force-plate reporting follows a disciplined framework: pick 1-2 output metrics (the obvious performance result, e.g. jump height), 1-3 driver metrics (what produces the output, e.g. braking/propulsive force), 1-3 strategy metrics (how the athlete achieved it, e.g. phase durations), optional symmetry metrics (L/R differences), and add "fluffy" metrics (peak power, average power, RFD) only with a specific, defensible rationale. **Adopted practice, framework not Eric's own** [hd-odsf-metrics.md — origin: Hawkin Dynamics]
- NordBord hamstring testing was retired for roster-wide football monitoring (after starting January 2023) because a 25-30 minute per-group session could not be sustained across 120+ athletes without large, uncontrolled gaps in the data, and staff turnover ended the coordination needed to run it at scale. The decision rule stated: keep a demanding test only where you have "smaller numbers, clear clinical purpose, dedicated oversight" (now used for targeted return-to-play groups paired with joint-specific isometric testing); drop it where you can't guarantee consistent, comparable collection. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]

## Load monitoring and GPS

- The core GPS technology stack is Catapult (device/OpenField software) with Kitman Labs as the central athlete-management system for cross-technology storage, scaling, and visualization. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
- Core GPS metrics tracked: maximum velocity, total distance, player load, field time, heart-rate bands, velocity/acceleration/deceleration effort bands, and Inertial Movement Analysis (IMA) for indoor sessions without GPS coverage. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.11-13, Data Dictionary]
- A documented step-by-step SOP exists for the full GPS session lifecycle: charging, alarm-setting, activity creation, live period management, post-session sync, data cleaning (spike detection), tagging, and PDF export/reporting. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.9-11]
- No sport-specific or position-specific GPS/load thresholds currently exist in the documented data dictionary — it is generic and vendor-organized, and building contextualized per-sport thresholds is named as unfinished, prioritized work. **Explicit (gap, stated as a gap)** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]
- Heavy GPS/load-monitoring data was described as having bred a "culture of fear" in the field broadly (do less, to protect recovery), which the course material argues actually leaves athletes under-prepared for competition. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10]
- Daily subjective wellness surveys, rolled out across multiple sports via the AMS app starting summer 2022, were abandoned after roughly one academic year because athletes learned to game the consistent, low-effort answers the survey rewarded; the data looked clean but carried no real signal. Wellness surveys are still used, deliberately, in return-to-play scenarios and with athletes managing chronic health conditions, where subjective context still adds value objective data can't supply. **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]

## Speed and sprint

- Linear sprint testing uses a 2-point start for team-sport athletes (for reliability), athlete self-selected start timing, at least two maximal-effort reps over 30-40 meters. **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
- Split times are interpreted by physical quality, not just total time: 0-10m is read as an acceleration score (reflecting maximal strength/power/slow stretch-shortening-cycle development), 30-40m as a speed score (reflecting sprint-specific/fast stretch-shortening-cycle development), and 40m peak velocity is derived from the 30-40m split divided by 10. **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
- SmartSpeed timing gates are the standard tool for sprint, agility, and reaction-time testing across the department. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
- Speed is taught as the quality with the shortest ground-contact-time demand (~0.08s male, ~0.10s female at max velocity) and is described as harder to train and more genetically constrained than strength or power, but as the biggest separator between good and great athletes at the elite level. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.11]

## Strength and power

- The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill, each level a required foundation for the next) is repeatedly described as the department's programming "compass." **Inferred (transcript + shared course material)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10; week1-lecture.md pp.23,26]
- Exercise selection is organized on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises (Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of "sport specific." **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16; week1-lecture.md pp.32-36]
- The Principle of Dynamic Correspondence (Verkhoshansky) — matching amplitude/direction of movement, region of force production, dynamics of effort, rate/timing of force production, and regime of muscular work to the sport skill — governs whether an exercise actually transfers, rather than surface resemblance to the sport. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.14; week1-lecture.md p.34]
- Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.13; week1-lecture.md p.31]
- Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work. In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule. **Inferred (transcript + shared slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.21]
- Undulating/non-linear periodization (Parker/Miller/Panariello), waving volume week to week (e.g., medium-high, medium, high, low over four weeks) is stated as the personally preferred model over strict linear progression, specifically to avoid staleness while still building tolerance for higher loads. **Inferred (transcript, speaker unconfirmed but first-person: "For me personally, this is a more preferential model to use")** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-26]
- Prilepin's chart (total reps and reps-per-set by %1RM) is the default guide for daily rep/set assignment within a training block, used consistently across strength and power teaching. **Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.19; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.15]
- Strength's residual training effect is treated as roughly 30 days — a minimal retention dose is still trained within that window, even during lower-strength-emphasis blocks. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-25]
- Tracy Fober's maxim ("use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer") is adopted as a guiding standard: prioritize movement quality and confidence-through-competence over chasing hypertrophy or 1RM numbers, especially early in a training cycle. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.21; week1-lecture.md p.46]

## Conditioning and energy systems

- Conditioning is defined two ways: (1) how well an athlete can meet the energy requirements of their specific sport/activity, and (2) how well they sustain strength, speed, and power output across a full competition. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.22]
- All three energy systems (alactic ~10-12s highest power, glycolytic/anaerobic-lactic ~60-90s medium capacity, aerobic hours-long lowest power/highest capacity) are always active simultaneously; programming targets the adaptation, not the drill label. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.19; class-4-2026.md p.15]
- A sport cannot maximize all three energy systems at once — priority has to be picked based on what the competition actually demands (e.g., for football: prepared for fall camp first, then the first game). **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.31]
- For football specifically, the stated priority stack is: Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands; Goal 2, the same two systems for game demands; glycolytic conditioning is treated as a "worst case scenario" to be absorbed incidentally through camp and practice rather than programmed as a primary target. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md pp.34, 39]
- Anaerobic (lactate) threshold heart-rate zones are assigned by athlete body size rather than a single number: roughly 165 bpm for big/tall athletes, 170 for medium, 175 for small, with Zone 1-4 bands set as percentages of that individual threshold. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md pp.28-29]
- The traits easiest to build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest — this ordering is used to sequence what needs the most frequent re-exposure. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.47]
- Training intensities between roughly 75-90% of maximal effort are labeled (via Francis) "no man's land" — too fast to build alactic power cleanly, too slow to build real aerobic capacity — and are treated as a zone to generally avoid as a primary training target. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.48]
- "Everything we do is some form of conditioning": lifting, agility work, and skill drills each load a specific energy system (power vs. capacity, alactic/glycolytic/aerobic) and should be classified and counted as conditioning, not treated as separate from it. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.31, tables pp.35-42]
- For speed-power athletes, the aerobic system's main value is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP between bouts), not distance capacity — a better-developed aerobic system means more available energy on play 10, 11, or 12 of a drive, not longer continuous running ability. **Inferred (transcript)** [2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md p.9]
- Aerobic-system training is kept below anaerobic threshold with roughly a 1:1 to 1:2 work:rest ratio and a general speed ceiling around 4.5 m/s, specifically to avoid spilling over into glycolytic-system stress. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.51; 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.11-12]
- Joel Jamieson's *Ultimate MMA Conditioning* is recommended as the single best practical resource for energy-system development, on the basis that its methods transfer cleanly to non-combat sports despite the MMA framing. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md pp.49-50; 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.11-12]

## Rehab and return to play

- Applied Performance's stated role in return-to-performance is to supply information that supports Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine's decisions on training and RTP periodization — a support/advisory role, not a stated final-decision role. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
- KPI-threshold identification for diagnostic screening and performance testing is named as a departmental operating principle, but no specific RTP criteria, battery, or phased-return protocol appears anywhere in this corpus. **Explicit (principle) / gap (no criteria stated)** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
- Daily wellness-style subjective monitoring, dropped for general roster use, is explicitly kept in return-to-play scenarios specifically because subjective context still fills a gap objective testing can't. **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- NordBord hamstring testing, dropped for roster-wide use, is explicitly retained for smaller, targeted return-to-play groups paired with joint-specific isometric testing (ForceFrame-style). **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]

*This is the thinnest discipline in the corpus — see Interview prep.*

## Injury risk and prevention

- Injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through sound progression of load, training means, and density, in collaboration with Athletic Medicine — an explicit refusal to claim injury prevention as achievable. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.4; week1-lecture.md p.9]
- Bodyweight-control competency is treated as a marker of injury risk in its own right: an athlete who can bench 400 lb but can't do 10 clean push-ups has "something out of whack" that needs fixing regardless of their strength numbers. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5]
- Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27]
- No formal injury-risk model (ACWR, tissue-capacity tracking, a biomechanical screening protocol with defined red flags) is attributed to Eric anywhere in this corpus; the detailed treatment of ACWR and injury-risk modeling that does exist (Clemson curriculum) is reference material only, not confirmed Baylor practice.

## Recovery and sleep

- Recovery capacity must be "earned" by training hard enough first; recovery technology (Theragun, Normatec, cryo) is treated as useful but not a substitute for managing training stress and dose correctly. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.9]
- Recovery appears in the department's own subcategory list of Athletic Performance (alongside strength, conditioning, speed, agility, power, nutrition, applied performance, sports psychology, RTP), but no specific recovery protocol, sleep target, or monitoring tool is described anywhere in this corpus. **Explicit (named as a subcategory) / gap (no protocol stated)** [week1-lecture.md p.11]

## Nutrition and body composition

- Performance Nutrition is explicitly a separate Health & Wellness unit from Applied Performance, owning individual nutrition consultations, supplement education, body composition and bone density assessment, and the training table/fueling stations. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.5]
- Body composition testing is capped at no more than 4 times per year. **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md, "Anthropometrics"]
- Anthropometrics (height, weight, muscle-to-fat ratio) are described as strongly associated with success in most sports and worth tracking even though they are owned by Performance Nutrition rather than Applied Performance. **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md, "Anthropometrics"]
- No nutrition decision rules, body-composition targets, or thresholds are attributed to Eric anywhere in this corpus; this appears to be a deliberate department-design choice (Performance Nutrition owns it) rather than an oversight.

## Coaching, skill acquisition and constraints-led approach

- A trained "coach's eye," built through repetition and attention, is treated as at least as important as any technology for daily assessment: "you don't need a fancy test or anything to do that. ## Tensions and contradictions

1. **The task's own premise doesn't fully hold.** Both class transcripts (Class 1 and Class 3) are diarized entirely under a single Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line — including Class 3, which the Spring 2026 teaching schedule assigns solo to Rash (`spring-2026-teaching.md`: "Feb. 5 | Conditioning - Alactic-Aerobic | Rash"). Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name instead of doing real per-speaker diarization. This means roughly 30,000 words of the richest, most first-person material in this corpus cannot be confidently attributed to Rash specifically versus Ruf or Wenger. Every transcript-sourced bullet above is marked Inferred for this reason, even where the underlying statement is a confident, first-person claim.

2. **Department reporting model is not internally consistent.** The Playbook (p.6) frames Applied Performance as a peer discipline inside Health & Wellness that "enables" Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Nutrition, and Mental Health to answer their own questions. But Week 1 course material lists "Applied Performance" as one of many training sub-categories nested under Athletic Performance itself (p.11), and the same transcript narration describes Rash's role as "helping program and plan the training" — a support-staff framing, not a peer-department framing. Which model actually governs day-to-day authority is not reconciled anywhere in these documents.

3. **Coach's-eye-first versus objective-first is argued both ways.** The course material repeatedly argues that "you don't need a fancy test... you have to have a good coach's eye" and criticizes the GPS/load-monitoring era for breeding a fear-driven under-training culture. Eric's own SportSmith writing moves the opposite direction on daily monitoring specifically: he replaced subjective wellness surveys with objective force-plate mRSI because subjective self-report couldn't be trusted. Both share a skepticism of trendy or convenient data, but they land on opposite defaults (trust the trained eye vs. require an objective number) for the daily-monitoring question specifically.

4. **The Assessment Manual (V12) reads as an older document than the current technology stack.** It builds its 1RM-estimation protocol around GymAware, and its CMJ description references a "contact mat" for jump height. The current Playbook technology stack and the Development Plan both center velocity-based training on Perch, not GymAware, and the current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol runs all CMJ variants exclusively on ForceDecks force plates, with no contact mat mentioned. This suggests the Assessment Manual predates the current VALD/Perch-centered stack and may be a legacy document rather than the currently operative protocol — worth confirming directly with Eric before treating any of its specifics as current practice.

5. **Testing cueing instructions conflict across two protocol documents for the same test.** The Assessment Manual's CMJ instructions say explicitly: "Do not coach the strategy of jumping." The current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol gives testers specific verbal cues to give athletes during CMJ, squat-jump, and hop-test administration ("keep chest up," "land softly," "land stiff-legged on only the toes"). These may be reconcilable (safety/technique cues vs. jump-strategy cues are different things), but the two documents read differently on how much a tester should say out loud.

6. **Two different anaerobic-threshold heart-rate methods appear back to back in the same slide deck without being reconciled.** One slide gives an age-based formula (max HR = 220-age for men, 226-age for women, threshold at ~85% of that), and the very next slides give a body-size-based table (big/medium/small athlete, ~165/170/175 bpm threshold) as the operational standard used elsewhere throughout the conditioning material. Which one is actually used day to day is not stated. [class-4-2026.md pp.27-29]

7. **The Development Plan's own critique cuts against the corpus it's part of.** It states the current Baylor Playbook "has no educational component whatsoever" and reads "like a vendor product reference manual," even though Eric personally co-teaches a full graduate-level course covering much of the same material the Playbook is missing. The department's teaching capacity clearly exists; it just hasn't been captured back into the Playbook or a formal intern curriculum yet.

8. **The Playbook's NordBord documentation has not caught up with practice.** The Playbook's Technology Overview and Workflows still document a full, unqualified, roster-style NordBord data-collection SOP. The SportSmith piece describes explicitly retiring roster-wide NordBord testing for football starting after January 2023, keeping it only for small, targeted return-to-play groups. The written SOP has not been updated to reflect that decision.

9. **A personally-stated periodization preference is stated inside an unreliable-speaker transcript.** "For me personally, this is a more preferential model to use" (about undulating over linear periodization) is a strong, direct, first-person preference claim — but it comes from the same unreliably-diarized Class 1 transcript described in Tension 1, so it cannot be confirmed as Eric's own stated preference without his direct confirmation.

10. **Older vs. current unit-goal templates show almost no adopted content.** The Geyer and Skodinski Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are staff-authored templates for individual sport programming philosophy; Geyer's is mostly filled in (periodization model, weekly split, KPI tests for softball), Skodinski's is nearly blank (just the section headers). Neither is attributed to Eric, and there's no equivalent document in this corpus showing Eric's own answers to the same template questions — a real gap if Flint wants Eric's own unit-goal-style programming philosophy in his own words.

    62	
    63	**When NOT to apply** — The intramuscular-pressure data (Fig 4.13) are from electrically
    64	stimulated cat soleus and gastrocnemius (Petrofsky & Hendershot, 1984), not human voluntary
    65	contraction; treat the specific kPa values as animal-model data illustrating the
    66	tension-pressure relationship, not human norms. The Rohmert-curve endurance data (Fig 4.14)
    67	are specifically finger-flexor endurance (Petrofsky, 1980), a small, distal muscle group;
    68	the shape of the curve (hyperbolic decline, female advantage) should not be assumed to hold
    69	identically for large, proximal muscle groups without separate verification. The 27-28
    70	Celsius optimum-temperature finding and the bodyfat-endurance link are each from single
    71	cited sources without reported effect sizes. The text points to "(Fig 4.14)" for the
    72	temperature optimum (PDF p. 238, printed p. 227), but Fig 4.14 plots endurance against %MVC
    73	and shows no temperature data; do not cite the figure for the temperature claim.
    74	
    75	**Example** — Inference: a coach prescribing a sustained isometric hold at low relative
    76	intensity could expect it to be comparatively non-fatiguing per the 10-15%-of-maximum
    77	threshold, while a sustained near-maximal hold held to fatigue would need the multi-minute
    78	recovery windows this entry describes before endurance returns. Whether a given hold is
    79	under 10-15% of maximum is not shown in the source.
    80	
    81	**Related** — [[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]],
    82	[[principle--breath-holding-and-valsalva-support-spinal-stability-in-maximal-lifting]] (Ch3,
    83	a related discussion of intramuscular/intrathoracic pressure during sustained maximal
    84	effort).

    13	
    14	# Isometric Strength Gains Spread Further From the Training Angle When the Muscle Trains in a Lengthened Position
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Many studies report isometric training producing maximum strength gains at
    17	or very close to the trained joint angle, leading some athletes to avoid isometric training
    18	altogether; the authors argue this "angular specificity" framing needs critical revision,
    19	citing other studies showing isometric training also produces significant strength increase
    20	up to about 15 degrees either side of the training angle. Because every type of muscle
    21	contraction has its own force/torque-versus-joint-angle curve (see 2.1.2), the authors argue
    22	it is "highly unlikely" that strength gain would be confined to one precise angle and
    23	nowhere else, and prefer the term "regional specificity" over "angular specificity" (or
    24	muscle-length specificity). Thepault-Mathieu et al (1988) found this regional specificity is
    25	strongest when the muscle trains in its most shortened position and weakest when it trains
    26	most lengthened: males training isometrically for 5 weeks (5 sets of 5 reps, 5 seconds each,
    27	3 times weekly) at 25 degrees of elbow flexion (full extension = 0 degrees) gained 54%
    28	strength at the training angle but only about 25% averaged over the rest of the range; a
    29	group training at 80 degrees gained 30% at the training angle and about 25% over the rest of
    30	the range; a group training at 120 degrees gained 25% at the training angle but only about
    31	7% over the rest of the range. The authors' summary: isometric training of a relatively
    32	lengthened muscle can produce substantial strength increase "not only near the region of
    33	training, but also throughout the range of movement." They caution this finding should not
    34	be read as meaning isometric training can replace other strength-training forms, since a
    35	specific type of static or dynamic strength depends on the neuromuscular factors governing
    36	how force is exerted in a given situation. (PDF pp. 237-238, printed pp. 226-227, "4.2.4
    37	Isometric Training," "Isometric Training and Angular Specificity.")
    38	
    39	**Why it works** — The authors give the biomechanical basis (a distinct force/torque-vs-angle
    40	curve exists for every contraction type) for why strict single-angle specificity is
    41	implausible, but they do not give a mechanism for why the Thepault-Mathieu et al (1988)
    42	lengthened-position condition specifically produced the broadest transfer across the range
    43	(54%/25 degrees training angle giving about 25% elsewhere, versus 120 degrees training angle
    44	giving only about 7% elsewhere). Inference: a plausible explanation, not stated in the text,
    45	is that training at longer muscle lengths recruits a different or broader distribution of
    46	sarcomere lengths and joint-angle-dependent moment arms than training at a shortened length,
    47	though this is not confirmed by the source.
    48	
    49	**When to apply** — Use this as a rationale for choosing a relatively lengthened joint
    50	position when isometric training is intended to transfer strength gains across a wider
    51	portion of the range of motion, rather than assuming isometric work only strengthens the
    52	exact trained angle. Use the "regional specificity" framing, not "angular specificity," when
    53	discussing isometric training's carryover with coaches or athletes.
    54	
    55	**When NOT to apply** — This is a single study (Thepault-Mathieu et al, 1988) with a specific
    56	protocol (5 weeks, 5x5 at 5 seconds, 3x weekly, elbow flexion only) and three training
    57	angles; the specific percentages (54%, 30%, 25% at-angle gains; roughly 25%, 25%, 7%
    58	remainder-of-range gains) should not be generalised to other joints, muscle groups, or
    59	protocols without direct testing. The authors' own caution stands: this finding does not
    60	mean isometric training can substitute for dynamic strength training generally.
    61	
    62	**Example** — The book's own example is the Thepault-Mathieu et al (1988) three-group study
    63	described above; no further invented example is added here.
    64	
    65	**Related** — [[claim--hettinger-muller-isometric-strength-gain-rate]],
    66	[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]] (Ch2, a related but
    67	broader claim about joint-angle transfer that this entry's regional-specificity nuance
    68	qualifies).

    13	
    14	# Isometric Contraction Is Not One Thing: Voluntary vs Reflexive, Slow vs Explosive
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors argue isometric training is not simply holding a static
    17	contraction for a set time: a true isometric contraction requires the muscle to raise
    18	tension from rest to a maximal or sub-maximal value over a rise ("attack") time, sustain
    19	that tension for a resistance phase, then decrease it to rest or a lower value over a decay
    20	time. Verified against the page image (Fig 4.11, PDF p. 236, printed p. 225): the authors
    21	categorise isometric contraction into voluntary isometrics (splitting further into slow
    22	isometrics and voluntary explosive isometrics) and reflexive isometrics (splitting further
    23	into reflexive explosive isometrics and oscillatory isometrics). A voluntary isometric
    24	contraction can be produced deliberately; a reflexive one occurs involuntarily via the
    25	muscle's reflex response between the eccentric and concentric phases of plyometric
    26	activities such as the depth jump or weightlifting clean-and-jerk. Verified against the page
    27	image (Fig 4.12, PDF p. 236, printed p. 225): the figure contrasts slow isometrics (gradual
    28	rise, long resistance plateau) with explosive isometrics (steep rise, short resistance
    29	phase); the caption says reflexive explosive action has an even steeper rise and a much
    30	shorter resistance phase ("The slope of the rise is even greater and the duration of the
    31	resistance phase is much shorter during reflexive explosive isometric action"). On
    32	oscillatory isometrics, the authors say the technique "may also be useful in producing
    33	powerful contractions over a small range of movement," citing research showing that "the
    34	maximum tension that can be produced voluntarily during sinusoidally pulsed brief isometric
    35	jerks at 5 Hz is the same as the maximum sustained tension" (Soechting & Roberts, 1975);
    36	Basmajian (1978) read this as emphasising fibre recruitment and motor-unit synchronisation
    37	(PDF p. 235, printed p. 224). That is the only evidence the book gives for the oscillatory
    38	box, and it describes voluntarily produced jerks, while Fig 4.11 (PDF p. 236, printed p.
    39	225) files oscillatory isometrics under reflexive isometrics; the book does not reconcile
    40	the two. The authors argue that because the steepness of the isometric force-time curve,
    41	and the higher magnitude of maximum isometric versus dynamic maximum force at equivalent
    42	joint angles, both support developing explosive strength isometrically when the training
    43	accent is on speed of force development, "it is doubtful whether it is always productive to
    44	maintain a rigid distinction between dynamic and isometric exercise": as resistance grows
    45	very large, dynamic work becomes progressively more isometric, so isometric work is "really
    46	the limiting case of dynamic work as the velocity of movement tends to zero." Because the
    47	inhibitory effects usually associated with voluntary muscle action are not encountered in
    48	reflexive isometric contraction, "even greater explosive force can be displayed
    49	isometrically than dynamically." The authors add that "negative evaluations of this method
    50	are premature" (PDF p. 236, printed p. 225). A related but separate finding on impulsive
    51	loading: short bouts of low-frequency mechanical vibration (10-35 Hz) applied to the body
    52	have been shown to speed recovery, modulate muscle activity, raise strength/power stable
    53	state, lower arterial pressure and enhance oxidative processes (Kopysov, 1978; Lebedev &
    54	Peliakov, 1991), and whole-body vibration at 26 Hz through the lower extremities has been
    55	shown to produce marked increases in jumping power (Bosco et al, 1998); the authors note
    56	this fuels an open debate about whether plyometric training effects are driven mainly by
    57	elastic-energy storage/release, neural facilitation, or intrinsic muscle changes (Ingen
    58	Schenau et al, 1997). (PDF pp. 235-236, printed pp. 224-225, "4.2.4 Isometric Training,"
    59	Figs 4.11-4.12.)
    60	
    61	**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism for the voluntary/reflexive distinction is neural:
    62	reflexive isometric contraction does not encounter the inhibitory effects usually associated
    63	with voluntary muscle action, permitting higher explosive force display (PDF p. 235, printed
    64	p. 224). Inference: the slow-vs-explosive distinction within each category follows from how
    65	quickly neural drive ramps up to the target tension level, which the force-time curve shape
    66	(Fig 4.12) captures directly.
    67	
    68	**When to apply** — Use this taxonomy when specifying what kind of isometric work a given
    69	drill is training: a sustained maximal hold at a joint angle is a slow voluntary isometric;
    70	a deliberately fast ramp to near-maximal tension is a voluntary explosive isometric; the
    71	brief isometric moment between the eccentric and concentric phases of a depth jump or
    72	clean-and-jerk is, per the authors, a reflexive explosive isometric that the athlete does
    73	not consciously initiate. Per the authors, distinguish "isometric training for developing
    74	absolute strength" from "isometric training for developing explosive strength" and select
    75	the appropriate type for the goal.
    76	
    77	**When NOT to apply** — The authors say the absolute-strength versus explosive-strength
    78	split within isometric training "still requires detailed experimental corroboration" (PDF p.
    79	236, printed p. 225). Inference: the oscillatory category rests on one cited study of
    80	voluntary 5 Hz jerks (Soechting & Roberts, 1975), so the evidence the book gives does not
    81	support its placement under reflexive isometrics. The vibration/whole-body-vibration findings are a
    82	separate line of evidence (Bosco et al, 1998, and others) that the authors connect to this
    83	discussion only by analogy (impulsive loading), not by stating vibration produces isometric
    84	contraction in the sense defined here; treat the two topics as related but distinct.
    85	
    86	**Example** — The book's own example is the depth jump and the weightlifting clean-and-jerk
    87	cited as sources of reflexive isometric contraction; no further invented example is added
    88	here.
    89	
    90	**Related** — [[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]] (Ch1, the broader
    91	concentric/eccentric/isometric/quasi-isometric terminology this taxonomy sits within),
    92	[[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]].

    13	
    14	# External vs Internal Isometrics, and Using a Held Supramaximal Load to Prime the Nervous System
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors distinguish "external isometrics" (contraction exerted against
    17	an external load) from "internal isometrics" (contraction exerted against opposing muscles
    18	within the body, as in bodybuilders' posing actions; see
    19	[[heuristic--loadless-training-broomstick-protocol]]). Isometric contractions can be
    20	submaximal or maximal, short or long duration, continuous or intermittent, sequenced across
    21	different joint angles, alternated between agonist and antagonist (or adductor/abductor,
    22	medial/lateral rotators), and alternated between intensities, including voluntary
    23	oscillation between high and low intensity to prolong the period of application. A
    24	separate practical technique: isometrically holding a heavy load at a "sticking point" can
    25	"decrease any deficiencies in that region or prime the nervous system to cope with greater
    26	levels of loading which will eventually be encountered during the process of gradual
    27	progressive overload"; the authors' specific example is "the mere supporting of a
    28	supramaximal load (e.g. 120-150% of one's 1RM) on the shoulders or quasi-isometric movement
    29	over the first few degrees of knee flexion of a squat," which can "accustom the body
    30	neuromuscularly and favourably enhance one's mental perception to undertake future squats
    31	which are going to be only slightly heavier than one's current 1RM." The authors also state
    32	that, "as pointed out earlier," isometric contraction released explosively "can decrease the
    33	reaction response time by as much as 7%, particularly if associated with a strong
    34	pre-stretch," against the traditional coaching belief that movement is most efficient
    35	starting from complete relaxation; "Verkhoshansky stresses" that a movement produced from
    36	complete relaxation is usually slower and less forceful. Historically, isometric effort was
    37	emphasised heavily by DeLorme, Hettinger and Muller, but with the rise of gymnasium machines
    38	and the decline of Charles Atlas's mail-order "dynamic tension" programmes, isometrics
    39	largely fell out of popular use, though physical therapists still use it in early
    40	injury-rehabilitation stages, and Russian coaches often prescribe the 75% concentric / 15%
    41	eccentric / 10% isometric strength-training regime "advocated by their scientists" for the
    42	average athlete. The authors also note that because one basic PNF principle holds that
    43	mobility (dynamic contraction) is more primitive than stability (isometric contraction),
    44	stability sits at a "higher level of muscular learning." (PDF p. 240, printed p. 229,
    45	"Other Aspects of Isometric Activity," "4.2.4 Isometric Training.")
    46	
    47	**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for the 7% reaction-time figure (PDF p.
    48	240, printed p. 229). Inference: it may connect to the earlier argument that reflexive
    49	isometric contraction escapes the inhibition associated with voluntary action (PDF p. 235,
    50	printed p. 224; see [[framework--isometric-contraction-categorization-voluntary-reflexive]]),
    51	but that argument is about force, and the text does not link the two. For supramaximal
    52	holding, no cellular mechanism is given; the stated effect is neuromuscular and perceptual
    53	familiarisation ("accustom the body neuromuscularly," "favourably enhance one's mental
    54	perception") rather than a measured strength-transfer pathway.
    55	
    56	**When to apply** — Use the external/internal isometrics distinction as vocabulary when
    57	specifying whether a drill uses an external load or purely internal agonist-antagonist
    58	tensing. Use supramaximal-hold work (120-150% of 1RM support holds, or quasi-isometric
    59	movement over the first few degrees of a squat) as a progressive-overload step that
    60	accustoms the athlete to loads slightly above current 1RM (PDF p. 240, printed p. 229). Use
    61	the 75/15/10 concentric/eccentric/isometric regime as a citable, if dated, historical
    62	reference point when discussing how much isometric work a general strength programme might
    63	include.
    64	
    65	**When NOT to apply** — The 7% reaction-time figure and the supramaximal-holding
    66	familiarisation effect are stated without reported sample sizes or controlled outcome data
    67	in this passage; treat them as the authors' summarised cla

15	    14	# Hettinger and Muller's Original Isometric-Training Finding: About 5% Strength Gain Per Week From One Daily 6-Second Effort at Two-Thirds Maximum
16	    15	
17	    16	**What it is** — Isometric exercises became popular in the mid-1950s in the search for
18	    17	economical, effective strength methods. Hettinger and Muller (1953, 1955) established that
19	    18	one daily effort at two-thirds of maximum, held for six seconds, performed for 10 weeks,
20	    19	increases strength by about 5% per week. Separately, Clark et al (1954) found that static
21	    20	strength continues to increase even after a four-week isometric programme has concluded.
22	    21	This early success prompted considerable research comparing isometric training's
23	    22	effectiveness against dynamic training, which produced "rather contradictory data" (see
24	    23	review by Verkhoshansky, 1970). The authors' general conclusion from that body of research:
25	    24	isometric training can be more effective than dynamic exercise specifically where the target
26	    25	exercise requires a large-magnitude muscle contraction at a certain stage of a movement, or
27	    26	"during the early stages of injury rehabilitation"; if the target exercise involves
28	    27	high-speed movement, sustained isometric training is less effective. The authors also note
29	    28	that because isometric training's usual purpose is developing absolute strength, tension
30	    29	should be increased slowly and held for a relatively long time, since prolonged tension
31	    30	maintenance demands the energy expenditure that stimulates adequate neuromuscular
32	    31	adaptation; some researchers found no essential difference in strength gain from varying
33	    32	isometric tension intensity, from which the authors infer that "the fundamental
34	    33	conditioning factor is not so much the magnitude of the isometric tension as its duration."
35	    34	(PDF pp. 234-235, printed pp. 223-224, "4.2.4 Isometric Training.")
36	    35	
37	    36	**Why it works** — The authors' stated reasoning: prolonged maintenance of muscular tension
38	    37	requires an energy expenditure that "stimulates adequate adaptation in the neuromuscular
39	    38	system, thereby determining its strength potential," and this can exceed the stimulus from
40	    39	brief transient dynamic tension. The authors give no cellular or neural mechanism for why
41	    40	duration outweighs magnitude; their conclusion rests on studies that did not find a
42	    41	strength-gain difference across tension intensities (p.224), not on a stated physiological
43	    42	pathway.
44	    43	
45	    44	**When to apply** — Use the 5%-per-week figure and the two-thirds-maximum, 6-second, daily,
46	    45	10-week protocol as a citable historical anchor for isometric-training dosing, and use the
47	    46	authors' scoping rule (isometrics favoured for large-magnitude contraction at a specific
48	    47	movement stage or early rehab; less favoured when the target skill is high-speed) to decide
49	    48	when isometric work is the better tool versus dynamic resistance training.
50	    49	
51	    50	**When NOT to apply** — This is 1950s data; the authors say later comparisons of isometric
52	    51	and dynamic training produced "rather contradictory data" (Verkhoshansky 1970 review, PDF
53	    52	235, printed p.224), and the text reports no modern replication. Treat "5% per week" as
54	    53	specific to Hettinger and Muller's exact protocol (two-thirds max, 6 seconds, daily, 10
55	    54	weeks), not a generalizable isometric-training growth rate. The "duration not magnitude"
56	    55	inference (PDF 235, printed p.224) sits against other statements in the same book and the
57	    56	library. On PDF 33, printed p.22, the authors cite Hettinger and Muller (1953) for a
58	    57	threshold stimulus of "not ... less than one-third of the maximal strength" for the average
59	    58	person, and add that as strength increases the stimulus "should be increased, and reach
60	    59	80-95% of the athlete's maximum" (see [[claim--strength-training-threshold-stimulus]]); on
61	    60	PDF 34, printed p.23, Korobkov, Gerasimov and Vasiliev (via Verkhoshansky 1977) report
62	    61	"approximately equivalent increases in strength" with loads of 20, 40, 60 and 80% of 1RM in
63	    62	the initial stages of training, which partly agrees with the p.224 inference for beginners.
64	    63	The book's own isometric protocol also sets explosive work at "70-80% of one's maximum
65	    64	strength" (PDF 237, printed p.226). Natera, as relayed in
66	    65	[[framework--isometric-training-variables-and-adaptations]] (Moyer), reports Oranchuk 2019
67	    66	as finding that "moderate-to-high intensity gives the best" peak-force gains. Hold length
68	    67	also differs across the section: 6 s here; "no more than 6 seconds (some authors recommend
69	    68	10 seconds)" and "no longer than 8 seconds" for non-explosive maximal holds (both PDF 237,
70	    69	printed p.226).
71	    70	
72	    71	**Example** — The book's own example is the Hettinger and Muller protocol itself (daily,
73	    72	6-second, two-thirds-maximum isometric effort for 10 weeks, yielding about 5% weekly
74	    73	strength gain); no further invented example is added here.
75	    74	
76	    75	**Related** — [[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]],
77	    76	[[claim--isometric-regional-specificity-not-strictly-angular]],
78	    77	[[claim--strength-training-threshold-stimulus]] (Ch1, the intensity-threshold rule this
79	    78	entry's duration inference sits against),
80	    79	[[framework--isometric-training-variables-and-adaptations]] (Moyer, Oranchuk 2019 as
81	    80	relayed).

83	     1	---

94	    12	---
95	    13	
96	    14	# Isometric Endurance Collapses Above 10-15% of Maximal Tension, and Recovers in Three Distinct Phases
97	    15	
98	    16	**What it is** — Isometric endurance at resistance exceeding 10-15% of a muscle's maximal
99	    17	strength is very short compared with dynamic exercise, because of metabolic demand and
100	    18	impaired blood flow to the exercising muscle under sustained contraction (Petrofsky &
101	    19	Phillips, 1986); below that threshold, contractions are considered non-fatiguing, since
102	    20	intramuscular pressure stays low and is readily exceeded by rising mean arterial pressure in
103	    21	the capillaries. Verified against the page image (Fig 4.13, PDF p. 238, printed p. 227, cat
104	    22	soleus and gastrocnemius, electrically stimulated, based on Petrofsky & Hendershot, 1984):
105	    23	intramuscular pressure rises roughly linearly with muscle tension, from about 0 kPa at 0%
106	    24	to about 20 kPa at 100% of maximal strength. As tension rises, intramuscular pressure rises
107	    25	with it and metabolism cannot keep pace, producing a hyperbolic drop in performance and
108	    26	marked fatigue increase (the Rohmert curve, first derived by Monod and Sherrer 1967, later
109	    27	by Rohmert 1968). Verified against the page image (Fig 4.14, PDF p. 238, printed p. 227,
110	    28	finger flexors, based on Petrofsky 1980): endurance time falls hyperbolically as %MVC
111	    29	(maximum voluntary contraction) rises, and females sustain the same tension level for
112	    30	longer than males at every tension level tested, a difference the authors say "has not
113	    31	been adequately explained yet." Muscle temperature also affects isometric endurance: hot
114	    32	packs reduce it and pre-exercise icing increases it. The authors write that "Research by
115	    33	Clarke et al (1958) discovered that there is an optimum core muscle temperature" above and
116	    34	below which isometric endurance fairly rapidly decreases, an optimum later placed near 27-28
117	    35	Celsius (Petrofsky & Phillips, 1986). Higher
118	    36	bodyfat percentage, associated with higher resting muscle temperature, is linked to lower
119	    37	isometric endurance in most situations. Dynamic exercise takes place more efficiently at
120	    38	higher temperatures, "apparently because of reduced environmental tissue viscosity," but in
121	    39	isometric contraction muscle fibres do not move, so viscosity plays an "insignificant role
122	    40	compared with that of muscle metabolism" (Petrofsky & Phillips, 1986). Recovery from
123	    41	isometric contraction proceeds in three phases (Petrofsky & Phillips, 1986): a rapid
124	    42	recovery of about 50% of endurance in the first 3 minutes; a slower recovery lasting about
125	    43	20 minutes, reaching about 90% of initial endurance; and complete recovery within at least
126	    44	24 hours; recovery from low-tension isometric contraction is slower during the first phases
127	    45	of recovery. (PDF pp. 238-239, printed pp. 227-228, "Isometric Endurance," "Recovery after
128	    46	Isometric Activity," Figs 4.13-4.14.)
129	    47	
130	    48	**Why it works** — The authors' stated mechanism is a mechanical-metabolic one: rising muscle
131	    49	tension raises intramuscular pressure, and above roughly 10-15% of maximal strength the
132	    50	contraction impairs the blood flow that metabolism needs, so the metabolism "is unable to
133	    51	meet the physiological demands of the exercise," producing the hyperbolic Rohmert-curve drop
134	    52	in endurance (PDF p. 238, printed p. 227). No mechanism is given for the sex difference in
135	    53	endurance or for the 27-28 Celsius optimum temperature beyond citing the studies that
136	    54	measured them.
137	    55	
138	    56	**When to apply** — Use the 10-15%-of-maximal-strength threshold as the authors' dividing
139	    57	line between "non-fatiguing" and rapidly fatiguing isometric holds when designing isometric
140	    58	protocols. Inference: use the three-phase timeline (about 50% back in 3 minutes, about 90%
141	    59	back in 20 minutes, full recovery by 24 hours) as the recovery of isometric endurance after
142	    60	a fatiguing sustained contraction; the source reports recovery "of endurance" (PDF p. 239,
143	    61	printed p. 228) and does not test brief maximal efforts.
144	    62	
145	    63	**When NOT to apply** — The intramuscular-pressure data (Fig 4.13) are from electrically
146	    64	stimulated cat soleus and gastrocnemius (Petrofsky & Hendershot, 1984), not human voluntary
147	    65	contraction; treat the specific kPa values as animal-model data illustrating the
148	    66	tension-pressure relationship, not human norms. The Rohmert-curve endurance data (Fig 4.14)
149	    67	are specifically finger-flexor endurance (Petrofsky, 1980), a small, distal muscle group;
150	    68	the shape of the curve (hyperbolic decline, female advantage) should not be assumed to hold
151	    69	identically for large, proximal muscle groups without separate verification. The 27-28
152	    70	Celsius optimum-temperature finding and the bodyfat-endurance link are each from single
153	    71	cited sources without reported effect sizes. The text points to "(Fig 4.14)" for the
154	    72	temperature optimum (PDF p. 238, printed p. 227), but Fig 4.14 plots endurance against %MVC
155	    73	and shows no temperature data; do not cite the figure for the temperature claim.
156	    74	
157	    75	**Example** — Inference: a coach prescribing a sustained isometric hold at low relative
158	    76	intensity could expect it to be comparatively non-fatiguing per the 10-15%-of-maximum
159	    77	threshold, while a sustained near-maximal hold held to fatigue would need the multi-minute
160	    78	recovery windows this entry describes before endurance returns. Whether a given hold is
161	    79	under 10-15% of maximum is not shown in the source.
162	    80	
163	    81	**Related** — [[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]],
164	    82	[[principle--breath-holding-and-valsalva-support-spinal-stability-in-maximal-lifting]] (Ch3,
165	    83	a related discussion of intramuscular/intrathoracic pressure during sustained maximal
166	    84	effort).

181	    14	# Isometric Strength Gains Spread Further From the Training Angle When the Muscle Trains in a Lengthened Position
182	    15	
183	    16	**What it is** — Many studies report isometric training producing maximum strength gains at
184	    17	or very close to the trained joint angle, leading some athletes to avoid isometric training
185	    18	altogether; the authors argue this "angular specificity" framing needs critical revision,
186	    19	citing other studies showing isometric training also produces significant strength increase
187	    20	up to about 15 degrees either side of the training angle. Because every type of muscle
188	    21	contraction has its own force/torque-versus-joint-angle curve (see 2.1.2), the authors argue
189	    22	it is "highly unlikely" that strength gain would be confined to one precise angle and
190	    23	nowhere else, and prefer the term "regional specificity" over "angular specificity" (or
191	    24	muscle-length specificity). Thepault-Mathieu et al (1988) found this regional specificity is
192	    25	strongest when the muscle trains in its most shortened position and weakest when it trains
193	    26	most lengthened: males training isometrically for 5 weeks (5 sets of 5 reps, 5 seconds each,
194	    27	3 times weekly) at 25 degrees of elbow flexion (full extension = 0 degrees) gained 54%
195	    28	strength at the training angle but only about 25% averaged over the rest of the range; a
196	    29	group training at 80 degrees gained 30% at the training angle and about 25% over the rest of
197	    30	the range; a group training at 120 degrees gained 25% at the training angle but only about
198	    31	7% over the rest of the range. The authors' summary: isometric training of a relatively
199	    32	lengthened muscle can produce substantial strength increase "not only near the region of
200	    33	training, but also throughout the range of movement." They caution this finding should not
201	    34	be read as meaning isometric training can replace other strength-training forms, since a
202	    35	specific type of static or dynamic strength depends on the neuromuscular factors governing
203	    36	how force is exerted in a given situation. (PDF pp. 237-238, printed pp. 226-227, "4.2.4
204	    37	Isometric Training," "Isometric Training and Angular Specificity.")
205	    38	
206	    39	**Why it works** — The authors give the biomechanical basis (a distinct force/torque-vs-angle
207	    40	curve exists for every contraction type) for why strict single-angle specificity is
208	    41	implausible, but they do not give a mechanism for why the Thepault-Mathieu et al (1988)
209	    42	lengthened-position condition specifically produced the broadest transfer across the range
210	    43	(54%/25 degrees training angle giving about 25% elsewhere, versus 120 degrees training angle
211	    44	giving only about 7% elsewhere). Inference: a plausible explanation, not stated in the text,
212	    45	is that training at longer muscle lengths recruits a different or broader distribution of
213	    46	sarcomere lengths and joint-angle-dependent moment arms than training at a shortened length,
214	    47	though this is not confirmed by the source.
215	    48	
216	    49	**When to apply** — Use this as a rationale for choosing a relatively lengthened joint
217	    50	position when isometric training is intended to transfer strength gains across a wider
218	    51	portion of the range of motion, rather than assuming isometric work only strengthens the
219	    52	exact trained angle. Use the "regional specificity" framing, not "angular specificity," when
220	    53	discussing isometric training's carryover with coaches or athletes.
221	    54	
222	    55	**When NOT to apply** — This is a single study (Thepault-Mathieu et al, 1988) with a specific
223	    56	protocol (5 weeks, 5x5 at 5 seconds, 3x weekly, elbow flexion only) and three training
224	    57	angles; the specific percentages (54%, 30%, 25% at-angle gains; roughly 25%, 25%, 7%
225	    58	remainder-of-range gains) should not be generalised to other joints, muscle groups, or
226	    59	protocols without direct testing. The authors' own caution stands: this finding does not
227	    60	mean isometric training can substitute for dynamic strength training generally.
228	    61	
229	    62	**Example** — The book's own example is the Thepault-Mathieu et al (1988) three-group study
230	    63	described above; no further invented example is added here.
231	    64	
232	    65	**Related** — [[claim--hettinger-muller-isometric-strength-gain-rate]],
233	    66	[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]] (Ch2, a related but
234	    67	broader claim about joint-angle transfer that this entry's regional-specificity nuance
235	    68	qualifies).
