249	    13	
250	    14	# Isometric Contraction Is Not One Thing: Voluntary vs Reflexive, Slow vs Explosive
251	    15	
252	    16	**What it is** — The authors argue isometric training is not simply holding a static
253	    17	contraction for a set time: a true isometric contraction requires the muscle to raise
254	    18	tension from rest to a maximal or sub-maximal value over a rise ("attack") time, sustain
255	    19	that tension for a resistance phase, then decrease it to rest or a lower value over a decay
256	    20	time. Verified against the page image (Fig 4.11, PDF p. 236, printed p. 225): the authors
257	    21	categorise isometric contraction into voluntary isometrics (splitting further into slow
258	    22	isometrics and voluntary explosive isometrics) and reflexive isometrics (splitting further
259	    23	into reflexive explosive isometrics and oscillatory isometrics). A voluntary isometric
260	    24	contraction can be produced deliberately; a reflexive one occurs involuntarily via the
261	    25	muscle's reflex response between the eccentric and concentric phases of plyometric
262	    26	activities such as the depth jump or weightlifting clean-and-jerk. Verified against the page
263	    27	image (Fig 4.12, PDF p. 236, printed p. 225): the figure contrasts slow isometrics (gradual
264	    28	rise, long resistance plateau) with explosive isometrics (steep rise, short resistance
265	    29	phase); the caption says reflexive explosive action has an even steeper rise and a much
266	    30	shorter resistance phase ("The slope of the rise is even greater and the duration of the
267	    31	resistance phase is much shorter during reflexive explosive isometric action"). On
268	    32	oscillatory isometrics, the authors say the technique "may also be useful in producing
269	    33	powerful contractions over a small range of movement," citing research showing that "the
270	    34	maximum tension that can be produced voluntarily during sinusoidally pulsed brief isometric
271	    35	jerks at 5 Hz is the same as the maximum sustained tension" (Soechting & Roberts, 1975);
272	    36	Basmajian (1978) read this as emphasising fibre recruitment and motor-unit synchronisation
273	    37	(PDF p. 235, printed p. 224). That is the only evidence the book gives for the oscillatory
274	    38	box, and it describes voluntarily produced jerks, while Fig 4.11 (PDF p. 236, printed p.
275	    39	225) files oscillatory isometrics under reflexive isometrics; the book does not reconcile
276	    40	the two. The authors argue that because the steepness of the isometric force-time curve,
277	    41	and the higher magnitude of maximum isometric versus dynamic maximum force at equivalent
278	    42	joint angles, both support developing explosive strength isometrically when the training
279	    43	accent is on speed of force development, "it is doubtful whether it is always productive to
280	    44	maintain a rigid distinction between dynamic and isometric exercise": as resistance grows
281	    45	very large, dynamic work becomes progressively more isometric, so isometric work is "really
282	    46	the limiting case of dynamic work as the velocity of movement tends to zero." Because the
283	    47	inhibitory effects usually associated with voluntary muscle action are not encountered in
284	    48	reflexive isometric contraction, "even greater explosive force can be displayed
285	    49	isometrically than dynamically." The authors add that "negative evaluations of this method
286	    50	are premature" (PDF p. 236, printed p. 225). A related but separate finding on impulsive
287	    51	loading: short bouts of low-frequency mechanical vibration (10-35 Hz) applied to the body
288	    52	have been shown to speed recovery, modulate muscle activity, raise strength/power stable
289	    53	state, lower arterial pressure and enhance oxidative processes (Kopysov, 1978; Lebedev &
290	    54	Peliakov, 1991), and whole-body vibration at 26 Hz through the lower extremities has been
291	    55	shown to produce marked increases in jumping power (Bosco et al, 1998); the authors note
292	    56	this fuels an open debate about whether plyometric training effects are driven mainly by
293	    57	elastic-energy storage/release, neural facilitation, or intrinsic muscle changes (Ingen
294	    58	Schenau et al, 1997). (PDF pp. 235-236, printed pp. 224-225, "4.2.4 Isometric Training,"
295	    59	Figs 4.11-4.12.)
296	    60	
297	    61	**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism for the voluntary/reflexive distinction is neural:
298	    62	reflexive isometric contraction does not encounter the inhibitory effects usually associated
299	    63	with voluntary muscle action, permitting higher explosive force display (PDF p. 235, printed
300	    64	p. 224). Inference: the slow-vs-explosive distinction within each category follows from how
301	    65	quickly neural drive ramps up to the target tension level, which the force-time curve shape
302	    66	(Fig 4.12) captures directly.
303	    67	
304	    68	**When to apply** — Use this taxonomy when specifying what kind of isometric work a given
305	    69	drill is training: a sustained maximal hold at a joint angle is a slow voluntary isometric;
306	    70	a deliberately fast ramp to near-maximal tension is a voluntary explosive isometric; the
307	    71	brief isometric moment between the eccentric and concentric phases of a depth jump or
308	    72	clean-and-jerk is, per the authors, a reflexive explosive isometric that the athlete does
309	    73	not consciously initiate. Per the authors, distinguish "isometric training for developing
310	    74	absolute strength" from "isometric training for developing explosive strength" and select
311	    75	the appropriate type for the goal.
312	    76	
313	    77	**When NOT to apply** — The authors say the absolute-strength versus explosive-strength
314	    78	split within isometric training "still requires detailed experimental corroboration" (PDF p.
315	    79	236, printed p. 225). Inference: the oscillatory category rests on one cited study of
316	    80	voluntary 5 Hz jerks (Soechting & Roberts, 1975), so the evidence the book gives does not
317	    81	support its placement under reflexive isometrics. The vibration/whole-body-vibration findings are a
318	    82	separate line of evidence (Bosco et al, 1998, and others) that the authors connect to this
319	    83	discussion only by analogy (impulsive loading), not by stating vibration produces isometric
320	    84	contraction in the sense defined here; treat the two topics as related but distinct.
321	    85	
322	    86	**Example** — The book's own example is the depth jump and the weightlifting clean-and-jerk
323	    87	cited as sources of reflexive isometric contraction; no further invented example is added
324	    88	here.
325	    89	
326	    90	**Related** — [[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]] (Ch1, the broader
327	    91	concentric/eccentric/isometric/quasi-isometric terminology this taxonomy sits within),
328	    92	[[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]].

342	    13	
343	    14	# External vs Internal Isometrics, and Using a Held Supramaximal Load to Prime the Nervous System
344	    15	
345	    16	**What it is** — The authors distinguish "external isometrics" (contraction exerted against
346	    17	an external load) from "internal isometrics" (contraction exerted against opposing muscles
347	    18	within the body, as in bodybuilders' posing actions; see
348	    19	[[heuristic--loadless-training-broomstick-protocol]]). Isometric contractions can be
349	    20	submaximal or maximal, short or long duration, continuous or intermittent, sequenced across
350	    21	different joint angles, alternated between agonist and antagonist (or adductor/abductor,
351	    22	medial/lateral rotators), and alternated between intensities, including voluntary
352	    23	oscillation between high and low intensity to prolong the period of application. A
353	    24	separate practical technique: isometrically holding a heavy load at a "sticking point" can
354	    25	"decrease any deficiencies in that region or prime the nervous system to cope with greater
355	    26	levels of loading which will eventually be encountered during the process of gradual
356	    27	progressive overload"; the authors' specific example is "the mere supporting of a
357	    28	supramaximal load (e.g. 120-150% of one's 1RM) on the shoulders or quasi-isometric movement
358	    29	over the first few degrees of knee flexion of a squat," which can "accustom the body
359	    30	neuromuscularly and favourably enhance one's mental perception to undertake future squats
360	    31	which are going to be only slightly heavier than one's current 1RM." The authors also state
361	    32	that, "as pointed out earlier," isometric contraction released explosively "can decrease the
362	    33	reaction response time by as much as 7%, particularly if associated with a strong
363	    34	pre-stretch," against the traditional coaching belief that movement is most efficient
364	    35	starting from complete relaxation; "Verkhoshansky stresses" that a movement produced from
365	    36	complete relaxation is usually slower and less forceful. Historically, isometric effort was
366	    37	emphasised heavily by DeLorme, Hettinger and Muller, but with the rise of gymnasium machines
367	    38	and the decline of Charles Atlas's mail-order "dynamic tension" programmes, isometrics
368	    39	largely fell out of popular use, though physical therapists still use it in early
369	    40	injury-rehabilitation stages, and Russian coaches often prescribe the 75% concentric / 15%
370	    41	eccentric / 10% isometric strength-training regime "advocated by their scientists" for the
371	    42	average athlete. The authors also note that because one basic PNF principle holds that
372	    43	mobility (dynamic contraction) is more primitive than stability (isometric contraction),
373	    44	stability sits at a "higher level of muscular learning." (PDF p. 240, printed p. 229,
374	    45	"Other Aspects of Isometric Activity," "4.2.4 Isometric Training.")
375	    46	
376	    47	**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for the 7% reaction-time figure (PDF p.
377	    48	240, printed p. 229). Inference: it may connect to the earlier argument that reflexive
378	    49	isometric contraction escapes the inhibition associated with voluntary action (PDF p. 235,
379	    50	printed p. 224; see [[framework--isometric-contraction-categorization-voluntary-reflexive]]),
380	    51	but that argument is about force, and the text does not link the two. For supramaximal
381	    52	holding, no cellular mechanism is given; the stated effect is neuromuscular and perceptual
382	    53	familiarisation ("accustom the body neuromuscularly," "favourably enhance one's mental
383	    54	perception") rather than a measured strength-transfer pathway.
384	    55	
385	    56	**When to apply** — Use the external/internal isometrics distinction as vocabulary when
386	    57	specifying whether a drill uses an external load or purely internal agonist-antagonist
387	    58	tensing. Use supramaximal-hold work (120-150% of 1RM support holds, or quasi-isometric
388	    59	movement over the first few degrees of a squat) as a progressive-overload step that
389	    60	accustoms the athlete to loads slightly above current 1RM (PDF p. 240, printed p. 229). Use
390	    61	the 75/15/10 concentric/eccentric/isometric regime as a citable, if dated, historical
391	    62	reference point when discussing how much isometric work a general strength programme might
392	    63	include.
393	    64	
394	    65	**When NOT to apply** — The 7% reaction-time figure and the supramaximal-holding
395	    66	familiarisation effect are stated without reported sample sizes or controlled outcome data
396	    67	in this passage; treat them as the authors' summarised claims, not independently verified
397	    68	percentages. The 75/15/10 regime is attributed generally to Russian coaches and "their
398	    69	scientists" without a specific citation, so treat it as a reported convention rather than
399	    70	an experimentally validated ratio. Inference: supramaximal holding (120-150% of 1RM) carries
400	    71	obvious injury risk without adequate rack and spotter safety, which this passage does not
401	    72	discuss.
402	    73	
403	    74	**Example** — The book's own example is the 120-150% 1RM shoulder support and the
404	    75	quasi-isometric first degrees of a squat, used to prepare for future squats only slightly
405	    76	heavier than the current 1RM (PDF p. 240, printed p. 229); no further invented example is
406	    77	added here.
407	    78

409	    80	[[framework--isometric-contraction-categorization-voluntary-reflexive]],
410	    81	[[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]].

424	    13	
425	    14	# Isometric Training's Six Advantages, Six Drawbacks, and the Authors' Recommended Execution Protocol
426	    15	
427	    16	**What it is** — The authors list six advantages proponents claim for isometric training:
428	    17	(1) it requires very simple apparatus; (2) it can locally exercise any muscle group at a
429	    18	specific joint angle, which dynamic work can only briefly pass through, since movement
430	    19	inertia usually carries the load past the angle of greatest mechanical effect; (3) it is
431	    20	time-productive, since each 6-second isometric contraction is "equivalent in its effect" to
432	    21	many dynamic ballistic contractions in which maximal force lasts no more than 0.1 second,
433	    22	meaning 10 minutes of targeted isometric tension can replace "a fatiguing hour" of dynamic
434	    23	weight training; (4) it produces an insignificant increase in muscle mass and bodymass
435	    24	compared with dynamic strength work, particularly pressing exercises; (5) it costs far less
436	    25	time and energy than dynamic weight training, letting an athlete preserve a high
437	    26	speed-strength level during a crucial competition period; (6) it offers more potential than
438	    27	dynamic exercise for using visual and kinaesthetic cues to hold a given position, an
439	    28	advantage for studying and correcting technical errors. Six drawbacks are also listed:
440	    29	isometrics fatigue the nervous system; may harm the cardiovascular system in some
441	    30	individuals via prolonged breath-holding and elevated blood pressure; disturb coordination;
442	    31	enhance muscle performance only near the specific trained joint angle; decrease speed of
443	    32	movement; and diminish soft-tissue elasticity and functional range of dynamic movement.
444	    33	Proper breathing, adequate rest/relaxation between exercises, and limiting contraction length
445	    34	to "no more than 6 seconds (some authors recommend 10 seconds)" can minimise these harmful
446	    35	after-effects. The authors give four "methods of execution ... recommended for developing
447	    36	absolute strength with isometric exercises" (PDF p. 237, printed p. 226): (1) pressing against an immovable
448	    37	structure or a partner's resistance, with the drawback that strength change can only be
449	    38	judged subjectively without a dynamometer; (2) holding a raised load for a set period, with a
450	    39	quasi-isometric variant shifting the load slowly across the range with stops at different
451	    40	joint angles; (3) pushing a weight from a lower support up to press against an upper stop
452	    41	(a power rack), giving a brief dynamic phase before the isometric hold and letting the
453	    42	athlete lift several times between stops; (4) using a dynamometer or other resistance
454	    43	device to control and display tension magnitude. For non-explosive isometrics, the authors
455	    44	give a specific protocol: apply force gradually, hold maximal tension no longer than 8
456	    45	seconds, perform 6 repetitions, rest 5-10 seconds between reps, limit total isometric
457	    46	training to 10 minutes per session, and finish with relaxation exercises; for developing
458	    47	explosive strength instead, tension should be generated at maximum speed to 70-80% of
459	    48	maximum strength, and reflexive explosive isometric action from plyometric movements "can be
460	    49	extremely effective" for this. The book gives three hold limits on the same page: "no more
461	    50	than 6 seconds," "some authors recommend 10," and "no longer than 8 seconds" for
462	    51	non-explosive maximal holds; it does not reconcile them (PDF p. 237, printed p. 226; the
463	    52	Hettinger and Muller protocol in [[claim--hettinger-muller-isometric-strength-gain-rate]]
464	    53	also uses 6 s). (PDF pp. 236-237, printed pp. 225-226, "4.2.4 Isometric Training.")
465	    54	
466	    55	**Why it works** — The authors give a specific mechanism only for advantage (2), regarding
467	    56	joint-angle specificity of loading, and advantage (3), the time-efficiency claim, which rests
468	    57	on comparing sustained near-maximal isometric tension duration against the brief (about 0.1
469	    58	second) duration of maximal force during a ballistic dynamic contraction. Inference: the
470	    59	remaining advantages and drawbacks are stated as observations rather than derived from a
471	    60	single unifying mechanism.
472	    61	
473	    62	**When to apply** — Use the 8-second hold, 6-repetition, 5-10-second-rest, 10-minute-session
474	    63	protocol as the authors' recommended baseline for non-explosive isometric training aimed at
475	    64	absolute strength, and the 70-80%-max, maximum-speed protocol for explosive-strength-focused
476	    65	isometric work. Weigh the six advantages against the six drawbacks for a given athlete and
477	    66	context. The source says only that isometrics "may have a harmful effect on the
478	    67	cardiovascular system in some individuals" (PDF p. 237, printed p. 226). Inference: that
479	    68	caution is most relevant for athletes with existing cardiovascular risk factors, and the
480	    69	coordination-disturbance and range-of-movement drawbacks argue for pairing isometric work
481	    70	with dynamic training rather than using it as a sole training means.
482	    71	
483	    72	**When NOT to apply** — This protocol and these advantages/drawbacks are the authors' own
484	    73	synthesis from an era (1950s-1970s citations) predating modern force-plate or dynamometer-based
485	    74	isometric dosing research; do not treat the "equivalent to a fatiguing hour of training"
486	    75	comparison (advantage 3) as a rigorously measured equivalence, since no controlled outcome
487	    76	comparison is cited for that specific claim. The drawbacks (cardiovascular risk, coordination
488	    77	disturbance, reduced movement speed, reduced tissue elasticity) argue against using isometric
489	    78	training as an athlete's sole or dominant training means, per the authors' own framing.
490	    79	
491	    80	**Example** — Inference: a coach using isometric mid-thigh pulls to reinforce a specific
492	    81	sticking-point joint angle is applying advantage (2) directly; the same coach should still
493	    82	program dynamic work elsewhere in the week to offset the coordination and movement-speed
494	    83	drawbacks this entry lists.
495	    84

514	    14	# Loadless Training: Tensing Muscles Maximally Against an Unloaded Broomstick to Train Without Equipment
515	    15	
516	    16	**What it is** — "Loadless training" (the Russian term; bodybuilders' "posing" training is
517	    17	the related practice) has an athlete voluntarily tense agonists and antagonists maximally
518	    18	without an external load, as if overcoming a maximal weight. In the early 1900s Anokhin and
519	    19	Froshek proposed developing strength through motivated tensing of agonists and antagonists
520	    20	at every joint, as bodybuilders do when tensing before judges, but the technique was not
521	    21	studied scientifically until after 1965. Kovalik (1978) ran a doctoral thesis on this
522	    22	"voluntary loadless muscle tensing," aiming to develop a supplementary training system
523	    23	imposing less joint stress than weight training, particularly for younger lifters whose
524	    24	skeletal systems have not matured. His subjects performed Olympic and supplementary lifts
525	    25	(e.g. snatch pull, front squat) with a broomstick while trying to generate maximum muscle
526	    26	tension as if overcoming a maximal weight; this produced definite muscle strengthening and
527	    27	technical-skill improvement, but Kovalik concluded it must be used cautiously in Olympic
528	    28	weightlifting because it might disrupt optimal extensor-flexor strength ratios. Loadless
529	    29	training is described as "especially useful if one has no access to training facilities or
530	    30	if one is recuperating from musculoskeletal injuries"; "combined with pushups and
531	    31	free-standing squats, loadless training can be used to good effect on trips away from
532	    32	home." It can be performed isometrically (joint held at a specific angle),
533	    33	quasi-isometrically (joint moved powerfully through a full range), or dynamically (imitating
534	    34	a weight-training movement with unloaded muscular tension against a broomstick). Kovalik
535	    35	recommended 5 sets per exercise; the authors add that "research indicates" 3-10 s rest
536	    36	between sets, and they give, without a source, the rest of the protocol: during
537	    37	quasi-isometric loadless training, avoid long periods of intense breath-holding and instead
538	    38	breathe out slowly in synchrony with the slow tensing of each movement; each movement
539	    39	should involve strong simultaneous tension in agonists and antagonists, starting from full
540	    40	extension and ending with stretching beyond full extension and back, over 10-15 seconds;
541	    41	the holding phase at the end of each movement (e.g. the overhead jerk position) should be
542	    42	held with maximal tension for 6-8 seconds. Rotating joints in different planes and moving
543	    43	limbs in diagonal and spiral patterns follows PNF principles and can enhance loadless
544	    44	training as supplementary strengthening. The authors also describe tensing several muscle
545	    45	groups while clearly visualising sporting movements: this "active visualisation, as opposed
546	    46	to the passive, relaxed visualisation recommended by many sports psychologists, can be
547	    47	useful adjunct to skills training, provided it does not alter the dynamic structure of
548	    48	normal competitive patterns." (PDF pp. 240-241, printed pp. 229-230, "Loadless Training.")
549	    49	
550	    50	**Why it works** — The authors' stated support is that "the value of this type of training
551	    51	is corroborated by research which has revealed that dynamic stretching against resistance
552	    52	may strengthen muscle and connective tissue" (PDF p. 241, printed p. 230; no citation
553	    53	given), plus Kovalik's finding of strengthening and technical-skill improvement. Their
554	    54	stated rationale for its specific value is reduced joint stress compared with weight
555	    55	training (relevant for immature skeletons or injury recovery) and portability (no equipment
556	    56	required). Inference: the caution about disrupting extensor-flexor ratios may reflect that
557	    57	voluntary tensing without an external load, and without the proprioceptive feedback a load
558	    58	gives, does not reproduce the same relative muscle-group demand as loaded lifting; the book
559	    59	gives no reason for the caution.
560	    60	
561	    61	**When to apply** — Use loadless training as a supplementary strengthening tool when
562	    62	equipment is unavailable (e.g. travel, combined with pushups and free-standing squats) or
563	    63	while recuperating from musculoskeletal injuries, and for younger or skeletally immature
564	    64	lifters where reduced joint loading is a priority. Follow the protocol given on PDF p. 241,
565	    65	printed p. 230 (Kovalik's 5 sets; 3-10 s rest; slow exhalation during quasi-isometric
566	    66	tensing; 10-15 s per movement; 6-8 s holding phase).
567	    67	
568	    68	**When NOT to apply** — Kovalik's own caution applies directly: use loadless training
569	    69	cautiously in competitive Olympic weightlifting programming specifically, since it may
570	    70	disrupt the optimal extensor-flexor strength ratio the sport requires. This is a single
571	    71	doctoral thesis (Kovalik, 1978) without reported sample size or a control condition compared
572	    72	against standard weight training in this passage; treat it as a supplementary method, not a
573	    73	substitute for loaded resistance training. The authors' own proviso on active visualisation
574	    74	also applies: it should not alter the dynamic structure of normal competitive patterns.
575	    75	
576	    76	**Example** — The book's own example is Kovalik's broomstick snatch pull and front squat,
577	    77	performed with maximal tension as if overcoming a maximal weight; no further invented
578	    78	example is added here.
579	    79	
580	    80	**Related** — [[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]],
581	    81	[[heuristic--isometric-priming-and-external-internal-classification]].

    13	
    14	# Hettinger and Muller's Original Isometric-Training Finding: About 5% Strength Gain Per Week From One Daily 6-Second Effort at Two-Thirds Maximum
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Isometric exercises became popular in the mid-1950s in the search for
    17	economical, effective strength methods. Hettinger and Muller (1953, 1955) established that
    18	one daily effort at two-thirds of maximum, held for six seconds, performed for 10 weeks,
    19	increases strength by about 5% per week. Separately, Clark et al (1954) found that static
    20	strength continues to increase even after a four-week isometric programme has concluded.
    21	This early success prompted considerable research comparing isometric training's
    22	effectiveness against dynamic training, which produced "rather contradictory data" (see
    23	review by Verkhoshansky, 1970). The authors' general conclusion from that body of research:
    24	isometric training can be more effective than dynamic exercise specifically where the target
    25	exercise requires a large-magnitude muscle contraction at a certain stage of a movement, or
    26	"during the early stages of injury rehabilitation"; if the target exercise involves
    27	high-speed movement, sustained isometric training is less effective. The authors also note
    28	that because isometric training's usual purpose is developing absolute strength, tension
    29	should be increased slowly and held for a relatively long time, since prolonged tension
    30	maintenance demands the energy expenditure that stimulates adequate neuromuscular
    31	adaptation; some researchers found no essential difference in strength gain from varying
    32	isometric tension intensity, from which the authors infer that "the fundamental
    33	conditioning factor is not so much the magnitude of the isometric tension as its duration."
    34	(PDF pp. 234-235, printed pp. 223-224, "4.2.4 Isometric Training.")
    35	
    36	**Why it works** — The authors' stated reasoning: prolonged maintenance of muscular tension
    37	requires an energy expenditure that "stimulates adequate adaptation in the neuromuscular
    38	system, thereby determining its strength potential," and this can exceed the stimulus from
    39	brief transient dynamic tension. The authors give no cellular or neural mechanism for why
    40	duration outweighs magnitude; their conclusion rests on studies that did not find a
    41	strength-gain difference across tension intensities (p.224), not on a stated physiological
    42	pathway.
    43	
    44	**When to apply** — Use the 5%-per-week figure and the two-thirds-maximum, 6-second, daily,
    45	10-week protocol as a citable historical anchor for isometric-training dosing, and use the
    46	authors' scoping rule (isometrics favoured for large-magnitude contraction at a specific
    47	movement stage or early rehab; less favoured when the target skill is high-speed) to decide
    48	when isometric work is the better tool versus dynamic resistance training.
    49	
    50	**When NOT to apply** — This is 1950s data; the authors say later comparisons of isometric
    51	and dynamic training produced "rather contradictory data" (Verkhoshansky 1970 review, PDF
    52	235, printed p.224), and the text reports no modern replication. Treat "5% per week" as
    53	specific to Hettinger and Muller's exact protocol (two-thirds max, 6 seconds, daily, 10
    54	weeks), not a generalizable isometric-training growth rate. The "duration not magnitude"
    55	inference (PDF 235, printed p.224) sits against other statements in the same book and the
    56	library. On PDF 33, printed p.22, the authors cite Hettinger and Muller (1953) for a
    57	threshold stimulus of "not ... less than one-third of the maximal strength" for the average
    58	person, and add that as strength increases the stimulus "should be increased, and reach
    59	80-95% of the athlete's maximum" (see [[claim--strength-training-threshold-stimulus]]); on
    60	PDF 34, printed p.23, Korobkov, Gerasimov and Vasiliev (via Verkhoshansky 1977) report
    61	"approximately equivalent increases in strength" with loads of 20, 40, 60 and 80% of 1RM in
    62	the initial stages of training, which partly agrees with the p.224 inference for beginners.
    63	The book's own isometric protocol also sets explosive work at "70-80% of one's maximum
    64	strength" (PDF 237, printed p.226). Natera, as relayed in
    65	[[framework--isometric-training-variables-and-adaptations]] (Moyer), reports Oranchuk 2019
    66	as finding that "moderate-to-high intensity gives the best" peak-force gains. Hold length
    67	also differs across the section: 6 s here; "no more than 6 seconds (some authors recommend
    68	10 seconds)" and "no longer than 8 seconds" for non-explosive maximal holds (both PDF 237,
    69	printed p.226).
    70	
    71	**Example** — The book's own example is the Hettinger and Muller protocol itself (daily,
    72	6-second, two-thirds-maximum isometric effort for 10 weeks, yielding about 5% weekly
    73	strength gain); no further invented example is added here.
    74	
    75	**Related** — [[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]],
    76	[[claim--isometric-regional-specificity-not-strictly-angular]],
    77	[[claim--strength-training-threshold-stimulus]] (Ch1, the intensity-threshold rule this
    78	entry's duration inference sits against),
    79	[[framework--isometric-training-variables-and-adaptations]] (Moyer, Oranchuk 2019 as
    80	relayed).

    13	
    14	# Isometric Endurance Collapses Above 10-15% of Maximal Tension, and Recovers in Three Distinct Phases
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Isometric endurance at resistance exceeding 10-15% of a muscle's maximal
    17	strength is very short compared with dynamic exercise, because of metabolic demand and
    18	impaired blood flow to the exercising muscle under sustained contraction (Petrofsky &
    19	Phillips, 1986); below that threshold, contractions are considered non-fatiguing, since
    20	intramuscular pressure stays low and is readily exceeded by rising mean arterial pressure in
    21	the capillaries. Verified against the page image (Fig 4.13, PDF p. 238, printed p. 227, cat
    22	soleus and gastrocnemius, electrically stimulated, based on Petrofsky & Hendershot, 1984):
    23	intramuscular pressure rises roughly linearly with muscle tension, from about 0 kPa at 0%
    24	to about 20 kPa at 100% of maximal strength. As tension rises, intramuscular pressure rises
    25	with it and metabolism cannot keep pace, producing a hyperbolic drop in performance and
    26	marked fatigue increase (the Rohmert curve, first derived by Monod and Sherrer 1967, later
    27	by Rohmert 1968). Verified against the page image (Fig 4.14, PDF p. 238, printed p. 227,
    28	finger flexors, based on Petrofsky 1980): endurance time falls hyperbolically as %MVC
    29	(maximum voluntary contraction) rises, and females sustain the same tension level for
    30	longer than males at every tension level tested, a difference the authors say "has not
    31	been adequately explained yet." Muscle temperature also affects isometric endurance: hot
    32	packs reduce it and pre-exercise icing increases it. The authors write that "Research by
    33	Clarke et al (1958) discovered that there is an optimum core muscle temperature" above and
    34	below which isometric endurance fairly rapidly decreases, an optimum later placed near 27-28
    35	Celsius (Petrofsky & Phillips, 1986). Higher
    36	bodyfat percentage, associated with higher resting muscle temperature, is linked to lower
    37	isometric endurance in most situations. Dynamic exercise takes place more efficiently at
    38	higher temperatures, "apparently because of reduced environmental tissue viscosity," but in
    39	isometric contraction muscle fibres do not move, so viscosity plays an "insignificant role
    40	compared with that of muscle metabolism" (Petrofsky & Phillips, 1986). Recovery from
    41	isometric contraction proceeds in three phases (Petrofsky & Phillips, 1986): a rapid
    42	recovery of about 50% of endurance in the first 3 minutes; a slower recovery lasting about
    43	20 minutes, reaching about 90% of initial endurance; and complete recovery within at least
    44	24 hours; recovery from low-tension isometric contraction is slower during the first phases
    45	of recovery. (PDF pp. 238-239, printed pp. 227-228, "Isometric Endurance," "Recovery after
    46	Isometric Activity," Figs 4.13-4.14.)
    47	
    48	**Why it works** — The authors' stated mechanism is a mechanical-metabolic one: rising muscle
    49	tension raises intramuscular pressure, and above roughly 10-15% of maximal strength the
    50	contraction impairs the blood flow that metabolism needs, so the metabolism "is unable to
    51	meet the physiological demands of the exercise," producing the hyperbolic Rohmert-curve drop
    52	in endurance (PDF p. 238, printed p. 227). No mechanism is given for the sex difference in
    53	endurance or for the 27-28 Celsius optimum temperature beyond citing the studies that
    54	measured them.
    55	
    56	**When to apply** — Use the 10-15%-of-maximal-strength threshold as the authors' dividing
    57	line between "non-fatiguing" and rapidly fatiguing isometric holds when designing isometric
    58	protocols. Inference: use the three-phase timeline (about 50% back in 3 minutes, about 90%
    59	back in 20 minutes, full recovery by 24 hours) as the recovery of isometric endurance after
    60	a fatiguing sustained contraction; the source reports recovery "of endurance" (PDF p. 239,
    61	printed p. 228) and does not test brief maximal efforts.
    62	
    63	**When NOT to apply** — The intramuscular-pressure data (Fig 4.13) are from electrically
    64	stimulated cat soleus and gastrocnemius (Petrofsky & Hendershot, 1984), not human voluntary
    65	contraction; treat the specific kPa values as animal-model data illustrating the
    66	tension-pressure relationship, not human norms. The Rohmert-curve endurance data (Fig 4.14)
    67	are specifically finger-flexor endurance (Petrofsky, 1980), a small, distal muscle group;
    68	the shape of the curve (hyperbolic decline, female advantage) should not be assumed to hold
    69	identically for large, proximal muscle groups without separate verification. The 27-28
    70	Celsius optimum-temperature finding and the bodyfat-endurance link are each from single
    71	cited sources without reported effect sizes. The text points to "(Fig 4.14)" for the
    72	temperature optimum (PDF p. 238, printed p. 227), but Fig 4.14 plots endurance against %MVC
    73	and shows no temperature data; do not cite the figure for the temperature claim.
    74	
    75	**Example** — Inference: a coach prescribing a sustained isometric hold at low relative
    76	intensity could expect it to be comparatively non-fatiguing per the 10-15%-of-maximum
    77	threshold, while a sustained near-maximal hold held to fatigue would need the multi-minute
    78	recovery windows this entry describes before endurance returns. Whether a given hold is
    79	under 10-15% of maximum is not shown in the source.
    80	
    81	**Related** — [[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]],
    82	[[principle--breath-holding-and-valsalva-support-spinal-stability-in-maximal-lifting]] (Ch3,
    83	a related discussion of intramuscular/intrathoracic pressure during sustained maximal
    84	effort).

    12	---
    13	
    14	# Isometric Strength Gains Spread Further From the Training Angle When the Muscle Trains in a Lengthened Position
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Many studies report isometric training producing maximum strength gains at
    17	or very close to the trained joint angle, leading some athletes to avoid isometric training
    18	altogether; the authors argue this "angular specificity" framing needs critical revision,
    19	citing other studies showing isometric training also produces significant strength increase
    20	up to about 15 degrees either side of the training angle. Because every type of muscle
    21	contraction has its own force/torque-versus-joint-angle curve (see 2.1.2), the authors argue
    22	it is "highly unlikely" that strength gain would be confined to one precise angle and
    23	nowhere else, and prefer the term "regional specificity" over "angular specificity" (or
    24	muscle-length specificity). Thepault-Mathieu et al (1988) found this regional specificity is
    25	strongest when the muscle trains in its most shortened position and weakest when it trains
    26	most lengthened: males training isometrically for 5 weeks (5 sets of 5 reps, 5 seconds each,
    27	3 times weekly) at 25 degrees of elbow flexion (full extension = 0 degrees) gained 54%
    28	strength at the training angle but only about 25% averaged over the rest of the range; a
    29	group training at 80 degrees gained 30% at the training angle and about 25% over the rest of
    30	the range; a group training at 120 degrees gained 25% at the training angle but only about
    31	7% over the rest of the range. The authors' summary: isometric training of a relatively
    32	lengthened muscle can produce substantial strength increase "not only near the region of
    33	training, but also throughout the range of movement." They caution this finding should not
    34	be read as meaning isometric training can replace other strength-training forms, since a
    35	specific type of static or dynamic strength depends on the neuromuscular factors governing
    36	how force is exerted in a given situation. (PDF pp. 237-238, printed pp. 226-227, "4.2.4
    37	Isometric Training," "Isometric Training and Angular Specificity.")
    38	
    39	**Why it works** — The authors give the biomechanical basis (a distinct force/torque-vs-angle
    40	curve exists for every contraction type) for why strict single-angle specificity is
    41	implausible, but they do not give a mechanism for why the Thepault-Mathieu et al (1988)
    42	lengthened-position condition specifically produced the broadest transfer across the range
    43	(54%/25 degrees training angle giving about 25% elsewhere, versus 120 degrees training angle
    44	giving only about 7% elsewhere). Inference: a plausible explanation, not stated in the text,
    45	is that training at longer muscle lengths recruits a different or broader distribution of
    46	sarcomere lengths and joint-angle-dependent moment arms than training at a shortened length,
    47	though this is not confirmed by the source.
    48	
    49	**When to apply** — Use this as a rationale for choosing a relatively lengthened joint
    50	position when isometric training is intended to transfer strength gains across a wider
    51	portion of the range of motion, rather than assuming isometric work only strengthens the
    52	exact trained angle. Use the "regional specificity" framing, not "angular specificity," when
    53	discussing isometric training's carryover with coaches or athletes.
    54	
    55	**When NOT to apply** — This is a single study (Thepault-Mathieu et al, 1988) with a specific
    56	protocol (5 weeks, 5x5 at 5 seconds, 3x weekly, elbow flexion only) and three training
    57	angles; the specific percentages (54%, 30%, 25% at-angle gains; roughly 25%, 25%, 7%
    58	remainder-of-range gains) should not be generalised to other joints, muscle groups, or
    59	protocols without direct testing. The authors' own caution stands: this finding does not
    60	mean isometric training can substitute for dynamic strength training generally.
    61	
    62	**Example** — The book's own example is the Thepault-Mathieu et al (1988) three-group study
    63	described above; no further invented example is added here.
    64	
    65	**Related** — [[claim--hettinger-muller-isometric-strength-gain-rate]],
    66	[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]] (Ch2, a related but
    67	broader claim about joint-angle transfer that this entry's regional-specificity nuance
    68	qualifies).

     9	confidence: supported
    10	ingest-tier: full-text
    11	created: 2026-09-27
    12	---
    13	
    14	# Isometric Contraction Is Not One Thing: Voluntary vs Reflexive, Slow vs Explosive
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors argue isometric training is not simply holding a static
    17	contraction for a set time: a true isometric contraction requires the muscle to raise
    18	tension from rest to a maximal or sub-maximal value over a rise ("attack") time, sustain
    19	that tension for a resistance phase, then decrease it to rest or a lower value over a decay
    20	time. Verified against the page image (Fig 4.11, PDF p. 236, printed p. 225): the authors
    21	categorise isometric contraction into voluntary isometrics (splitting further into slow
    22	isometrics and voluntary explosive isometrics) and reflexive isometrics (splitting further
    23	into reflexive explosive isometrics and oscillatory isometrics). A voluntary isometric
    24	contraction can be produced deliberately; a reflexive one occurs involuntarily via the
    25	muscle's reflex response between the eccentric and concentric phases of plyometric
    26	activities such as the depth jump or weightlifting clean-and-jerk. Verified against the page
    27	image (Fig 4.12, PDF p. 236, printed p. 225): the figure contrasts slow isometrics (gradual
    28	rise, long resistance plateau) with explosive isometrics (steep rise, short resistance
    29	phase); the caption says reflexive explosive action has an even steeper rise and a much
    30	shorter resistance phase ("The slope of the rise is even greater and the duration of the
    31	resistance phase is much shorter during reflexive explosive isometric action"). On
    32	oscillatory isometrics, the authors say the technique "may also be useful in producing
    33	powerful contractions over a small range of movement," citing research showing that "the
    34	maximum tension that can be produced voluntarily during sinusoidally pulsed brief isometric
    35	jerks at 5 Hz is the same as the maximum sustained tension" (Soechting & Roberts, 1975);
    36	Basmajian (1978) read this as emphasising fibre recruitment and motor-unit synchronisation
    37	(PDF p. 235, printed p. 224). That is the only evidence the book gives for the oscillatory
    38	box, and it describes voluntarily produced jerks, while Fig 4.11 (PDF p. 236, printed p.
    39	225) files oscillatory isometrics under reflexive isometrics; the book does not reconcile
    40	the two. The authors argue that because the steepness of the isometric force-time curve,
    41	and the higher magnitude of maximum isometric versus dynamic maximum force at equivalent
    42	joint angles, both support developing explosive strength isometrically when the training
    43	accent is on speed of force development, "it is doubtful whether it is always productive to
    44	maintain a rigid distinction between dynamic and isometric exercise": as resistance grows
    45	very large, dynamic work becomes progressively more isometric, so isometric work is "really
    46	the limiting case of dynamic work as the velocity of movement tends to zero." Because the
    47	inhibitory effects usually associated with voluntary muscle action are not encountered in
    48	reflexive isometric contraction, "even greater explosive force can be displayed
    49	isometrically than dynamically." The authors add that "negative evaluations of this method
    50	are premature" (PDF p. 236, printed p. 225). A related but separate finding on impulsive
    51	loading: short bouts of low-frequency mechanical vibration (10-35 Hz) applied to the body
    52	have been shown to speed recovery, modulate muscle activity, raise strength/power stable
    53	state, lower arterial pressure and enhance oxidative processes (Kopysov, 1978; Lebedev &
    54	Peliakov, 1991), and whole-body vibration at 26 Hz through the lower extremities has been
    55	shown to produce marked increases in jumping power (Bosco et al, 1998); the authors note
    56	this fuels an open debate about whether plyometric training effects are driven mainly by
    57	elastic-energy storage/release, neural facilitation, or intrinsic muscle changes (Ingen
    58	Schenau et al, 1997). (PDF pp. 235-236, printed pp. 224-225, "4.2.4 Isometric Training,"
    59	Figs 4.11-4.12.)
    60	
    61	**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism for the voluntary/reflexive distinction is neural:
    62	reflexive isometric contraction does not encounter the inhibitory effects usually associated
    63	with voluntary muscle action, permitting higher explosive force display (PDF p. 235, printed
    64	p. 224). Inference: the slow-vs-explosive distinction within each category follows from how
    65	quickly neural drive ramps up to the target tension level, which the force-time curve shape
    66	(Fig 4.12) captures directly.
    67	
    68	**When to apply** — Use this taxonomy when specifying what kind of isometric work a given
    69	drill is training: a sustained maximal hold at a joint angle is a slow voluntary isometric;
    70	a deliberately fast ramp to near-maximal tension is a voluntary explosive isometric; the
    71	brief isometric moment between the eccentric and concentric phases of a depth jump or
    72	clean-and-jerk is, per the authors, a reflexive explosive isometric that the athlete does
    73	not consciously initiate. Per the authors, distinguish "isometric training for developing
    74	absolute strength" from "isometric training for developing explosive strength" and select
    75	the appropriate type for the goal.
    76	
    77	**When NOT to apply** — The authors say the absolute-strength versus explosive-strength
    78	split within isometric training "still requires detailed experimental corroboration" (PDF p.
    79	236, printed p. 225). Inference: the oscillatory category rests on one cited study of
    80	voluntary 5 Hz jerks (Soechting & Roberts, 1975), so the evidence the book gives does not
    81	support its placement under reflexive isometrics. The vibration/whole-body-vibration findings are a
    82	separate line of evidence (Bosco et al, 1998, and others) that the authors connect to this
    83	discussion only by analogy (impulsive loading), not by stating vibration produces isometric
    84	contraction in the sense defined here; treat the two topics as related but distinct.
    85	
    86	**Example** — The book's own example is the depth jump and the weightlifting clean-and-jerk
    87	cited as sources of reflexive isometric contraction; no further invented example is added
    88	here.
    89	
    90	**Related** — [[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]] (Ch1, the broader
    91	concentric/eccentric/isometric/quasi-isometric terminology this taxonomy sits within),
    92	[[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]].

    13	
    14	# External vs Internal Isometrics, and Using a Held Supramaximal Load to Prime the Nervous System
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors distinguish "external isometrics" (contraction exerted against
    17	an external load) from "internal isometrics" (contraction exerted against opposing muscles
    18	within the body, as in bodybuilders' posing actions; see
    19	[[heuristic--loadless-training-broomstick-protocol]]). Isometric contractions can be
    20	submaximal or maximal, short or long duration, continuous or intermittent, sequenced across
    21	different joint angles, alternated between agonist and antagonist (or adductor/abductor,
    22	medial/lateral rotators), and alternated between intensities, including voluntary
    23	oscillation between high and low intensity to prolong the period of application. A
    24	separate practical technique: isometrically holding a heavy load at a "sticking point" can
    25	"decrease any deficiencies in that region or prime the nervous system to cope with greater
    26	levels of loading which will eventually be encountered during the process of gradual
    27	progressive overload"; the authors' specific example is "the mere supporting of a
    28	supramaximal load (e.g. 120-150% of one's 1RM) on the shoulders or quasi-isometric movement
    29	over the first few degrees of knee flexion of a squat," which can "accustom the body
    30	neuromuscularly and favourably enhance one's mental perception to undertake future squats
    31	which are going to be only slightly heavier than one's current 1RM." The authors also state
    32	that, "as pointed out earlier," isometric contraction released explosively "can decrease the
    33	reaction response time by as much as 7%, particularly if associated with a strong
    34	pre-stretch," against the traditional coaching belief that movement is most efficient
    35	starting from complete relaxation; "Verkhoshansky stresses" that a movement produced from
    36	complete relaxation is usually slower and less forceful. Historically, isometric effort was
    37	emphasised heavily by DeLorme, Hettinger and Muller, but with the rise of gymnasium machines
    38	and the decline of Charles Atlas's mail-order "dynamic tension" programmes, isometrics
    39	largely fell out of popular use, though physical therapists still use it in early
    40	injury-rehabilitation stages, and Russian coaches often prescribe the 75% concentric / 15%
    41	eccentric / 10% isometric strength-training regime "advocated by their scientists" for the
    42	average athlete. The authors also note that because one basic PNF principle holds that
    43	mobility (dynamic contraction) is more primitive than stability (isometric contraction),
    44	stability sits at a "higher level of muscular learning." (PDF p. 240, printed p. 229,
    45	"Other Aspects of Isometric Activity," "4.2.4 Isometric Training.")
    46	
    47	**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for the 7% reaction-time figure (PDF p.
    48	240, printed p. 229). Inference: it may connect to the earlier argument that reflexive
    49	isometric contraction escapes the inhibition associated with voluntary action (PDF p. 235,
    50	printed p. 224; see [[framework--isometric-contraction-categorization-voluntary-reflexive]]),
    51	but that argument is about force, and the text does not link the two. For supramaximal
    52	holding, no cellular mechanism is given; the stated effect is neuromuscular and perceptual
    53	familiarisation ("accustom the body neuromuscularly," "favourably enhance one's mental
    54	perception") rather than a measured strength-transfer pathway.
    55	
    56	**When to apply** — Use the external/internal isometrics distinction as vocabulary when
    57	specifying whether a drill uses an external load or purely internal agonist-antagonist
    58	tensing. Use supramaximal-hold work (120-150% of 1RM support holds, or quasi-isometric
    59	movement over the first few degrees of a squat) as a progressive-overload step that
    60	accustoms the athlete to loads slightly above current 1RM (PDF p. 240, printed p. 229). Use
    61	the 75/15/10 concentric/eccentric/isometric regime as a citable, if dated, historical
    62	reference point when discussing how much isometric work a general strength programme might
    63	include.
    64	
    65	**When NOT to apply** — The 7% reaction-time figure and the supramaximal-holding
    66	familiarisation effect are stated without reported sample sizes or controlled outcome data
    67	in this passage; treat them as the authors' summarised claims, not independently verified
    68	percentages. The 75/15/10 regime is attributed generally to Russian coaches and "their
    69	scientists" without a specific citation, so treat it as a reported convention rather than
    70	an experimentally validated ratio. Inference: supramaximal holding (120-150% of 1RM) carries
    71	obvious injury risk without adequate rack and spotter safety, which this passage does not
    72	discuss.
    73	
    74	**Example** — The book's own example is the 120-150% 1RM shoulder support and the
    75	quasi-isometric first degrees of a squat, used to prepare for future squats only slightly
    76	heavier than the current 1RM (PDF p. 240, printed p. 229); no further invented example is
    77	added here.
    78	
    79	**Related** — [[heuristic--loadless-training-broomstick-protocol]],
    80	[[framework--isometric-contraction-categorization-voluntary-reflexive]],
    81	[[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]].

    13	
    14	# Isometric Training's Six Advantages, Six Drawbacks, and the Authors' Recommended Execution Protocol
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors list six advantages proponents claim for isometric training:
    17	(1) it requires very simple apparatus; (2) it can locally exercise any muscle group at a
    18	specific joint angle, which dynamic work can only briefly pass through, since movement
    19	inertia usually carries the load past the angle of greatest mechanical effect; (3) it is
    20	time-productive, since each 6-second isometric contraction is "equivalent in its effect" to
    21	many dynamic ballistic contractions in which maximal force lasts no more than 0.1 second,
    22	meaning 10 minutes of targeted isometric tension can replace "a fatiguing hour" of dynamic
    23	weight training; (4) it produces an insignificant increase in muscle mass and bodymass
    24	compared with dynamic strength work, particularly pressing exercises; (5) it costs far less
    25	time and energy than dynamic weight training, letting an athlete preserve a high
    26	speed-strength level during a crucial competition period; (6) it offers more potential than
    27	dynamic exercise for using visual and kinaesthetic cues to hold a given position, an
    28	advantage for studying and correcting technical errors. Six drawbacks are also listed:
    29	isometrics fatigue the nervous system; may harm the cardiovascular system in some
    30	individuals via prolonged breath-holding and elevated blood pressure; disturb coordination;
    31	enhance muscle performance only near the specific trained joint angle; decrease speed of
    32	movement; and diminish soft-tissue elasticity and functional range of dynamic movement.
    33	Proper breathing, adequate rest/relaxation between exercises, and limiting contraction length
    34	to "no more than 6 seconds (some authors recommend 10 seconds)" can minimise these harmful
    35	after-effects. The authors give four "methods of execution ... recommended for developing
    36	absolute strength with isometric exercises" (PDF p. 237, printed p. 226): (1) pressing against an immovable
    37	structure or a partner's resistance, with the drawback that strength change can only be
    38	judged subjectively without a dynamometer; (2) holding a raised load for a set period, with a
    39	quasi-isometric variant shifting the load slowly across the range with stops at different
    40	joint angles; (3) pushing a weight from a lower support up to press against an upper stop
    41	(a power rack), giving a brief dynamic phase before the isometric hold and letting the
    42	athlete lift several times between stops; (4) using a dynamometer or other resistance
    43	device to control and display tension magnitude. For non-explosive isometrics, the authors
    44	give a specific protocol: apply force gradually, hold maximal tension no longer than 8
    45	seconds, perform 6 repetitions, rest 5-10 seconds between reps, limit total isometric
    46	training to 10 minutes per session, and finish with relaxation exercises; for developing
    47	explosive strength instead, tension should be generated at maximum speed to 70-80% of
    48	maximum strength, and reflexive explosive isometric action from plyometric movements "can be
    49	extremely effective" for this. The book gives three hold limits on the same page: "no more
    50	than 6 seconds," "some authors recommend 10," and "no longer than 8 seconds" for
    51	non-explosive maximal holds; it does not reconcile them (PDF p. 237, printed p. 226; the
    52	Hettinger and Muller protocol in [[claim--hettinger-muller-isometric-strength-gain-rate]]
    53	also uses 6 s). (PDF pp. 236-237, printed pp. 225-226, "4.2.4 Isometric Training.")
    54	
    55	**Why it works** — The authors give a specific mechanism only for advantage (2), regarding
    56	joint-angle specificity of loading, and advantage (3), the time-efficiency claim, which rests
    57	on comparing sustained near-maximal isometric tension duration against the brief (about 0.1
    58	second) duration of maximal force during a ballistic dynamic contraction. Inference: the
    59	remaining advantages and drawbacks are stated as observations rather than derived from a
    60	single unifying mechanism.
    61	
    62	**When to apply** — Use the 8-second hold, 6-repetition, 5-10-second-rest, 10-minute-session
    63	protocol as the authors' recommended baseline for non-explosive isometric training aimed at
    64	absolute strength, and the 70-80%-max, maximum-speed protocol for explosive-strength-focused
    65	isometric work. Weigh the six advantages against the six drawbacks for a given athlete and
    66	context. The source says only that isometrics "may have a harmful effect on the
    67	cardiovascular system in some individuals" (PDF p. 237, printed p. 226). Inference: that
    68	caution is most relevant for athletes with existing cardiovascular risk factors, and the
    69	coordination-disturbance and range-of-movement drawbacks argue for pairing isometric work
    70	with dynamic training rather than using it as a sole training means.
    71	
    72	**When NOT to apply** — This protocol and these advantages/drawbacks are the authors' own
    73	synthesis from an era (1950s-1970s citations) predating modern force-plate or dynamometer-based
    74	isometric dosing research; do not treat the "equivalent to a fatiguing hour of training"
    75	comparison (advantage 3) as a rigorously measured equivalence, since no controlled outcome
    76	comparison is cited for that specific claim. The drawbacks (cardiovascular risk, coordination
    77	disturbance, reduced movement speed, reduced tissue elasticity) argue against using isometric
    78	training as an athlete's sole or dominant training means, per the authors' own framing.
    79	
    80	**Example** — Inference: a coach using isometric mid-thigh pulls to reinforce a specific
    81	sticking-point joint angle is applying advantage (2) directly; the same coach should still
    82	program dynamic work elsewhere in the week to offset the coordination and movement-speed
    83	drawbacks this entry lists.
    84	
    85	**Related** — [[framework--isometric-contraction-categorization-voluntary-reflexive]],
    86	[[claim--hettinger-muller-isometric-strength-gain-rate]],
    87	[[principle--breath-holding-and-valsalva-support-spinal-stability-in-maximal-lifting]] (Ch3,
    88	the cardiovascular/breath-holding caution this entry's drawback 2 overlaps with).

    13	
    14	# Loadless Training: Tensing Muscles Maximally Against an Unloaded Broomstick to Train Without Equipment
    15	
    16	**What it is** — "Loadless training" (the Russian term; bodybuilders' "posing" training is
    17	the related practice) has an athlete voluntarily tense agonists and antagonists maximally
    18	without an external load, as if overcoming a maximal weight. In the early 1900s Anokhin and
    19	Froshek proposed developing strength through motivated tensing of agonists and antagonists
    20	at every joint, as bodybuilders do when tensing before judges, but the technique was not
    21	studied scientifically until after 1965. Kovalik (1978) ran a doctoral thesis on this
    22	"voluntary loadless muscle tensing," aiming to develop a supplementary training system
    23	imposing less joint stress than weight training, particularly for younger lifters whose
    24	skeletal systems have not matured. His subjects performed Olympic and supplementary lifts
    25	(e.g. snatch pull, front squat) with a broomstick while trying to generate maximum muscle
    26	tension as if overcoming a maximal weight; this produced definite muscle strengthening and
    27	technical-skill improvement, but Kovalik concluded it must be used cautiously in Olympic
    28	weightlifting because it might disrupt optimal extensor-flexor strength ratios. Loadless
    29	training is described as "especially useful if one has no access to training facilities or
    30	if one is recuperating from musculoskeletal injuries"; "combined with pushups and
    31	free-standing squats, loadless training can be used to good effect on trips away from
    32	home." It can be performed isometrically (joint held at a specific angle),
    33	quasi-isometrically (joint moved powerfully through a full range), or dynamically (imitating
    34	a weight-training movement with unloaded muscular tension against a broomstick). Kovalik
    35	recommended 5 sets per exercise; the authors add that "research indicates" 3-10 s rest
    36	between sets, and they give, without a source, the rest of the protocol: during
    37	quasi-isometric loadless training, avoid long periods of intense breath-holding and instead
    38	breathe out slowly in synchrony with the slow tensing of each movement; each movement
    39	should involve strong simultaneous tension in agonists and antagonists, starting from full
    40	extension and ending with stretching beyond full extension and back, over 10-15 seconds;
    41	the holding phase at the end of each movement (e.g. the overhead jerk position) should be
    42	held with maximal tension for 6-8 seconds. Rotating joints in different planes and moving
    43	limbs in diagonal and spiral patterns follows PNF principles and can enhance loadless
    44	training as supplementary strengthening. The authors also describe tensing several muscle
    45	groups while clearly visualising sporting movements: this "active visualisation, as opposed
    46	to the passive, relaxed visualisation recommended by many sports psychologists, can be
    47	useful adjunct to skills training, provided it does not alter the dynamic structure of
    48	normal competitive patterns." (PDF pp. 240-241, printed pp. 229-230, "Loadless Training.")
    49	
    50	**Why it works** — The authors' stated support is that "the value of this type of training
    51	is corroborated by research which has revealed that dynamic stretching against resistance
    52	may strengthen muscle and connective tissue" (PDF p. 241, printed p. 230; no citation
    53	given), plus Kovalik's finding of strengthening and technical-skill improvement. Their
    54	stated rationale for its specific value is reduced joint stress compared with weight
    55	training (relevant for immature skeletons or injury recovery) and portability (no equipment
    56	required). Inference: the caution about disrupting extensor-flexor ratios may reflect that
    57	voluntary tensing without an external load, and without the proprioceptive feedback a load
    58	gives, does not reproduce the same relative muscle-group demand as loaded lifting; the book
    59	gives no reason for the caution.
    60	
    61	**When to apply** — Use loadless training as a supplementary strengthening tool when
    62	equipment is unavailable (e.g. travel, combined with pushups and free-standing squats) or
    63	while recuperating from musculoskeletal injuries, and for younger or skeletally immature
    64	lifters where reduced joint loading is a priority. Follow the protocol given on PDF p. 241,
    65	printed p. 230 (Kovalik's 5 sets; 3-10 s rest; slow exhalation during quasi-isometric
    66	tensing; 10-15 s per movement; 6-8 s holding phase).
    67	
    68	**When NOT to apply** — Kovalik's own caution applies directly: use loadless training
    69	cautiously in competitive Olympic weightlifting programming specifically, since it may
    70	disrupt the optimal extensor-flexor strength ratio the sport requires. This is a single
    71	doctoral thesis (Kovalik, 1978) without reported sample size or a control condition compared
    72	against standard weight training in this passage; treat it as a supplementary method, not a
    73	substitute for loaded resistance training. The authors' own proviso on active visualisation
    74	also applies: it should not alter the dynamic structure of normal competitive patterns.
    75	
    76	**Example** — The book's own example is Kovalik's broomstick snatch pull and front squat,
    77	performed with maximal tension as if overcoming a maximal weight; no further invented
    78	example is added here.
    79	
    80	**Related** — [[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]],
    81	[[heuristic--isometric-priming-and-external-internal-classification]].

13	    12	---
14	    13	
15	    14	# Eccentric Training Damages Tissue and Causes Soreness at First, but Adaptation Removes Both Within 2-3 Weeks While Eccentric Work Capacity Rises
16	    15	
17	    16	**What it is** — Because the muscle complex lengthens under eccentric contraction, its series
18	    17	elastic component (SEC) is exposed to greater strain than under concentric conditions,
19	    18	raising injury potential; most muscle strains and ruptures occur during the eccentric phase
20	    19	of movement (Garrett, 1986). A single session of intense eccentric exercise commonly causes
21	    20	pronounced delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS), peaking 24-72 hours after exercise and
22	    21	resolving within several days (Friden et al, 1983a), accompanied by reduced dynamic strength
23	    22	and damage to myofibrils and connective-tissue elements such as the Z bands (a SEC
24	    23	component). Friden et al (1983b) also examined longer eccentric-training exposure (3
25	    24	sessions weekly over 8 weeks total) and found post-exercise soreness stopped occurring after
26	    25	2-3 weeks, while the ability to perform eccentric work increased by 375%; biopsies showed no
27	    26	Z-band damage at that point, suggesting adaptation to eccentric exercise had occurred.
28	    27	Schwane and Armstrong (1983) corroborated this with downhill running in rats, which produced
29	    28	a superior training effect to level or uphill running and prevented injury more effectively.
30	    29	The authors state that "eccentric exercise tends to produce greater and more rapid increases
31	    30	in muscle strength and hypertrophy than concentric exercise (Hortobagyi et al, 2000)". The
32	    31	book states this on printed p.231 (PDF p. 242) after calling the comparative training
33	    32	findings "often contradictory" on printed p.230 (PDF p. 241); see
34	    33	[[claim--eccentric-vs-concentric-training-adaptation-contradictory-findings]]. It is sometimes
35	    34	suggested this stems from eccentric exercise's greater tissue damage; however, Komulainen et
36	    35	al (2000) found the increase in myofibrillar cross-sectional area in unchanged (non-damaged)
37	    36	muscle fibres was much the same after concentric exercise as after the more damaging
38	    37	eccentric exercise, a result the authors say "do not support the hypothesis that fibre
39	    38	hypertrophy depends on the extent of the fibre damage in exercised muscles." (PDF p. 242,
40	    39	printed p. 231, "4.2.5 Eccentric Training.")
41	    40	
42	    41	**Why it works** — For the soreness/damage mechanism, the stated pathway is mechanical:
43	    42	eccentric lengthening exposes the SEC to greater strain than concentric conditions, so "the
44	    43	potential for injury increases" (PDF p. 242, printed p. 231). The book reports DOMS as
45	    44	"accompanied by" Z-band and myofibril damage; it does not state that the damage causes the
46	    45	soreness. For the adaptation over repeated sessions, no cellular mechanism is given beyond the biopsy finding that Z-band damage no
47	    46	longer occurs after 2-3 weeks of repeated exposure; Inference: this is consistent with a
48	    47	protective structural or neural adaptation (increased sarcomere number in series, improved
49	    48	motor-unit recruitment patterns, or connective-tissue remodelling) that the text does not
50	    49	itself specify. For the Hortobagyi-versus-Komulainen tension, the authors present Komulainen
51	    50	et al's finding as evidence against a damage-drives-hypertrophy causal model, without
52	    51	proposing an alternative mechanism for why eccentric training produces faster
53	    52	strength/hypertrophy gains if not primarily through greater damage.
54	    53	
55	    54	**When to apply** — Use the Friden et al (1983b) adaptation finding (soreness and Z-band
56	    55	damage both disappear within 2-3 weeks of regular eccentric exposure, while eccentric work capacity rises sharply,
57	    56	here 375% in 8 weeks) as the rationale for introducing eccentric-emphasis training
58	    57	gradually and consistently rather than sporadically, to reach the adapted, lower-injury-risk
59	    58	state faster. Inference: the downhill-running finding in rats (Schwane & Armstrong, 1983)
60	    59	could serve as a supporting rationale for progressive eccentric loading in return-to-running
61	    60	or tendon/muscle rehabilitation programming, although it is rat data applied to humans, alongside the tendon-adaptation hypothesis already noted in
62	    61	[[claim--eccentric-vs-concentric-training-adaptation-contradictory-findings]].
63	    62	
64	    63	**When NOT to apply** — The rat downhill-running data (Schwane & Armstrong, 1983) is an
65	    64	animal model; do not assume the same magnitude of protective adaptation transfers directly
66	    65	to human eccentric training without separate verification. The Komulainen et al (2000)
67	    66	finding that hypertrophy does not depend on damage extent contradicts the popular
68	    67	"damage-drives-adaptation" narrative for eccentric training; do not cite eccentric training's
69	    68	greater soreness or damage as itself the reason to prefer it for hypertrophy, since this
70	    69	specific study found comparable myofibrillar growth in undamaged fibres regardless of
71	    70	contraction type. The 375% eccentric-work-capacity increase is from one study (Friden et al,
72	    71	1983b) with a specific 8-week, 3x-weekly protocol; it measures work capacity, not maximal
73	    72	strength specifically.
74	    73	
75	    74	**Example** — Inference: introducing a new eccentric-emphasis exercise (e.g. slow eccentric
76	    75	Nordic curls) should start conservatively and progress gradually over roughly the first 2-3
77	    76	weeks, per Friden et al's repeated-bout timeline, before expecting soreness to diminish and
78	    77	before assuming the tissue has reached its adapted, more damage-resistant state.
79	    78	
80	    79	**Related** — [[claim--eccentric-vs-concentric-training-adaptation-contradictory-findings]],
81	    80	[[claim--eccentric-strength-and-energetics-vs-concentric]] (Ch3),
82	    81	[[claim--collagen-loading-curve-and-injury-risk]] (Ch1, related connective-tissue loading
83	    82	and injury-risk material).

97	    13	
98	    14	# Eccentric-Training Studies Disagree on Whether It Beats Concentric Training for Strength Gains
99	    15	
100	    16	**What it is** — Eccentric contraction is metabolically more efficient than concentric
101	    17	contraction and capable of generating higher forces (Kaneko et al, 1984; Komi, 1973; Rodgers
102	    18	& Berger, 1974), and the concentric-eccentric force gap widens as contraction velocity
103	    19	increases: maximum eccentric force rises while maximum concentric force falls as velocity
104	    20	increases, even though EMG for the muscle group stays reasonably constant (Komi, 1973; see
105	    21	also [[claim--eccentric-strength-and-energetics-vs-concentric]] for the underlying
106	    22	force/energy-cost data from Ch3). Training-adaptation findings, however, are described as
107	    23	"often contradictory": Johnson et al (1976) found no significant difference between
108	    24	concentric and eccentric training methods; Komi and Buskirk (1972), using an isokinetic
109	    25	dynamometer, found eccentric training produced greater eccentric, concentric AND isometric
110	    26	strength increases than concentric training, while concentric training increased only
111	    27	concentric and eccentric strength; Friden et al (1983b) found eccentric training to failure
112	    28	produced marked increases in eccentric strength-endurance but minimal change in concentric
113	    29	strength-endurance. The high-speed, large-acceleration SMART (Seated Movement Aerobic and
114	    30	Resistive Training, "Supersitting") system created by Lisa Ericson (1992) for work with
115	    31	disabled populations tends to increase both concentric and eccentric strength-endurance
116	    32	together. The authors note other researchers report adaptation differences tied to training
117	    33	velocity, measurement velocity and the specific muscle group tested, while very few studies
118	    34	compare functional strength and power changes across free weights, auxotonic (variable
119	    35	resistance) activities, or natural sporting movements, concluding "the central role played
120	    36	by the specificity principle clearly has a profound effect on the experimental analysis." A
121	    37	separate mechanistic note: the superior eccentric strengthening seen at high isokinetic
122	    38	velocities (over 180 degrees/second) may reflect selective tensile-strength increase in
123	    39	tendon and other series elastic components rather than the contractile elements, with a
124	    40	training/rehabilitation implication that high-velocity progressive-overload eccentric work
125	    41	may build the musculotendinous junction's capacity to resist high-impact forces from
126	    42	running, jumping and other impulsive actions. (PDF p. 241, printed p. 230, "4.2.5 Eccentric
127	    43	Training.") Against this, one page later the authors state plainly that "eccentric exercise
128	    44	tends to produce greater and more rapid increases in muscle strength and hypertrophy than
129	    45	concentric exercise (Hortobagyi et al, 2000)" (PDF p. 242, printed p. 231); see
130	    46	[[claim--eccentric-training-damage-adaptation-and-injury-risk-tradeoff]].
131	    47	
132	    48	**Why it works** — The authors give a partial mechanism for the velocity-dependent
133	    49	concentric-eccentric force gap (already established in Ch3's force-velocity treatment, see
134	    50	[[claim--eccentric-strength-and-energetics-vs-concentric]] and
135	    51	[[framework--force-time-curve-adaptation-pattern-by-movement-type]]), but give no mechanism
136	    52	reconciling why different training studies (Johnson 1976 vs Komi & Buskirk 1972 vs Friden
137	    53	1983b) reach different conclusions about which training mode transfers best; the authors'
138	    54	own explanation is methodological (training velocity, measurement velocity, particular
139	    55	muscle groups, and the specificity principle; PDF p. 241, printed p. 230), not
140	    56	physiological.
141	    57	
142	    58	**When to apply** — Inference: when deciding between eccentric-emphasis and concentric-emphasis
143	    59	training for a given goal, treat "eccentric training is superior" as a contested claim
144	    60	depending heavily on which outcome is measured (eccentric strength specifically tends to
145	    61	respond best to eccentric training across these studies; broader transfer to concentric or
146	    62	functional strength is less consistent). The high-velocity eccentric/tendon-adaptation
147	    63	hypothesis is the authors' stated "training and rehabilitation implication" for
148	    64	progressive high-velocity eccentric work (PDF p. 241, printed p. 230); applying it to a
149	    65	specific tendinopathy (e.g. patellar or Achilles) is an extension the book does not make.
150	    66	
151	    67	**When NOT to apply** — Contested because the book calls the findings "often contradictory"
152	    68	(PDF p. 241, printed p. 230) and then states eccentric superiority as known (PDF p. 242,
153	    69	printed p. 231). Handford et al 2024
154	    70	([[research-papers/handford-2024-a-conceptual-framework-of-different-eccentric-training-methods]])
155	    71	states its eccentric taxonomy is not evidence that any one method is superior (its p. 9).
156	    72	This entry summarises training-adaptation studies from a narrow era (1972-1992) with sample
157	    73	sizes not given in the text and differing protocols (isokinetic dynamometer
158	    74	training in Komi & Buskirk; training-to-failure in Friden; a seated aerobic-resistive system
159	    75	in Ericson) that are not directly comparable to one another. Do not treat "eccentric training
160	    76	increases concentric, eccentric and isometric strength" (Komi & Buskirk's specific finding)
161	    77	as a settled general principle; Johnson et al (1976) found no such advantage under a
162	    78	different protocol. The tendon-adaptation hypothesis for high-velocity eccentric work is
163	    79	explicitly framed as a possible explanation ("may be due to"), not a confirmed mechanism.
164	    80	
165	    81	**Example** — Inference: a rehabilitation programme using slow, controlled eccentric squats
166	    82	for general lower-body strength is applying a different training stimulus than one using
167	    83	fast, high-velocity eccentric work (over 180 degrees/second) aimed at tendon/musculotendinous
168	    84	junction adaptation; per this entry, the evidence for broad strength transfer is
169	    85	stronger in some cited studies than others, while the tendon-specific rationale applies
170	    86	mainly to the high-velocity case.
171	    87	
172	    88	**Related** — [[claim--eccentric-strength-and-energetics-vs-concentric]] (Ch3, the
173	    89	underlying force-magnitude and energy-cost data this entry's training studies build on),
174	    90	[[claim--eccentric-training-damage-adaptation-and-injury-risk-tradeoff]] (this section's
175	    91	companion entry on DOMS, tissue damage and the repeated-bout effect).
