190	    14	# The Isokinetic Training Method: How It Works, and Five Advantages Claimed by Its Early Proponents
191	    15	
192	    16	**What it is** — The isokinetic method, popular in the USA in the late 1960s and early
193	    17	1970s, uses a device (e.g. a centrifugal clutch or hydraulic system) that automatically
194	    18	adjusts resistance to control movement speed and, in principle, keep a maximal load on the
195	    19	muscles throughout the full working range; the limiting factor is movement speed, not the
196	    20	magnitude of resistance as in weightlifting, and resistance rises as speed rises. Depending
197	    21	on the apparatus, isokinetics may be concentric or eccentric, though most commercial
198	    22	machines of the era offered only the concentric mode; the device's resistance
199	    23	automatically accommodates each joint angle to the muscle's momentary capability, provided
200	    24	the athlete sustains sufficient motivation. Counsilman (1971, 1972), an early populariser
201	    25	for athletic training, claimed the isokinetic method's basic advantage over others is that
202	    26	it forces maximal-effort work throughout, producing larger, faster strength increases for
203	    27	particular actions even in very strong athletes; the authors state this specific claim "is
204	    28	incorrect," since isokinetic force is usually lower than isometric force throughout the
205	    29	range of joint movement, and maximal strength production is not possible under isokinetic
206	    30	conditions. Even so, the authors report some isokinetic benefits have been corroborated in
207	    31	specific sports (swimming, rowing) by considerable research (Chu & Smith, 1971;
208	    32	Rosentsweig & Hinson, 1972; Hinson & Rosentsweig, 1972; Wilson, 1972), which promote five
209	    33	advantages: (1) the device accommodates to the athlete's own capability throughout the
210	    34	range rather than the athlete accommodating to a fixed resistance, automatically adjusting
211	    35	for fatigue, pain or strength gain and thereby minimising injury risk; (2) prolonged warm-up
212	    36	becomes largely unnecessary, and a demanding workout is possible in five minutes, with no
213	    37	per-athlete adjustment needed on team equipment; (3) fewer repetitions can produce
214	    38	significant strength gains, since each repetition loads the muscle intensively throughout
215	    39	the full range; (4) real-time results display (computer monitor or graph) lets the athlete
216	    40	compete against themselves or others; (5) eliminating most eccentric activity on most
217	    41	isokinetic machines reduces post-exercise soreness. The authors caution that the studies
218	    42	behind these five points were not conducted with top-level international athletes, and did
219	    43	not specify training-phase context (general versus specific preparation). Several studies
220	    44	comparing isometric, dynamic and isokinetic regimes (Thistle et al, 1967; Rosentsweig &
221	    45	Hinson, 1972) found isokinetic exercise produced the greatest electrical (EMG) activity,
222	    46	largest muscle hypertrophy, and "highly effective maintenance of muscular strength" for
223	    47	specific muscle groups in the average person, with more significant strength gains in shorter periods and
224	    48	shorter sessions than other regimes in laboratory studies; transfer of this effect to
225	    49	multi-dimensional functional sporting activity, or across athletes of different
226	    50	qualification, "has not been proved." Isokinetic training also gives limited speed
227	    51	specificity over some ranges of sporting movement, since the trainer can control joint-action
228	    52	speed, but cannot reproduce force-time curves matching specific sports movements. The
229	    53	authors add that "increase in isokinetic strength of the quadriceps does not result in a
230	    54	comparable increase in squatting strength," and that "few, if any, of the studies examined
231	    55	the effect of isokinetic training on starting-strength, acceleration-strength, explosive
232	    56	strength, eccentric strength, strength deficit ... or neuromuscular skill," nor the effect
233	    57	of prolonged isokinetic training on "the elite competitor" (PDF p. 243, printed p. 232).
234	    58	(PDF pp. 242-243, printed pp. 231-232, "4.2.6 Isokinetic and Other Training Means,"
235	    59	"4.2.6.1 The Isokinetic Training Method.")
236	    60	
237	    61	**Why it works** — The authors state the accommodating-resistance mechanism directly
238	    62	(resistance adjusts automatically to applied force at each joint angle), but immediately
239	    63	qualify Counsilman's stronger claim (that this guarantees superior, faster strength gains)
240	    64	as incorrect on physiological grounds, since isokinetic force output is lower than isometric
241	    65	force at the same joint angle throughout the range.
242	    66	
243	    67	**When to apply** — Use this framework's five advantages as the historical case FOR
244	    68	isokinetic training, while treating Counsilman's "forces maximal effort throughout, superior
245	    69	to other methods" claim as specifically refuted by the authors. Inference: the swimming and
246	    70	rowing support cited here is consistent with isokinetics being most defensible for sports
247	    71	whose own movements are already closer to constant-velocity through part of their range (see
248	    72	[[claim--isokinetic-devices-cannot-be-truly-isokinetic-physics-limitation]], which records
249	    73	the authors' view that isokinetic testing or training is "non-functional, except possibly
250	    74	for swimmers," PDF p. 244, printed p. 233).
251	    75	
252	    76	**When NOT to apply** — The cited supporting studies used non-elite athlete samples and did
253	    77	not report training-phase context, per the authors' own caution; do not extend these
254	    78	findings to elite/international athletes or to specific-preparation training phases without
255	    79	separate verification. This entry's advantages should be read alongside
256	    80	[[claim--isokinetic-devices-cannot-be-truly-isokinetic-physics-limitation]] and
257	    81	[[heuristic--isokinetic-testing-limitations-for-functional-sport-specificity]], both of which
258	    82	the authors use to substantially qualify how much practical value these advantages carry for
259	    83	competitive athletes. The book cites Thistle et al 1967 as establishing isokinetic benefits
260	    84	(PDF p. 243, printed p. 232) and later says Thistle's proposition that strength is best
261	    85	developed with maximal tension throughout the movement "is neither proved nor is it
262	    86	universally accepted" (PDF p. 246, printed p. 235).
263	    87	
264	    88	**Example** — The book's own example is the swimming and rowing research cited above (Chu &
265	    89	Smith 1971; Rosentsweig & Hinson 1972; Hinson & Rosentsweig 1972; Wilson 1972); no further
266	    90	invented example is added here.
267	    91	
268	    92	**Related** — [[claim--isokinetic-devices-cannot-be-truly-isokinetic-physics-limitation]],
269	    93	[[heuristic--isokinetic-testing-limitations-for-functional-sport-specificity]],
270	    94	[[heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength]] (Ch2, a
271	    95	related caution against inferring dynamic functional strength from isometric or isokinetic
272	    96	dynamometer output).

287	    14	# There Is No Single "Optimal" Quadriceps:Hamstring Ratio: It Changes With Sport, Joint Angle and Test Velocity
288	    15	
289	    16	**What it is** — It is often claimed the optimal quadriceps-to-hamstring strength ratio is
290	    17	60:40, but Russian scientists found this ratio depends on the specific sport (Vorobyev,
291	    18	1978): they "determined that this ratio (measured when knee extension torque is greatest)
292	    19	should be nearer 80:20 for weightlifters and jumpers," while a treadmill-movement
293	    20	measurement gives runners a ratio of approximately 50:50. A related popular belief, that
294	    21	injuries are far more common once left/right lower-extremity strength differs by more than
295	    22	10%, is also questioned. The authors cite "recent research" finding that neither
296	    23	recommendation is supported by scientifically controlled experiments that correct torque
297	    24	outputs for the effect of gravity and avoid stretching the hamstrings (Stephens & Reid,
298	    25	1988). The flexor/extensor-ratio recommendation is additionally vague because the ratio
299	    26	varies across the joint's range of motion. Verified against the page image (Fig 4.16, PDF p.
300	    27	245, printed p. 234): the figure plots the ratio of isokinetic knee-extensor to knee-flexor
301	    28	torque (y-axis 0.5 to 3.5) against joint angle at 36, 108 and 180 degrees/second, from
302	    29	Cybex dynamometer data; the caption gives no source and no population, and states that
303	    30	"joint angle varies between partial knee flexion in the seated position to full extension
304	    31	at 90 degrees." The text reads the figure: the ratio at the knee at 80 degrees (in Fig 4.16's
305	    32	convention, where 90 degrees is full extension, so near full extension) is about 75:25 at 36
306	    33	degrees/second (a ratio near 3.0 on the figure) but 68:32 at 180 degrees/second (near 2.1);
307	    34	the ratio equals the traditional 60:40 figure (1.5) only at approximately 50 degrees. Since
308	    35	the ratio changes with both joint angle and measurement velocity, the authors conclude "it
309	    36	is meaningless to prescribe an optimal ratio for any joint," and it would be more relevant
310	    37	to refer to a characteristic curve over a full range of movement for a given angular
311	    38	velocity. The page is internally inconsistent: it reports Vorobyev's sport-specific targets
312	    39	(80:20, 50:50) as what the ratio "should be," then calls any optimal ratio "meaningless"
313	    40	(both PDF p. 244, printed p. 233). (PDF pp. 244-245, printed pp. 233-234, "4.2.6.2
314	    41	Limitations of the Isokinetic Method," "Recommended Strength Ratios," Fig 4.16.)
315	    42	
316	    43	**Why it works** — The authors give no physiological mechanism for why the ratio shifts with
317	    44	sport, joint angle or velocity. Their argument is empirical: the figure shows the ratio
318	    45	changing across angle and velocity, so a single number cannot describe it. Inference: a
319	    46	single-number ratio averages over torque variation that differs between the extensors and
320	    47	flexors across the range and across contraction speed.
321	    48	
322	    49	**When to apply** — Use this as a caution against citing a single flexor/extensor or
323	    50	left/right strength-ratio target (e.g. "60:40 quad:hamstring," "no more than 10% L/R
324	    51	difference") as universally optimal or diagnostic of injury risk. If a ratio must be used,
325	    52	specify the joint angle, the angle convention and the angular velocity it was measured at,
326	    53	and prefer a full-range characteristic curve over a single number when data allow, per the
327	    54	authors.
328	    55	
329	    56	Eric's baseline: NordBord hamstring testing is "explicitly retained for smaller, targeted
330	    57	return-to-play groups paired with joint-specific isometric testing (ForceFrame-style)"
331	    58	(`method-baseline.md`, Rehab and return to play); the corpus sets no flexor/extensor ratio
332	    59	target.
333	    60	
334	    61	Inference: this section bears on how such ratio data are read for return-to-play decisions.
335	    62	
336	    63	**When NOT to apply** — Fig 4.16 is uncited Cybex data at 36, 108 and 180 degrees/second on
337	    64	an unspecified population; Vorobyev (1978) supplies the sport-specific ratios and Stephens &
338	    65	Reid (1988) the gravity-correction critique. The specific ratio-versus-angle values should
339	    66	not be treated as universal constants for every athlete or joint. Inference: the figure's
340	    67	convention (90 degrees = full extension) is the reverse of the common 0 degrees = extension
341	    68	convention, so its angles cannot be compared directly with most modern reports. Do
342	    69	not use this entry to conclude ratio testing is worthless; the claim is that a single
343	    70	"optimal ratio" number is misleading, not that ratio measurement itself carries no
344	    71	information (see [[claim--natural-asymmetry-caution-against-isokinetic-symmetry-correction]]
345	    72	for the related but distinct caution about using isokinetic ratios to drive "correction").
346	    73	Inference: the Vorobyev targets were measured at a named point (greatest knee-extension
347	    74	torque), which partly meets the authors' angle objection but not their velocity objection.
348	    75	
349	    76	**Example** — Inference: a rehabilitation report citing "this athlete's quad:hamstring ratio
350	    77	is below the healthy 60:40 standard" should specify the joint angle and test velocity the
351	    78	ratio was measured at, since per Fig 4.16 the same limb could show a ratio above 60:40 at
352	    79	one angle/velocity and at or below it at another.
353	    80	
354	    81	**Related** — [[claim--natural-asymmetry-caution-against-isokinetic-symmetry-correction]]
355	    82	(Ch3.3.4.4, a related caution against using isokinetic ratios to "correct" asymmetry),
356	    83	[[heuristic--isokinetic-testing-limitations-for-functional-sport-specificity]],
357	    84	[[claim--pursuing-perfect-bilateral-symmetry-can-be-counterproductive]].

372	    14	# No Machine Can Be Truly Isokinetic: Isokinetic Tests Miss the Acceleration Phases Where the Authors Say Most Injuries Occur, and the Elastic-Energy Contribution of Natural Movement
373	    15	
374	    16	**What it is** — The authors call the assumption that isokinetic dynamometers are
375	    17	"accurately constant angular velocity devices" a "faulty basic assumption": the laws of
376	    18	physics make it impossible, since a body at rest must accelerate to reach a terminal
377	    19	velocity, sustain it, then decelerate back to rest, meaning every movement (isokinetic or
378	    20	otherwise) has periods of positive or negative acceleration; producing entirely isokinetic
379	    21	conditions throughout would require infinite acceleration, which "contradicts the laws of
380	    22	science." Manufacturers can only minimise, never eliminate, these non-isokinetic transition
381	    23	phases. The authors make two separate points about why this matters. (a) They assert, citing
382	    24	no source, that "most injuries occur during these transition phases when a limb is changing
383	    25	its velocity or tension is changing in the musculotendinous system," and that isokinetic
384	    26	testing "can reveal no useful information about what is happening to the muscles then." (b)
385	    27	Separately, "a most serious problem is that isokinetic testing can give no information on
386	    28	the major contribution played by the storage and release of elastic energy in the soft
387	    29	tissues during dynamic, natural actions such as walking, running, jumping or throwing." The
388	    30	authors' summary: "isokinetic testing or training is non-functional, except possibly for
389	    31	swimmers whose movements are approximately isokinetic over part of their range."
390	    32	Biomechanical analysis of force-time and rate-of-force-development curves for resisted free
391	    33	movement confirms distinct qualities (maximal strength, starting strength, acceleration
392	    34	strength, explosive strength, see Fig 2.13), and the curves obtained isokinetically are "so
393	    35	radically different from their free movement equivalents that they are of minimal value
394	    36	either for functional analysis or specific neuromuscular conditioning." (PDF p. 244, printed
395	    37	p. 233, "4.2.6.2 Limitations of the Isokinetic Method," "Fundamental Biomechanics of
396	    38	Isokinetic Devices.")
397	    39	
398	    40	**Why it works** — The physics is Newtonian: any object moving from rest, sustaining a
399	    41	velocity, and returning to rest must accelerate and decelerate, and true isokinetic motion
400	    42	throughout would demand infinite acceleration at the start and end. The two consequences are
401	    43	separate claims: (a) most injuries, the authors assert without citation, occur in
402	    44	transition phases the device cannot measure; (b) separately, isokinetic testing captures
403	    45	none of the elastic-energy storage and release of natural actions, which is a property of
404	    46	natural movement, not of the device's transition phases.
405	    47	
406	    48	**When to apply** — Use this as the physics-level foundation for treating isokinetic test or
407	    49	training data as descriptive of a narrow, artificial condition (the device's controlled
408	    50	constant-velocity phase) rather than as a general index of an athlete's dynamic capability.
409	    51	Inference: this reinforces the terminology point already in this library (see
410	    52	[[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]]) that commercial "isokinetic" devices are
411	    53	more accurately "quasi-isokinetic."
412	    54	
413	    55	**When NOT to apply** — The authors' own exception is swimming, where movement is
414	    56	"approximately isokinetic over part of their range," making isokinetic testing/training
415	    57	comparatively more relevant there than for running, jumping, throwing or lifting. Do not read
416	    58	this entry as claiming isokinetic devices provide zero useful information; the claims are
417	    59	narrower: (a) per the authors' uncited assertion, they miss the transition
418	    60	(acceleration/deceleration) phases where most injuries occur; (b) separately, they capture
419	    61	none of the elastic-energy contribution of natural actions. The sweeping "non-functional"
420	    62	verdict also sits against the book's own use of isokinetic data elsewhere (Fig 4.16 Cybex
421	    63	ratio curves, PDF p. 245, printed p. 234; Komi & Buskirk's isokinetic-dynamometer training
422	    64	study, PDF p. 241, printed p. 230); see
423	    65	[[heuristic--isokinetic-testing-limitations-for-functional-sport-specificity]] for why that
424	    66	sibling is contested.
425	    67	
426	    68	**Example** — Inference: a hamstring isokinetic strength test at a fixed angular velocity
427	    69	(e.g. 60 degrees/second) can characterise force output during that constant-velocity phase,
428	    70	but per this claim it cannot characterise what happens during the initial acceleration into
429	    71	that velocity or the deceleration out of it. The book does not name the sprinting hamstring
430	    72	or say where its injury risk concentrates.
431	    73	
432	    74	**Related** — [[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]] (Ch1, "isokinetic" as a
433	    75	misleading term for the same physical reason given here),
434	    76	[[heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength]] (Ch2),
435	    77	[[heuristic--isokinetic-testing-limitations-for-functional-sport-specificity]],
436	    78	[[framework--isokinetic-method-claimed-advantages-and-mechanism]].

451	    14	# Three Grounds (Anatomy, Physiology, Specificity) on Which Isokinetic Testing and Training Misrepresent Functional Sport Movement
452	    15	
453	    16	**What it is** — Building on the physics limitation already covered (see
454	    17	[[claim--isokinetic-devices-cannot-be-truly-isokinetic-physics-limitation]]), the authors
455	    18	give a detailed, itemised critique of relying on isokinetic dynamometers (e.g. Cybex,
456	    19	Orthotron) for testing and rehabilitation. (1) **Functional anatomy**: nearby-joint angle
457	    20	changes the torque produced about the joint in question (e.g. hip angle changes knee
458	    21	extension torque, important to weightlifters, jumpers and sprinters), but seated isokinetic
459	    22	testing typically immobilises the hips with straps, creating "non-functional conditions" that
460	    23	measure torque specific to the seated posture, not any actual sporting posture; testing is
461	    24	also rarely combined with EMG or myotonometry to identify which specific muscles (e.g.
462	    25	vastus medialis vs lateralis, affected by lateral/medial rotation) actually contribute to the
463	    26	measured torque, and open-chain testing (foot not contacting the ground) alters how popliteus
464	    27	and gastrocnemius contribute to knee flexion, both important in running, lifting and jumping;
465	    28	seated testing also ignores medial rotation contributions (sartorius, gracilis,
466	    29	semimembranosus, semitendinosus) and lateral rotation (biceps femoris). (2) **Muscle
467	    30	physiology**: most sporting actions begin from intense isometric or explosive-isometric
468	    31	contraction with stored tendon elastic energy, a state isokinetic testing/training involves
469	    32	only insignificantly; the myotatic stretch reflex (stronger with faster stretch) is central
470	    33	to explosive running, jumping, lifting and throwing but cannot be recruited under isokinetic
471	    34	conditions, and "the elimination of most of these reflex actions by isokinetic apparatus
472	    35	ensures that isokinetic testing and training is only of value during the early general
473	    36	conditioning or rehabilitation phase, but of no real significance during the specific
474	    37	preparation or competitive phases of sports training" (PDF p. 246, printed p. 235); agonist-antagonist cocontraction and ballistic (preprogrammed,
475	    38	feedback-independent) movement are both common in sport but isokinetic conditions permit
476	    39	neither; torque under isokinetic conditions is usually much lower than isometric torque at
477	    40	the same joint angle, contradicting the claim (Thistle et al, 1967) that isokinetics keeps
478	    41	tension maximal throughout; reciprocal inhibition (antagonist pre-contraction raising
479	    42	agonist force, used in PNF and common in plyometric rebounding) is not permitted by most
480	    43	isokinetic devices; and bilateral versus unilateral force-production patterns differ, so
481	    44	isokinetic limb-to-limb comparisons "can be very misleading," since a dominant limb's
482	    45	superiority is often one of skill, not strength (e.g. it is common, but the authors imply
483	    46	misguided, for therapists to isokinetically strengthen a footballer's weaker kicking limb
484	    47	when the support leg's job is producing stabilising strength). (3) **Specificity**:
485	    48	indiscriminate isokinetic use neglects the specificity principle across ten dimensions (type
486	    49	of muscle contraction, movement pattern, region of movement, velocity of movement, force of
487	    50	contraction, muscle fibre recruitment, metabolism, biochemical adaptation, flexibility,
488	    51	fatigue), citing Sale and McDougall (1981) that strength gains are apparent only when
489	    52	measured during the same movement type used in training; this specificity concern
490	    53	"culminated" in Verkhoshansky's principle of dynamic correspondence (see 4.3). On this
491	    54	basis, isokinetic training and measurement are "so functionally different from normal
492	    55	sporting movement as to be relatively useless for giving any information that is accurately
493	    56	applicable to the competitive athlete" (PDF p. 247, printed p. 236). The authors' concluding analogy: relying on a single isokinetic model
494	    57	to assess strength and endurance is "tantamount to permanently accepting" the early
495	    58	planetary-electron atomic model just because it is easy to work with; a more versatile,
496	    59	"kinesiological polygraph" combining high-speed video, EMG, myotensiometers, accelerometers
497	    60	and force plates is what multi-faceted human movement actually demands, and sporting
498	    61	performance itself remains the ultimate test of any training or rehabilitation regime. The
499	    62	authors also name the APRE system (based on DeLorme's original work, see 5.2.2) as an
500	    63	inexpensive, effective alternative to isokinetics, and point to Osternig (1986) for a
501	    64	detailed review of isokinetic strengths and weaknesses. (PDF pp. 244-247, printed pp.
502	    65	233-236, "4.2.6.2 Limitations of the Isokinetic Method," "Functional Anatomy," "Muscle
503	    66	Physiology," "The Importance of Specificity," "Concluding Remarks.")
504	    67	
505	    68	**Why it works** — Each of the itemised points above carries its own stated mechanism (listed
506	    69	inline): joint-coupling effects on torque, missing EMG/myotonometry verification, absent
507	    70	elastic-energy and stretch-reflex contribution, absent cocontraction/ballistic patterning,
508	    71	absent reciprocal inhibition, and bilateral-versus-unilateral force-pattern differences. The
509	    72	authors' unifying argument is that isokinetic devices remove or distort each of these
510	    73	naturally-occurring features of dynamic sport movement, so a test built on removing them
511	    74	cannot validly characterise performance that depends on them.
512	    75	
513	    76	**When to apply** — Use this itemised list as a detailed checklist when deciding whether a
514	    77	specific isokinetic finding (a strength deficit, an asymmetry, a rehabilitation
515	    78	"clearance" threshold) should influence a functional/sport-specific training or return-to-play
516	    79	decision: check whether the isokinetic condition tested (seated, seat-strapped, single-joint,
517	    80	no elastic energy, no stretch reflex, no cocontraction, no reciprocal inhibition, bilateral
518	    81	comparison) resembles the sporting movement in question closely enough for the finding to
519	    82	transfer. Per the authors, confine isokinetic work to early general conditioning or
520	    83	rehabilitation (PDF p. 246, printed p. 235). This heuristic substantially extends, with a Ch4-specific itemised mechanism list,
521	    84	the caution already recorded in
522	    85	[[heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength]] (Ch2, citing
523	    86	the book's own "futile" statement about isometric/isokinetic dynamometers); a reciprocal link
524	    87	from that entry to this one is recommended.
525	    88	
526	    89	**When NOT to apply** — Marked contested, inheriting the same internal tension already
527	    90	recorded in [[heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength]]:
528	    91	the book itself relies on isokinetic and isometric dynamometer data elsewhere (e.g. the
529	    92	Fig 4.16 Cybex ratio curves, PDF p. 245, printed p. 234, in
530	    93	[[heuristic--isokinetic-strength-ratios-vary-by-angle-and-velocity]]; Komi & Buskirk's
531	    94	isokinetic-dynamometer training study, PDF p. 241, printed p. 230; Figs 2.8-2.9 isokinetic
532	    95	vs isometric torque, cited on PDF p. 243, printed p. 232 and PDF p. 246, printed p. 235) to
533	    96	establish real findings, without fully reconciling that reliance with this section's
534	    97	sweeping "non-functional" critique. Do not read this entry as claiming isokinetic devices have zero diagnostic value
535	    98	(the authors themselves call them "useful for measuring isokinetic actions... in two
536	    99	dimensions"); the claim is that extrapolating isokinetic results to full sporting movement
537	   100	"is scientifically unacceptable and misleading."
538	   101	
539	   102	**Example** — Inference: a therapist isokinetically strengthening a footballer's weaker
540	   103	kicking (non-support) leg, per the authors' own named example, may be targeting the wrong
541	   104	quality if the support leg's job (stabilising strength under bilateral/unilateral,
542	   105	cocontractive demand) is actually more functionally relevant to on-field performance than the
543	   106	kicking leg's isolated, isokinetically-measured torque.
544	   107	
545	   108	**Related** — [[heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength]]
546	   109	(Ch2, the entry this one substantially extends with Ch4-specific mechanisms; reciprocal link
547	   110	recommended), [[claim--isokinetic-devices-cannot-be-truly-isokinetic-physics-limitation]],
548	   111	[[heuristic--isokinetic-strength-ratios-vary-by-angle-and-velocity]],
549	   112	[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Ch1, the ten-dimension specificity

565	    14	# The Static-Dynamic Method: Pairing a Brief Isometric Hold With Explosive Concentric Work in One Repetition
566	    15	
567	    16	**What it is** — The static-dynamic method sequentially combines isometric and dynamic
568	    17	(auxotonic) muscular activity within one exercise. Two variants are given as experimentally
569	    18	effective: (1) a 2-3 second isometric contraction at 80% of maximum, immediately followed by
570	    19	explosive concentric dynamic work with a 30%-of-maximum load; (2) a constant load of 75-80%
571	    20	of maximum used for both the isometric and dynamic components, illustrated with a half-squat
572	    21	example: the athlete sinks into a half-squat with a barbell on the shoulders, holds that
573	    22	position for 2 seconds, then jumps upward with maximal acceleration before landing carefully
574	    23	and repeating. Experimentally, variant (1) proved better than dynamic exercise alone for
575	    24	developing speed-strength. For variant (2) the source reads: "The second variant has an
576	    25	equivalent affect on the improvement of speed-strength and absolute strength (Dobrovolsky,
577	    26	1972, 1973)." The comparator is unclear: this may mean an equal effect on both qualities,
578	    27	or an effect equivalent to dynamic exercise; the text does not say. (PDF p. 247, printed p.
579	    28	236, "4.2.6.3 Static-Dynamic Methods.")
580	    29	
581	    30	**Why it works** — No specific mechanism is given for why pairing a brief isometric hold with
582	    31	subsequent explosive concentric work outperforms dynamic-only training for speed-strength in
583	    32	variant (1); Inference: this is plausibly related to the same explosive-isometric-to-concentric
584	    33	transition mechanism already described for depth jumps and the shock method (see
585	    34	[[framework--kinetic-energy-stimulation-mechanical-basis-and-advantages]] and
586	    35	[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]), where the isometric phase primes the
587	    36	neuromuscular system immediately before the explosive concentric effort, though the authors
588	    37	do not state this connection explicitly for the static-dynamic method here.
589	    38	
590	    39	**When to apply** — Use variant (1) (2-3s isometric hold at 80% max, then explosive
591	    40	concentric at 30% max) when the specific goal is speed-strength development, per the cited
592	    41	finding that it outperformed dynamic-only training for that quality. Use variant (2) (a
593	    42	half-squat hold then jump at 75-80% max) when both speed-strength and absolute strength are
594	    43	targets, per the source's statement that it affects both. Inference: if the sentence means
595	    44	its effect only equals dynamic exercise, its value would lie mainly in variety or in the
596	    45	loaded-jump pattern itself; the text does not settle which reading is meant.
597	    46	
598	    47	**When NOT to apply** — This is a single-source finding (Dobrovolsky, 1972, 1973) without
599	    48	reported sample size, training-age context, or long-term outcome data beyond the immediate
600	    49	comparison to dynamic-only training; treat the specific load percentages (80%/30%, 75-80%)
601	    50	as the cited protocol's own parameters, not universally optimal figures. Variant (2)'s
602	    51	half-squat-and-jump with load requires careful technique and landing control, which this
603	    52	passage does not itself detail as a safety protocol.
604	    53	
605	    54	**Example** — The book's own example is the half-squat-hold-then-jump description above
606	    55	(variant 2); no further invented example is added here.
607	    56	
608	    57	**Related** — [[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]],

610	    59	[[heuristic--choice-of-muscle-training-regime-favor-combination]] (this section's companion

    13	
    14	# Eccentric Training Damages Tissue and Causes Soreness at First, but Adaptation Removes Both Within 2-3 Weeks While Eccentric Work Capacity Rises
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Because the muscle complex lengthens under eccentric contraction, its series
    17	elastic component (SEC) is exposed to greater strain than under concentric conditions,
    18	raising injury potential; most muscle strains and ruptures occur during the eccentric phase
    19	of movement (Garrett, 1986). A single session of intense eccentric exercise commonly causes
    20	pronounced delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS), peaking 24-72 hours after exercise and
    21	resolving within several days (Friden et al, 1983a), accompanied by reduced dynamic strength
    22	and damage to myofibrils and connective-tissue elements such as the Z bands (a SEC
    23	component). Friden et al (1983b) also examined longer eccentric-training exposure (3
    24	sessions weekly over 8 weeks total) and found post-exercise soreness stopped occurring after
    25	2-3 weeks, while the ability to perform eccentric work increased by 375%; biopsies showed no
    26	Z-band damage at that point, suggesting adaptation to eccentric exercise had occurred.
    27	Schwane and Armstrong (1983) corroborated this with downhill running in rats, which produced
    28	a superior training effect to level or uphill running and prevented injury more effectively.
    29	The authors state that "eccentric exercise tends to produce greater and more rapid increases
    30	in muscle strength and hypertrophy than concentric exercise (Hortobagyi et al, 2000)". The
    31	book states this on printed p.231 (PDF p. 242) after calling the comparative training
    32	findings "often contradictory" on printed p.230 (PDF p. 241); see
    33	[[claim--eccentric-vs-concentric-training-adaptation-contradictory-findings]]. It is sometimes
    34	suggested this stems from eccentric exercise's greater tissue damage; however, Komulainen et
    35	al (2000) found the increase in myofibrillar cross-sectional area in unchanged (non-damaged)
    36	muscle fibres was much the same after concentric exercise as after the more damaging
    37	eccentric exercise, a result the authors say "do not support the hypothesis that fibre
    38	hypertrophy depends on the extent of the fibre damage in exercised muscles." (PDF p. 242,
    39	printed p. 231, "4.2.5 Eccentric Training.")
    40	
    41	**Why it works** — For the soreness/damage mechanism, the stated pathway is mechanical:
    42	eccentric lengthening exposes the SEC to greater strain than concentric conditions, so "the
    43	potential for injury increases" (PDF p. 242, printed p. 231). The book reports DOMS as
    44	"accompanied by" Z-band and myofibril damage; it does not state that the damage causes the
    45	soreness. For the adaptation over repeated sessions, no cellular mechanism is given beyond the biopsy finding that Z-band damage no
    46	longer occurs after 2-3 weeks of repeated exposure; Inference: this is consistent with a
    47	protective structural or neural adaptation (increased sarcomere number in series, improved
    48	motor-unit recruitment patterns, or connective-tissue remodelling) that the text does not
    49	itself specify. For the Hortobagyi-versus-Komulainen tension, the authors present Komulainen
    50	et al's finding as evidence against a damage-drives-hypertrophy causal model, without
    51	proposing an alternative mechanism for why eccentric training produces faster
    52	strength/hypertrophy gains if not primarily through greater damage.
    53	
    54	**When to apply** — Use the Friden et al (1983b) adaptation finding (soreness and Z-band
    55	damage both disappear within 2-3 weeks of regular eccentric exposure, while eccentric work capacity rises sharply,
    56	here 375% in 8 weeks) as the rationale for introducing eccentric-emphasis training
    57	gradually and consistently rather than sporadically, to reach the adapted, lower-injury-risk
    58	state faster. Inference: the downhill-running finding in rats (Schwane & Armstrong, 1983)
    59	could serve as a supporting rationale for progressive eccentric loading in return-to-running
    60	or tendon/muscle rehabilitation programming, although it is rat data applied to humans, alongside the tendon-adaptation hypothesis already noted in
    61	[[claim--eccentric-vs-concentric-training-adaptation-contradictory-findings]].
    62	
    63	**When NOT to apply** — The rat downhill-running data (Schwane & Armstrong, 1983) is an
    64	animal model; do not assume the same magnitude of protective adaptation transfers directly
    65	to human eccentric training without separate verification. The Komulainen et al (2000)
    66	finding that hypertrophy does not depend on damage extent contradicts the popular
    67	"damage-drives-adaptation" narrative for eccentric training; do not cite eccentric training's
    68	greater soreness or damage as itself the reason to prefer it for hypertrophy, since this
    69	specific study found comparable myofibrillar growth in undamaged fibres regardless of
    70	contraction type. The 375% eccentric-work-capacity increase is from one study (Friden et al,
    71	1983b) with a specific 8-week, 3x-weekly protocol; it measures work capacity, not maximal
    72	strength specifically.
    73	
    74	**Example** — Inference: introducing a new eccentric-emphasis exercise (e.g. slow eccentric
    75	Nordic curls) should start conservatively and progress gradually over roughly the first 2-3
    76	weeks, per Friden et al's repeated-bout timeline, before expecting soreness to diminish and
    77	before assuming the tissue has reached its adapted, more damage-resistant state.
    78	
    79	**Related** — [[claim--eccentric-vs-concentric-training-adaptation-contradictory-findings]],
    80	[[claim--eccentric-strength-and-energetics-vs-concentric]] (Ch3),
    81	[[claim--collagen-loading-curve-and-injury-risk]] (Ch1, related connective-tissue loading
    82	and injury-risk material).

    13	
    14	# Eccentric-Training Studies Disagree on Whether It Beats Concentric Training for Strength Gains
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Eccentric contraction is metabolically more efficient than concentric
    17	contraction and capable of generating higher forces (Kaneko et al, 1984; Komi, 1973; Rodgers
    18	& Berger, 1974), and the concentric-eccentric force gap widens as contraction velocity
    19	increases: maximum eccentric force rises while maximum concentric force falls as velocity
    20	increases, even though EMG for the muscle group stays reasonably constant (Komi, 1973; see
    21	also [[claim--eccentric-strength-and-energetics-vs-concentric]] for the underlying
    22	force/energy-cost data from Ch3). Training-adaptation findings, however, are described as
    23	"often contradictory": Johnson et al (1976) found no significant difference between
    24	concentric and eccentric training methods; Komi and Buskirk (1972), using an isokinetic
    25	dynamometer, found eccentric training produced greater eccentric, concentric AND isometric
    26	strength increases than concentric training, while concentric training increased only
    27	concentric and eccentric strength; Friden et al (1983b) found eccentric training to failure
    28	produced marked increases in eccentric strength-endurance but minimal change in concentric
    29	strength-endurance. The high-speed, large-acceleration SMART (Seated Movement Aerobic and
    30	Resistive Training, "Supersitting") system created by Lisa Ericson (1992) for work with
    31	disabled populations tends to increase both concentric and eccentric strength-endurance
    32	together. The authors note other researchers report adaptation differences tied to training
    33	velocity, measurement velocity and the specific muscle group tested, while very few studies
    34	compare functional strength and power changes across free weights, auxotonic (variable
    35	resistance) activities, or natural sporting movements, concluding "the central role played
    36	by the specificity principle clearly has a profound effect on the experimental analysis." A
    37	separate mechanistic note: the superior eccentric strengthening seen at high isokinetic
    38	velocities (over 180 degrees/second) may reflect selective tensile-strength increase in
    39	tendon and other series elastic components rather than the contractile elements, with a
    40	training/rehabilitation implication that high-velocity progressive-overload eccentric work
    41	may build the musculotendinous junction's capacity to resist high-impact forces from
    42	running, jumping and other impulsive actions. (PDF p. 241, printed p. 230, "4.2.5 Eccentric
    43	Training.") Against this, one page later the authors state plainly that "eccentric exercise
    44	tends to produce greater and more rapid increases in muscle strength and hypertrophy than
    45	concentric exercise (Hortobagyi et al, 2000)" (PDF p. 242, printed p. 231); see
    46	[[claim--eccentric-training-damage-adaptation-and-injury-risk-tradeoff]].
    47	
    48	**Why it works** — The authors give a partial mechanism for the velocity-dependent
    49	concentric-eccentric force gap (already established in Ch3's force-velocity treatment, see
    50	[[claim--eccentric-strength-and-energetics-vs-concentric]] and
    51	[[framework--force-time-curve-adaptation-pattern-by-movement-type]]), but give no mechanism
    52	reconciling why different training studies (Johnson 1976 vs Komi & Buskirk 1972 vs Friden
    53	1983b) reach different conclusions about which training mode transfers best; the authors'
    54	own explanation is methodological (training velocity, measurement velocity, particular
    55	muscle groups, and the specificity principle; PDF p. 241, printed p. 230), not
    56	physiological.
    57	
    58	**When to apply** — Inference: when deciding between eccentric-emphasis and concentric-emphasis
    59	training for a given goal, treat "eccentric training is superior" as a contested claim
    60	depending heavily on which outcome is measured (eccentric strength specifically tends to
    61	respond best to eccentric training across these studies; broader transfer to concentric or
    62	functional strength is less consistent). The high-velocity eccentric/tendon-adaptation
    63	hypothesis is the authors' stated "training and rehabilitation implication" for
    64	progressive high-velocity eccentric work (PDF p. 241, printed p. 230); applying it to a
    65	specific tendinopathy (e.g. patellar or Achilles) is an extension the book does not make.
    66	
    67	**When NOT to apply** — Contested because the book calls the findings "often contradictory"
    68	(PDF p. 241, printed p. 230) and then states eccentric superiority as known (PDF p. 242,
    69	printed p. 231). Handford et al 2024
    70	([[research-papers/handford-2024-a-conceptual-framework-of-different-eccentric-training-methods]])
    71	states its eccentric taxonomy is not evidence that any one method is superior (its p. 9).
    72	This entry summarises training-adaptation studies from a narrow era (1972-1992) with sample
    73	sizes not given in the text and differing protocols (isokinetic dynamometer
    74	training in Komi & Buskirk; training-to-failure in Friden; a seated aerobic-resistive system
    75	in Ericson) that are not directly comparable to one another. Do not treat "eccentric training
    76	increases concentric, eccentric and isometric strength" (Komi & Buskirk's specific finding)
    77	as a settled general principle; Johnson et al (1976) found no such advantage under a
    78	different protocol. The tendon-adaptation hypothesis for high-velocity eccentric work is
    79	explicitly framed as a possible explanation ("may be due to"), not a confirmed mechanism.
    80	
    81	**Example** — Inference: a rehabilitation programme using slow, controlled eccentric squats
    82	for general lower-body strength is applying a different training stimulus than one using
    83	fast, high-velocity eccentric work (over 180 degrees/second) aimed at tendon/musculotendinous
    84	junction adaptation; per this entry, the evidence for broad strength transfer is
    85	stronger in some cited studies than others, while the tendon-specific rationale applies
    86	mainly to the high-velocity case.
    87	
    88	**Related** — [[claim--eccentric-strength-and-energetics-vs-concentric]] (Ch3, the
    89	underlying force-magnitude and energy-cost data this entry's training studies build on),
    90	[[claim--eccentric-training-damage-adaptation-and-injury-risk-tradeoff]] (this section's
    91	companion entry on DOMS, tissue damage and the repeated-bout effect).

    13	
    14	# The Isokinetic Training Method: How It Works, and Five Advantages Claimed by Its Early Proponents
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The isokinetic method, popular in the USA in the late 1960s and early
    17	1970s, uses a device (e.g. a centrifugal clutch or hydraulic system) that automatically
    18	adjusts resistance to control movement speed and, in principle, keep a maximal load on the
    19	muscles throughout the full working range; the limiting factor is movement speed, not the
    20	magnitude of resistance as in weightlifting, and resistance rises as speed rises. Depending
    21	on the apparatus, isokinetics may be concentric or eccentric, though most commercial
    22	machines of the era offered only the concentric mode; the device's resistance
    23	automatically accommodates each joint angle to the muscle's momentary capability, provided
    24	the athlete sustains sufficient motivation. Counsilman (1971, 1972), an early populariser
    25	for athletic training, claimed the isokinetic method's basic advantage over others is that
    26	it forces maximal-effort work throughout, producing larger, faster strength increases for
    27	particular actions even in very strong athletes; the authors state this specific claim "is
    28	incorrect," since isokinetic force is usually lower than isometric force throughout the
    29	range of joint movement, and maximal strength production is not possible under isokinetic
    30	conditions. Even so, the authors report some isokinetic benefits have been corroborated in
    31	specific sports (swimming, rowing) by considerable research (Chu & Smith, 1971;
    32	Rosentsweig & Hinson, 1972; Hinson & Rosentsweig, 1972; Wilson, 1972), which promote five
    33	advantages: (1) the device accommodates to the athlete's own capability throughout the
    34	range rather than the athlete accommodating to a fixed resistance, automatically adjusting
    35	for fatigue, pain or strength gain and thereby minimising injury risk; (2) prolonged warm-up
    36	becomes largely unnecessary, and a demanding workout is possible in five minutes, with no
    37	per-athlete adjustment needed on team equipment; (3) fewer repetitions can produce
    38	significant strength gains, since each repetition loads the muscle intensively throughout
    39	the full range; (4) real-time results display (computer monitor or graph) lets the athlete
    40	compete against themselves or others; (5) eliminating most eccentric activity on most
    41	isokinetic machines reduces post-exercise soreness. The authors caution that the studies
    42	behind these five points were not conducted with top-level international athletes, and did
    43	not specify training-phase context (general versus specific preparation). Several studies
    44	comparing isometric, dynamic and isokinetic regimes (Thistle et al, 1967; Rosentsweig &
    45	Hinson, 1972) found isokinetic exercise produced the greatest electrical (EMG) activity,
    46	largest muscle hypertrophy, and "highly effective maintenance of muscular strength" for
    47	specific muscle groups in the average person, with more significant strength gains in shorter periods and
    48	shorter sessions than other regimes in laboratory studies; transfer of this effect to
    49	multi-dimensional functional sporting activity, or across athletes of different
    50	qualification, "has not been proved." Isokinetic training also gives limited speed
    51	specificity over some ranges of sporting movement, since the trainer can control joint-action
    52	speed, but cannot reproduce force-time curves matching specific sports movements. The
    53	authors add that "increase in isokinetic strength of the quadriceps does not result in a
    54	comparable increase in squatting strength," and that "few, if any, of the studies examined
    55	the effect of isokinetic training on starting-strength, acceleration-strength, explosive
    56	strength, eccentric strength, strength deficit ... or neuromuscular skill," nor the effect
    57	of prolonged isokinetic training on "the elite competitor" (PDF p. 243, printed p. 232).
    58	(PDF pp. 242-243, printed pp. 231-232, "4.2.6 Isokinetic and Other Training Means,"
    59	"4.2.6.1 The Isokinetic Training Method.")
    60	
    61	**Why it works** — The authors state the accommodating-resistance mechanism directly
    62	(resistance adjusts automatically to applied force at each joint angle), but immediately
    63	qualify Counsilman's stronger claim (that this guarantees superior, faster strength gains)
    64	as incorrect on physiological grounds, since isokinetic force output is lower than isometric
    65	force at the same joint angle throughout the range.
    66	
    67	**When to apply** — Use this framework's five advantages as the historical case FOR
    68	isokinetic training, while treating Counsilman's "forces maximal effort throughout, superior
    69	to other methods" claim as specifically refuted by the authors. Inference: the swimming and
    70	rowing support cited here is consistent with isokinetics being most defensible for sports
    71	whose own movements are already closer to constant-velocity through part of their range (see
    72	[[claim--isokinetic-devices-cannot-be-truly-isokinetic-physics-limitation]], which records
    73	the authors' view that isokinetic testing or training is "non-functional, except possibly
    74	for swimmers," PDF p. 244, printed p. 233).
    75	
    76	**When NOT to apply** — The cited supporting studies used non-elite athlete samples and did
    77	not report training-phase context, per the authors' own caution; do not extend these
    78	findings to elite/international athletes or to specific-preparation training phases without
    79	separate verification. This entry's advantages should be read alongside
    80	[[claim--isokinetic-devices-cannot-be-truly-isokinetic-physics-limitation]] and
    81	[[heuristic--isokinetic-testing-limitations-for-functional-sport-specificity]], both of which
    82	the authors use to substantially qualify how much practical value these advantages carry for
    83	competitive athletes. The book cites Thistle et al 1967 as establishing isokinetic benefits
    84	(PDF p. 243, printed p. 232) and later says Thistle's proposition that strength is best
    85	developed with maximal tension throughout the movement "is neither proved nor is it
    86	universally accepted" (PDF p. 246, printed p. 235).
    87	
    88	**Example** — The book's own example is the swimming and rowing research cited above (Chu &
    89	Smith 1971; Rosentsweig & Hinson 1972; Hinson & Rosentsweig 1972; Wilson 1972); no further
    90	invented example is added here.
    91	
    92	**Related** — [[claim--isokinetic-devices-cannot-be-truly-isokinetic-physics-limitation]],
    93	[[heuristic--isokinetic-testing-limitations-for-functional-sport-specificity]],
    94	[[heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength]] (Ch2, a
    95	related caution against inferring dynamic functional strength from isometric or isokinetic
    96	dynamometer output).

    13	
    14	# There Is No Single "Optimal" Quadriceps:Hamstring Ratio: It Changes With Sport, Joint Angle and Test Velocity
    15	
    16	**What it is** — It is often claimed the optimal quadriceps-to-hamstring strength ratio is
    17	60:40, but Russian scientists found this ratio depends on the specific sport (Vorobyev,
    18	1978): they "determined that this ratio (measured when knee extension torque is greatest)
    19	should be nearer 80:20 for weightlifters and jumpers," while a treadmill-movement
    20	measurement gives runners a ratio of approximately 50:50. A related popular belief, that
    21	injuries are far more common once left/right lower-extremity strength differs by more than
    22	10%, is also questioned. The authors cite "recent research" finding that neither
    23	recommendation is supported by scientifically controlled experiments that correct torque
    24	outputs for the effect of gravity and avoid stretching the hamstrings (Stephens & Reid,
    25	1988). The flexor/extensor-ratio recommendation is additionally vague because the ratio
    26	varies across the joint's range of motion. Verified against the page image (Fig 4.16, PDF p.
    27	245, printed p. 234): the figure plots the ratio of isokinetic knee-extensor to knee-flexor
    28	torque (y-axis 0.5 to 3.5) against joint angle at 36, 108 and 180 degrees/second, from
    29	Cybex dynamometer data; the caption gives no source and no population, and states that
    30	"joint angle varies between partial knee flexion in the seated position to full extension
    31	at 90 degrees." The text reads the figure: the ratio at the knee at 80 degrees (in Fig 4.16's
    32	convention, where 90 degrees is full extension, so near full extension) is about 75:25 at 36
    33	degrees/second (a ratio near 3.0 on the figure) but 68:32 at 180 degrees/second (near 2.1);
    34	the ratio equals the traditional 60:40 figure (1.5) only at approximately 50 degrees. Since
    35	the ratio changes with both joint angle and measurement velocity, the authors conclude "it
    36	is meaningless to prescribe an optimal ratio for any joint," and it would be more relevant
    37	to refer to a characteristic curve over a full range of movement for a given angular
    38	velocity. The page is internally inconsistent: it reports Vorobyev's sport-specific targets
    39	(80:20, 50:50) as what the ratio "should be," then calls any optimal ratio "meaningless"
    40	(both PDF p. 244, printed p. 233). (PDF pp. 244-245, printed pp. 233-234, "4.2.6.2
    41	Limitations of the Isokinetic Method," "Recommended Strength Ratios," Fig 4.16.)
    42	
    43	**Why it works** — The authors give no physiological mechanism for why the ratio shifts with
    44	sport, joint angle or velocity. Their argument is empirical: the figure shows the ratio
    45	changing across angle and velocity, so a single number cannot describe it. Inference: a
    46	single-number ratio averages over torque variation that differs between the extensors and
    47	flexors across the range and across contraction speed.
    48	
    49	**When to apply** — Use this as a caution against citing a single flexor/extensor or
    50	left/right strength-ratio target (e.g. "60:40 quad:hamstring," "no more than 10% L/R
    51	difference") as universally optimal or diagnostic of injury risk. If a ratio must be used,
    52	specify the joint angle, the angle convention and the angular velocity it was measured at,
    53	and prefer a full-range characteristic curve over a single number when data allow, per the
    54	authors.
    55	
    56	Eric's baseline: NordBord hamstring testing is "explicitly retained for smaller, targeted
    57	return-to-play groups paired with joint-specific isometric testing (ForceFrame-style)"
    58	(`method-baseline.md`, Rehab and return to play); the corpus sets no flexor/extensor ratio
    59	target.
    60	
    61	Inference: this section bears on how such ratio data are read for return-to-play decisions.
    62	
    63	**When NOT to apply** — Fig 4.16 is uncited Cybex data at 36, 108 and 180 degrees/second on
    64	an unspecified population; Vorobyev (1978) supplies the sport-specific ratios and Stephens &
    65	Reid (1988) the gravity-correction critique. The specific ratio-versus-angle values should
    66	not be treated as universal constants for every athlete or joint. Inference: the figure's
    67	convention (90 degrees = full extension) is the reverse of the common 0 degrees = extension
    68	convention, so its angles cannot be compared directly with most modern reports. Do
    69	not use this entry to conclude ratio testing is worthless; the claim is that a single
    70	"optimal ratio" number is misleading, not that ratio measurement itself carries no
    71	information (see [[claim--natural-asymmetry-caution-against-isokinetic-symmetry-correction]]
    72	for the related but distinct caution about using isokinetic ratios to drive "correction").
    73	Inference: the Vorobyev targets were measured at a named point (greatest knee-extension
    74	torque), which partly meets the authors' angle objection but not their velocity objection.
    75	
    76	**Example** — Inference: a rehabilitation report citing "this athlete's quad:hamstring ratio
    77	is below the healthy 60:40 standard" should specify the joint angle and test velocity the
    78	ratio was measured at, since per Fig 4.16 the same limb could show a ratio above 60:40 at
    79	one angle/velocity and at or below it at another.
    80	
    81	**Related** — [[claim--natural-asymmetry-caution-against-isokinetic-symmetry-correction]]
    82	(Ch3.3.4.4, a related caution against using isokinetic ratios to "correct" asymmetry),
    83	[[heuristic--isokinetic-testing-limitations-for-functional-sport-specificity]],
    84	[[claim--pursuing-perfect-bilateral-symmetry-can-be-counterproductive]].

    14	# No Machine Can Be Truly Isokinetic: Isokinetic Tests Miss the Acceleration Phases Where the Authors Say Most Injuries Occur, and the Elastic-Energy Contribution of Natural Movement
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors call the assumption that isokinetic dynamometers are
    17	"accurately constant angular velocity devices" a "faulty basic assumption": the laws of
    18	physics make it impossible, since a body at rest must accelerate to reach a terminal
    19	velocity, sustain it, then decelerate back to rest, meaning every movement (isokinetic or
    20	otherwise) has periods of positive or negative acceleration; producing entirely isokinetic
    21	conditions throughout would require infinite acceleration, which "contradicts the laws of
    22	science." Manufacturers can only minimise, never eliminate, these non-isokinetic transition
    23	phases. The authors make two separate points about why this matters. (a) They assert, citing
    24	no source, that "most injuries occur during these transition phases when a limb is changing
    25	its velocity or tension is changing in the musculotendinous system," and that isokinetic
    26	testing "can reveal no useful information about what is happening to the muscles then." (b)
    27	Separately, "a most serious problem is that isokinetic testing can give no information on
    28	the major contribution played by the storage and release of elastic energy in the soft
    29	tissues during dynamic, natural actions such as walking, running, jumping or throwing." The
    30	authors' summary: "isokinetic testing or training is non-functional, except possibly for
    31	swimmers whose movements are approximately isokinetic over part of their range."
    32	Biomechanical analysis of force-time and rate-of-force-development curves for resisted free
    33	movement confirms distinct qualities (maximal strength, starting strength, acceleration
    34	strength, explosive strength, see Fig 2.13), and the curves obtained isokinetically are "so
    35	radically different from their free movement equivalents that they are of minimal value
    36	either for functional analysis or specific neuromuscular conditioning." (PDF p. 244, printed
    37	p. 233, "4.2.6.2 Limitations of the Isokinetic Method," "Fundamental Biomechanics of
    38	Isokinetic Devices.")
    39	
    40	**Why it works** — The physics is Newtonian: any object moving from rest, sustaining a
    41	velocity, and returning to rest must accelerate and decelerate, and true isokinetic motion
    42	throughout would demand infinite acceleration at the start and end. The two consequences are
    43	separate claims: (a) most injuries, the authors assert without citation, occur in
    44	transition phases the device cannot measure; (b) separately, isokinetic testing captures
    45	none of the elastic-energy storage and release of natural actions, which is a property of
    46	natural movement, not of the device's transition phases.
    47	
    48	**When to apply** — Use this as the physics-level foundation for treating isokinetic test or
    49	training data as descriptive of a narrow, artificial condition (the device's controlled
    50	constant-velocity phase) rather than as a general index of an athlete's dynamic capability.
    51	Inference: this reinforces the terminology point already in this library (see
    52	[[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]]) that commercial "isokinetic" devices are
    53	more accurately "quasi-isokinetic."
    54	
    55	**When NOT to apply** — The authors' own exception is swimming, where movement is
    56	"approximately isokinetic over part of their range," making isokinetic testing/training
    57	comparatively more relevant there than for running, jumping, throwing or lifting. Do not read
    58	this entry as claiming isokinetic devices provide zero useful information; the claims are
    59	narrower: (a) per the authors' uncited assertion, they miss the transition
    60	(acceleration/deceleration) phases where most injuries occur; (b) separately, they capture
    61	none of the elastic-energy contribution of natural actions. The sweeping "non-functional"
    62	verdict also sits against the book's own use of isokinetic data elsewhere (Fig 4.16 Cybex
    63	ratio curves, PDF p. 245, printed p. 234; Komi & Buskirk's isokinetic-dynamometer training
    64	study, PDF p. 241, printed p. 230); see
    65	[[heuristic--isokinetic-testing-limitations-for-functional-sport-specificity]] for why that
    66	sibling is contested.
    67	
    68	**Example** — Inference: a hamstring isokinetic strength test at a fixed angular velocity
    69	(e.g. 60 degrees/second) can characterise force output during that constant-velocity phase,
    70	but per this claim it cannot characterise what happens during the initial acceleration into
    71	that velocity or the deceleration out of it. The book does not name the sprinting hamstring
    72	or say where its injury risk concentrates.
    73	
    74	**Related** — [[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]] (Ch1, "isokinetic" as a
    75	misleading term for the same physical reason given here),
    76	[[heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength]] (Ch2),
    77	[[heuristic--isokinetic-testing-limitations-for-functional-sport-specificity]],
    78	[[framework--isokinetic-method-claimed-advantages-and-mechanism]].

    13	
    14	# Three Grounds (Anatomy, Physiology, Specificity) on Which Isokinetic Testing and Training Misrepresent Functional Sport Movement
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Building on the physics limitation already covered (see
    17	[[claim--isokinetic-devices-cannot-be-truly-isokinetic-physics-limitation]]), the authors
    18	give a detailed, itemised critique of relying on isokinetic dynamometers (e.g. Cybex,
    19	Orthotron) for testing and rehabilitation. (1) **Functional anatomy**: nearby-joint angle
    20	changes the torque produced about the joint in question (e.g. hip angle changes knee
    21	extension torque, important to weightlifters, jumpers and sprinters), but seated isokinetic
    22	testing typically immobilises the hips with straps, creating "non-functional conditions" that
    23	measure torque specific to the seated posture, not any actual sporting posture; testing is
    24	also rarely combined with EMG or myotonometry to identify which specific muscles (e.g.
    25	vastus medialis vs lateralis, affected by lateral/medial rotation) actually contribute to the
    26	measured torque, and open-chain testing (foot not contacting the ground) alters how popliteus
    27	and gastrocnemius contribute to knee flexion, both important in running, lifting and jumping;
    28	seated testing also ignores medial rotation contributions (sartorius, gracilis,
    29	semimembranosus, semitendinosus) and lateral rotation (biceps femoris). (2) **Muscle
    30	physiology**: most sporting actions begin from intense isometric or explosive-isometric
    31	contraction with stored tendon elastic energy, a state isokinetic testing/training involves
    32	only insignificantly; the myotatic stretch reflex (stronger with faster stretch) is central
    33	to explosive running, jumping, lifting and throwing but cannot be recruited under isokinetic
    34	conditions, and "the elimination of most of these reflex actions by isokinetic apparatus
    35	ensures that isokinetic testing and training is only of value during the early general
    36	conditioning or rehabilitation phase, but of no real significance during the specific
    37	preparation or competitive phases of sports training" (PDF p. 246, printed p. 235); agonist-antagonist cocontraction and ballistic (preprogrammed,
    38	feedback-independent) movement are both common in sport but isokinetic conditions permit
    39	neither; torque under isokinetic conditions is usually much lower than isometric torque at
    40	the same joint angle, contradicting the claim (Thistle et al, 1967) that isokinetics keeps
    41	tension maximal throughout; reciprocal inhibition (antagonist pre-contraction raising
    42	agonist force, used in PNF and common in plyometric rebounding) is not permitted by most
    43	isokinetic devices; and bilateral versus unilateral force-production patterns differ, so
    44	isokinetic limb-to-limb comparisons "can be very misleading," since a dominant limb's
    45	superiority is often one of skill, not strength (e.g. it is common, but the authors imply
    46	misguided, for therapists to isokinetically strengthen a footballer's weaker kicking limb
    47	when the support leg's job is producing stabilising strength). (3) **Specificity**:
    48	indiscriminate isokinetic use neglects the specificity principle across ten dimensions (type
    49	of muscle contraction, movement pattern, region of movement, velocity of movement, force of
    50	contraction, muscle fibre recruitment, metabolism, biochemical adaptation, flexibility,
    51	fatigue), citing Sale and McDougall (1981) that strength gains are apparent only when
    52	measured during the same movement type used in training; this specificity concern
    53	"culminated" in Verkhoshansky's principle of dynamic correspondence (see 4.3). On this
    54	basis, isokinetic training and measurement are "so functionally different from normal
    55	sporting movement as to be relatively useless for giving any information that is accurately
    56	applicable to the competitive athlete" (PDF p. 247, printed p. 236). The authors' concluding analogy: relying on a single isokinetic model
    57	to assess strength and endurance is "tantamount to permanently accepting" the early
    58	planetary-electron atomic model just because it is easy to work with; a more versatile,
    59	"kinesiological polygraph" combining high-speed video, EMG, myotensiometers, accelerometers
    60	and force plates is what multi-faceted human movement actually demands, and sporting
    61	performance itself remains the ultimate test of any training or rehabilitation regime. The
    62	authors also name the APRE system (based on DeLorme's original work, see 5.2.2) as an
    63	inexpensive, effective alternative to isokinetics, and point to Osternig (1986) for a
    64	detailed review of isokinetic strengths and weaknesses. (PDF pp. 244-247, printed pp.
    65	233-236, "4.2.6.2 Limitations of the Isokinetic Method," "Functional Anatomy," "Muscle
    66	Physiology," "The Importance of Specificity," "Concluding Remarks.")
    67	
    68	**Why it works** — Each of the itemised points above carries its own stated mechanism (listed
    69	inline): joint-coupling effects on torque, missing EMG/myotonometry verification, absent
    70	elastic-energy and stretch-reflex contribution, absent cocontraction/ballistic patterning,
    71	absent reciprocal inhibition, and bilateral-versus-unilateral force-pattern differences. The
    72	authors' unifying argument is that isokinetic devices remove or distort each of these
    73	naturally-occurring features of dynamic sport movement, so a test built on removing them
    74	cannot validly characterise performance that depends on them.
    75	
    76	**When to apply** — Use this itemised list as a detailed checklist when deciding whether a
    77	specific isokinetic finding (a strength deficit, an asymmetry, a rehabilitation
    78	"clearance" threshold) should influence a functional/sport-specific training or return-to-play
    79	decision: check whether the isokinetic condition tested (seated, seat-strapped, single-joint,
    80	no elastic energy, no stretch reflex, no cocontraction, no reciprocal inhibition, bilateral
    81	comparison) resembles the sporting movement in question closely enough for the finding to
    82	transfer. Per the authors, confine isokinetic work to early general conditioning or
    83	rehabilitation (PDF p. 246, printed p. 235). This heuristic substantially extends, with a Ch4-specific itemised mechanism list,
    84	the caution already recorded in
    85	[[heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength]] (Ch2, citing
    86	the book's own "futile" statement about isometric/isokinetic dynamometers); a reciprocal link
    87	from that entry to this one is recommended.
    88	
    89	**When NOT to apply** — Marked contested, inheriting the same internal tension already
    90	recorded in [[heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength]]:
    91	the book itself relies on isokinetic and isometric dynamometer data elsewhere (e.g. the
    92	Fig 4.16 Cybex ratio curves, PDF p. 245, printed p. 234, in
    93	[[heuristic--isokinetic-strength-ratios-vary-by-angle-and-velocity]]; Komi & Buskirk's
    94	isokinetic-dynamometer training study, PDF p. 241, printed p. 230; Figs 2.8-2.9 isokinetic
    95	vs isometric torque, cited on PDF p. 243, printed p. 232 and PDF p. 246, printed p. 235) to
    96	establish real findings, without fully reconciling that reliance with this section's
    97	sweeping "non-functional" critique. Do not read this entry as claiming isokinetic devices have zero diagnostic value
    98	(the authors themselves call them "useful for measuring isokinetic actions... in two
    99	dimensions"); the claim is that extrapolating isokinetic results to full sporting movement
   100	"is scientifically unacceptable and misleading."
   101	
   102	**Example** — Inference: a therapist isokinetically strengthening a footballer's weaker
   103	kicking (non-support) leg, per the authors' own named example, may be targeting the wrong
   104	quality if the support leg's job (stabilising strength under bilateral/unilateral,
   105	cocontractive demand) is actually more functionally relevant to on-field performance than the
   106	kicking leg's isolated, isokinetically-measured torque.
   107	
   108	**Related** — [[heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength]]
   109	(Ch2, the entry this one substantially extends with Ch4-specific mechanisms; reciprocal link
   110	recommended), [[claim--isokinetic-devices-cannot-be-truly-isokinetic-physics-limitation]],
   111	[[heuristic--isokinetic-strength-ratios-vary-by-angle-and-velocity]],
   112	[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Ch1, the ten-dimension specificity
   113	principle this section applies to isokinetics specifically).

    14	# The Static-Dynamic Method: Pairing a Brief Isometric Hold With Explosive Concentric Work in One Repetition
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The static-dynamic method sequentially combines isometric and dynamic
    17	(auxotonic) muscular activity within one exercise. Two variants are given as experimentally
    18	effective: (1) a 2-3 second isometric contraction at 80% of maximum, immediately followed by
    19	explosive concentric dynamic work with a 30%-of-maximum load; (2) a constant load of 75-80%
    20	of maximum used for both the isometric and dynamic components, illustrated with a half-squat
    21	example: the athlete sinks into a half-squat with a barbell on the shoulders, holds that
    22	position for 2 seconds, then jumps upward with maximal acceleration before landing carefully
    23	and repeating. Experimentally, variant (1) proved better than dynamic exercise alone for
    24	developing speed-strength. For variant (2) the source reads: "The second variant has an
    25	equivalent affect on the improvement of speed-strength and absolute strength (Dobrovolsky,
    26	1972, 1973)." The comparator is unclear: this may mean an equal effect on both qualities,
    27	or an effect equivalent to dynamic exercise; the text does not say. (PDF p. 247, printed p.
    28	236, "4.2.6.3 Static-Dynamic Methods.")
    29	
    30	**Why it works** — No specific mechanism is given for why pairing a brief isometric hold with
    31	subsequent explosive concentric work outperforms dynamic-only training for speed-strength in
    32	variant (1); Inference: this is plausibly related to the same explosive-isometric-to-concentric
    33	transition mechanism already described for depth jumps and the shock method (see
    34	[[framework--kinetic-energy-stimulation-mechanical-basis-and-advantages]] and
    35	[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]), where the isometric phase primes the
    36	neuromuscular system immediately before the explosive concentric effort, though the authors
    37	do not state this connection explicitly for the static-dynamic method here.
    38	
    39	**When to apply** — Use variant (1) (2-3s isometric hold at 80% max, then explosive
    40	concentric at 30% max) when the specific goal is speed-strength development, per the cited
    41	finding that it outperformed dynamic-only training for that quality. Use variant (2) (a
    42	half-squat hold then jump at 75-80% max) when both speed-strength and absolute strength are
    43	targets, per the source's statement that it affects both. Inference: if the sentence means
    44	its effect only equals dynamic exercise, its value would lie mainly in variety or in the
    45	loaded-jump pattern itself; the text does not settle which reading is meant.
    46	
    47	**When NOT to apply** — This is a single-source finding (Dobrovolsky, 1972, 1973) without
    48	reported sample size, training-age context, or long-term outcome data beyond the immediate
    49	comparison to dynamic-only training; treat the specific load percentages (80%/30%, 75-80%)
    50	as the cited protocol's own parameters, not universally optimal figures. Variant (2)'s
    51	half-squat-and-jump with load requires careful technique and landing control, which this
    52	passage does not itself detail as a safety protocol.
    53	
    54	**Example** — The book's own example is the half-squat-hold-then-jump description above
    55	(variant 2); no further invented example is added here.
    56	
    57	**Related** — [[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]],
    58	[[framework--kinetic-energy-stimulation-mechanical-basis-and-advantages]],
    59	[[heuristic--choice-of-muscle-training-regime-favor-combination]] (this section's companion
    60	entry, which places static-dynamic training within the broader argument for combining
    61	regimes).
