15	    14	# No Single Training Regime Is "Most Effective": The Authors Judge Combining Regimes the Most Rational Approach
16	    15	
17	    16	**What it is** — Asked which of the chapter's several muscular-work regimes (concentric,
18	    17	eccentric, isometric, isokinetic, static-dynamic, and combinations) is most effective, the
19	    18	authors argue a categorical answer is not possible, for three reasons: (1) comprehensive
20	    19	research comparing all regimes has not been conducted; one study comparing eccentric,
21	    20	concentric, isometric and combined regimes found some advantage of concentric over eccentric
22	    21	and isometric methods individually, but the combined-regime method showed "a clear
23	    22	advantage" over all of them (Pletnev, 1975); (2) comparative research is inherently difficult
24	    23	because training loads are hard to equate across different regimes; (3) it is
25	    24	"inappropriate to raise the question of the absolute effectiveness of any specific regime,"
26	    25	since each regime can be the most effective depending on the training situation, stage of
27	    26	the annual cycle, athlete level, the primary regime of muscular work demanded by the specific
28	    27	sport exercise, and the specific strength quality being trained. The authors' overall
29	    28	conclusion, stated with "reasonable certainty": the most rational way to enhance special
30	    29	strength preparation is to combine the various regimes of muscular work, a conclusion
31	    30	corroborated by multiple studies (Vorobyev, 1966; Andrianov & Vorobyev, 1969; Kuznetsov,
32	    31	1970; Verkhoshansky, 1970, 1972; Slobodyan, 1972; Tatyan, 1974; Pletnev, 1975; Khodykin,
33	    32	1975; Savin, 1974). Such a combination should be selected by considering its cumulative
34	    33	effect (see [[framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy]]) and
35	    34	its correspondence to the specific conditions of the sport. (PDF pp. 247-248, printed pp.
36	    35	236-237, "4.2.6.4 Choice of Muscle Training Regimes.") The authors earlier call any
37	    36	definitive statement about regimes "or combination of regimes" premature, because the
38	    37	comparative studies "are not very numerous," are "carried out with athletes of low
39	    38	qualification," and show "a tendency to deliberately favour that method which is
40	    39	fashionable" (PDF p. 242, printed p. 231); the "reasonable certainty" conclusion (PDF p.
41	    40	248, printed p. 237) is not reconciled with that. Only Pletnev (1975) is reported as a
42	    41	direct comparison ("a clear advantage"); the other citations are said to corroborate that
43	    42	combination is "the most rational means."
44	    43	
45	    44	**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for why combining regimes should be more
46	    45	effective than any one regime alone; Inference: a plausible explanation, not stated in the text, is that different
47	    46	regimes stress different components of the strength system (contractile tissue,
48	    47	elastic/connective tissue, neural drive, fibre-type-specific adaptation) somewhat
49	    48	independently, so combining them addresses more of the system than repeatedly stressing only
50	    49	one component.
51	    50	
52	    51	**When to apply** — Use this heuristic to resist single-method dogma ("isokinetics is best,"
53	    52	"only free weights work," "eccentric training is superior") when programming special
54	    53	strength training; per this section, the authors' own multi-study conclusion favours
55	    54	deliberately combining regimes (concentric, eccentric, isometric, static-dynamic,
56	    55	resistance, kinetic-energy) rather than committing to one, selected for cumulative effect
57	    56	and sport-specific correspondence.
58	    57	
59	    58	**When NOT to apply** — Contested because the authors call any definitive statement about
60	    59	"any regime or combination of regimes" premature (PDF p. 242, printed p. 231), citing
61	    60	low-qualification samples and fashion bias, then state the combination conclusion with
62	    61	"reasonable certainty" (PDF p. 248, printed p. 237). The corroborating citations (Vorobyev
63	    62	1966 through Savin 1974) give no individual effect sizes or protocols in this passage; treat "combining regimes is
64	    63	most rational" as the authors' summary conclusion across a body of era-specific Soviet sport
65	    64	science, not a single quantified finding. This heuristic does not specify which combination,
66	    65	in what proportion, or in what sequence to use for a given sport or athlete; it establishes
67	    66	only the authors' general principle that combining regimes is the most rational means,
68	    67	leaving the specific combination as a separate programming decision guided by cumulative-effect and
69	    68	dynamic-correspondence principles (see 4.3).
70	    69	
71	    70	**Example** — Inference: a strength block that mixes free-weight concentric-emphasis lifts,
72	    71	occasional isometric holds at sticking points, and periodic eccentric-emphasis work (rather
73	    72	than committing the whole block to one regime) is applying this heuristic directly; the
74	    73	specific mixture and sequencing would still need to be chosen using the cumulative-effect and
75	    74	sport-specificity criteria the authors name.
76	    75	
77	    76	**Related** — [[claim--static-dynamic-combined-isometric-concentric-method]],
78	    77	[[framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy]],
79	    78	[[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]] (Ch4.1, the related point that
80	    79	order and combination, not just choice of regime, change training outcomes).

95	    14	# Two Classes of Training Machine: Functional Resistance (Sport-Specific Pattern) vs Non-Functional Resistance (General Pattern)
96	    15	
97	    16	**What it is** — The authors distinguish two classes of strength machine: functional
98	    17	resistance (FR) machines, whose purpose is offering resistance in sport-specific movement
99	    18	patterns, and non-functional resistance (NFR) machines, whose sole purpose is offering
100	    19	general resistance in non-sport-specific patterns. They call this distinction vital, because
101	    20	Western "state-of-the-art" fitness centres are usually equipped almost entirely with NFR
102	    21	machines, so much so that adequate free weights or FR machines can be hard to find in them.
103	    22	"While the use of NFR machines may be adequate for the casual fitness client, it can be
104	    23	profoundly counterproductive for sport specific trainees if used in place of FR machines or
105	    24	free weights" (PDF p. 248, printed p. 237). They quote Zatsiorsky (1995) directly: "the important limitation of many strength training
106	    25	machines is that they are designed to train muscles, not movement. Because of this, they are
107	    26	not the most important training tool for athletes." FR devices are "supposed to imitate or
108	    27	train certain elements of an athletic exercise in order to provide the necessary specific
109	    28	loads in the different regimes of muscular work (Ratov, 1976)," and are reported effective for aspects of special strength training across many athlete types
110	    29	(Semenov, 1970; Petrova & Gorbunov, 1970; Verkhoshansky, 1970; Deniskin & Kuznetsov, 1972;
111	    30	Dobrovolski, 1972, 1973; Kuznetsov & Aiunts, 1974; Savin, 1974), because they permit strict
112	    31	regulation of load and the movement's spatial characteristics, letting a coach use the
113	    32	appropriate regime of muscular work and programme force-over-time characteristics while
114	    33	reproducing stereotypical training movements economically. The authors' example of a
115	    34	simple, cheap, versatile FR device is the "hi-lo" pulley machine, whose rope-attached
116	    35	handles (unlike fixed bars and pivots on most NFR machines) allow sport-specific movement
117	    36	patterns of great complexity; they estimate a circuit of just four pulley machines can
118	    37	provide training capacity that would otherwise need more than 40 "state of the art" NFR
119	    38	machines, and that a circuit of 10 pulley machines plus a few benches, jumping boards, bars,
120	    39	mats and wall-bars can serve more clients with a larger range of exercises than 100
121	    40	specialised machines, at under 15% of the cost. "Even then, the NFR machine-only facility
122	    41	would provide inferior multi-dimensional conditioning of the body" (PDF p. 249, printed p.
123	    42	238). A major FR advantage is visual/computerised feedback on movement
124	    43	quality and quantity for controlling training. The authors caution that simulating a sport
125	    44	movement against heavy machine loads can still significantly alter the movement's
126	    45	force-time characteristics and disrupt its neuromuscular programme; functionality is not
127	    46	automatic from an exercise merely resembling a sport action, but depends on the functional
128	    47	objective for which the exercise is used and how it is integrated into the long-term
129	    48	conditioning programme. (PDF pp. 248-249, printed pp. 237-238, "4.2.7 The Use of Training
130	    49	Machines," "4.2.7.1 Functional Resistance Machines.")
131	    50	
132	    51	**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is specificity: FR machines let a coach control load
133	    52	and the spatial/temporal pattern of the movement together, closer to the actual sport
134	    53	action, while still gaining measurement feedback; NFR machines use "fixed bars and pivots"
135	    54	(PDF p. 248, printed p. 237) in patterns that need not resemble any sport movement, training
136	    55	"muscles, not movement" per the quoted Zatsiorsky line.
137	    56	
138	    57	**When to apply** — Use this framework to audit a training facility or programme for FR
139	    58	versus NFR balance, per the authors' concern that Western commercial gyms over-provide NFR
140	    59	equipment. Prefer FR devices (pulley systems, cable machines with free movement paths,
141	    60	purpose-built sport-simulation devices) when the training goal requires reproducing a
142	    61	sport-specific spatial/temporal pattern with measurable load control.
143	    62	
144	    63	**When NOT to apply** — The authors' own caution applies: using any machine, FR or NFR, to
145	    64	simulate a sporting movement against heavy load can still disrupt the movement's natural
146	    65	force-time characteristics and neuromuscular programming; resemblance to a sport action does
147	    66	not automatically make an exercise "functional." See
148	    67	[[heuristic--nfr-machine-limitations-safety-and-appropriate-use]] for when NFR machines
149	    68	remain appropriate despite this section's general preference for FR devices and free
150	    69	weights.
151	    70	
152	    71	**Example** — The book's own example is the "hi-lo" pulley machine and the four-pulley
153	    72	versus forty-NFR-machine cost/capacity comparison described above; no further invented
154	    73	example is added here.
155	    74	
156	    75	**Related** — [[heuristic--nfr-machine-limitations-safety-and-appropriate-use]],
157	    76	[[claim--nfr-machine-marketing-claims-examined]].

172	    14	# NFR Machines: Real Limitations on Proprioception and Joint Loading, but Not Actually Safer Than Free Weights
173	    15	
174	    16	**What it is** — Non-functional resistance (NFR) machines can play a useful supplementary
175	    17	role but generally cannot match free weights and FR machines for multi-dimensional,
176	    18	full-range neuromuscular and musculoskeletal training. Many NFR machines force the user to
177	    19	sit or lie, minimising training effect on major stabilising muscles and involving fewer
178	    20	joints through fewer degrees of freedom; while potentially valuable early in rehabilitation,
179	    21	this is an incomplete way of training the body for functional development, since machines
180	    22	that stabilise major body regions and limit the number of moving joints diminish the
181	    23	capacity to train balance, coordination and proprioception. The authors give a worked
182	    24	example: a free-standing squat involves three joints (hip, knee, ankle), while a seated knee
183	    25	extension machine constrains the body to one joint (knee) to exercise the quadriceps, so for
184	    26	a comparable exercise intensity over the same range of motion, the machine increases
185	    27	shearing force across the knee; the squat additionally exercises the thigh adductors, spinal
186	    28	erectors and other stabilisers, and enhances balance and (via longitudinal compressive
187	    29	loading) bone density. Seated exercise also always imposes a greater lumbar-disc load than
188	    30	equivalent standing exercise: maintaining a neutral spinal curve while seated raises lumbar
189	    31	disc pressure by about 40% (Chaffin & Andersson, 1984); allowing the back to flex forward can
190	    32	raise this by as much as 90%; a well-designed lumbar-supporting backrest lowers the stress
191	    33	but lumbar disc pressure can still run about 75% higher than standing; stress increases
192	    34	further against resistance, especially with jerky movements, and seated positions cannot
193	    35	absorb shock loading via knee/hip/ankle flexion the way standing can. On safety
194	    36	specifically, the authors reject the common claim that NFR machines are much safer than free
195	    37	weights, citing no source for the comparison: injuries to the back and knees (leg press, hack-squat, hip-sled), shoulders and
196	    38	chest (bench press, pec-deck), elbow (bicep curl machines) and back (back-extension
197	    39	machines) are "just as common with machines as with free weights," and many machines (pec
198	    40	deck, bench press, leg press, calf raise, seated press) force the movement to start from the
199	    41	biomechanically least efficient, most harmful position for the relevant joint; spotters are
200	    42	just as necessary for machines as for free weights, and faulty technique is equally dangerous
201	    43	with either. Some machines (leg extension, lat pulley, seated bicep curl) genuinely are safer
202	    44	for someone with back weakness or injury, and can help in early rehabilitation, but
203	    45	"continual avoidance of stress to the regions involved eventually leads to their progressive
204	    46	weakening" if relied on long-term. NFR machines remain useful for isolating specific muscle
205	    47	groups (bodybuilding-style supplementary training) or for the primary stages of injury
206	    48	rehabilitation, but not as an all-round conditioning replacement for free weights and FR
207	    49	devices; one exception noted is the lat-pulley machine, generally more suitable and safer
208	    50	than the free-weight equivalent (bent-over rowing) for training latissimus dorsi. (PDF pp.
209	    51	249-250, printed pp. 238-239, "4.2.7.2 Non-Functional Resistance Machines," "4.2.7.4 The
210	    52	Training Safety of Machines.")
211	    53	
212	    54	**Why it works** — The proprioception/stability mechanism is that fixing more joints and
213	    55	supporting more of the body's weight through the machine itself removes the balance,
214	    56	coordination and multi-joint stabilisation demand that free, standing exercise imposes. The
215	    57	single-joint-versus-multi-joint mechanism is straightforward: constraining a comparable
216	    58	training stimulus to fewer joints concentrates the same relative stress onto those joints'
217	    59	structures (illustrated by the squat-versus-knee-extension shearing-force example). The
218	    60	lumbar-disc mechanism is postural: seated positions load the discs differently than standing,
219	    61	and cannot use lower-body joint flexion to absorb shock the way standing positions can.
220	    62	
221	    63	**When to apply** — Use NFR machines for early-stage rehabilitation of a specific injured
222	    64	joint or muscle group, for supplementary bodybuilding-style isolation work, or when back
223	    65	weakness/injury makes a machine (leg extension, lat pulley, seated bicep curl) genuinely
224	    66	safer than the free-weight equivalent.
225	    67	
226	    68	Eric's baseline: per the protocol documents (tagged Inferred in `method-baseline.md`, "Force
227	    69	plate and neuromuscular monitoring"), the department runs "the standard CMJ family" on
228	    70	ForceDecks, and "the isometric seated calf raise is run on the ForceDecks 'Mid-Thigh Pull'
229	    71	setting: 90-degree ankle/knee position."
230	    72	
231	    73	Inference: the seated calf raise is a fixed-angle isometric test, not NFR machine training,
232	    74	so this section's critique of seated machines does not bear on it directly.
233	    75	
234	    76	**When NOT to apply** — Do not rely on NFR machines long-term as a substitute for free
235	    77	weights or FR devices in a healthy, competitive athlete's programme, since progressive
236	    78	avoidance of stress to a region "eventually leads to... progressive weakening." Do not
237	    79	assume NFR machines are inherently safer than free weights; per the authors' uncited
238	    80	comparison (PDF p. 250, printed p. 239), injuries are "just as common with machines as with
239	    81	free weights," and spotting and technique matter with both. The lumbar-disc figures (40%,
240	    82	90%, 75%) come from one cited source, Chaffin & Andersson (1984), for the claim that seated
241	    83	exercise "always" loads the discs more than standing (PDF pp. 249-250, printed pp.
242	    84	238-239); the text cites only this one source, and this library holds no modern source on
243	    85	the point, so treat "always" as the authors' claim, not a checked finding.
244	    86	
245	    87	**Example** — Inference: using a seated knee-extension machine during the first two weeks
246	    88	after a knee injury (early rehabilitation, single-joint control) while progressing toward a
247	    89	free-standing squat as tolerance improves applies this heuristic's appropriate-use window; continuing
248	    90	to rely on the knee-extension machine as the primary quadriceps exercise once the athlete
249	    91	returns to full training would not, per the "progressive weakening" caution above.
250	    92	
251	    93	**Related** — [[framework--functional-vs-nonfunctional-resistance-machines]],
252	    94	[[claim--nfr-machine-marketing-claims-examined]].

267	    14	# The Authors Argue Variable-Resistance Machines' Core Marketing Premise Is a Physics Error, and That NFR Machines Need Many More Units to Match Free Weights
268	    15	
269	    16	**What it is** — Many machine manufacturers design variable-resistance machines to match a
270	    17	joint's natural torque curve, claiming superiority over free weights and other resistance
271	    18	devices on this basis. The authors identify a flawed premise behind this claim: manufacturers
272	    19	imply a free weight's resistance stays constant throughout a lift (e.g. a 50 kg biceps curl
273	    20	is presented as exerting a constant 50 kg / about 490 Newton force from start to finish). A
274	    21	simple application of Newton's Second Law (force proportional to acceleration) shows this is
275	    22	false: the resistance a free weight offers changes with acceleration from rest and at any
276	    23	point the trainee speeds up or slows down, "as can easily be demonstrated by force plate,
277	    24	cable tensiometer or high speed video analysis"; a skilled trainee already uses proprioception
278	    25	to perceive these changes and adjust resistance and direction more efficiently, the authors
279	    26	argue, than current machines can. Separately, on training efficiency, the authors give
280	    27	several specific machine-count comparisons: it takes at least 12 NFR machines to
281	    28	approximately equal the training effect of the clean-and-push-press, at least 4 to rival the
282	    29	free-standing squat, more than 3 to equal the standing dumbbell curl, and at least 5 to
283	    30	rival the flexed-knee deadlift; in total, more than 24 NFR machines are required to match the
284	    31	combined training effect of just four free-weight exercises (clean-and-push-press, squat,
285	    32	deadlift, biceps curl), at roughly 40 times the combined cost of the equivalent free weights
286	    33	and racks, with NFR machines also carrying higher maintenance costs and more frequent
287	    34	breakdowns in a well-used gymnasium than "virtually indestructible" free weights. (PDF pp.
288	    35	250-251, printed pp. 239-240, "4.2.7.3 Machines and the Variable Resistance Philosophy,"
289	    36	"4.2.7.5 The Efficiency of Machine Training.")
290	    37	
291	    38	**Why it works** — For the variable-resistance critique, the mechanism is Newtonian: force
292	    39	equals mass times acceleration, so any free weight's true resistance already varies with the
293	    40	trainee's own acceleration/deceleration throughout the lift, contradicting the marketing
294	    41	premise that free weights offer constant resistance needing a machine's correction. The
295	    42	authors give no mechanism for the machine counts. Inference: a compound free-weight exercise
296	    43	recruits and trains many more muscle groups, movement patterns and stabilising demands
297	    44	simultaneously than any single-joint NFR machine, so many NFR machines are needed in
298	    45	combination to approach the same total training stimulus.
299	    46	
300	    47	**When to apply** — Use the Newtonian-mechanics point to counter the specific marketing claim
301	    48	that free weights offer "constant" resistance (see When NOT to apply for its limit); per the
302	    49	authors, a skilled lifter's own proprioceptive control of bar speed already varies the true
303	    50	resistance throughout the lift (see also
304	    51	[[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]], Ch1). Use the machine-count/cost
305	    52	comparison when evaluating equipment-purchase decisions for a training facility: a small set
306	    53	of free-weight stations and racks may replicate the combined training effect of a much
307	    54	larger, more expensive NFR machine circuit, per this section's specific figures.
308	    55	
309	    56	**When NOT to apply** — The specific machine-count figures (12, 4, 3+, 5, 24+, roughly 40x
310	    57	cost) are the authors' own estimates for approximating specific free-weight exercises' total
311	    58	training effect with combinations of NFR machines; they do not cite a controlled study
312	    59	establishing these exact ratios, so treat them as illustrative rather than precisely
313	    60	measured. Inference: the Newtonian point shows free-weight resistance is not constant, but it
314	    61	does not show that free-weight resistance matches the joint's strength curve; the
315	    62	manufacturers' torque-angle argument (resistance varying with joint angle, which exists even
316	    63	at constant velocity) is not directly rebutted in this passage (PDF p. 250, printed p. 239).
317	    64	The authors do not argue that variable-resistance machines have zero value in this passage,
318	    65	only that their core "free weights are constant resistance" premise is incorrect. Inference:
319	    66	some variable-resistance designs may still offer useful features (feedback display, joint
320	    67	isolation for rehabilitation) independent of that specific flawed premise.
321	    68	
322	    69	**Example** — Inference: a facility manager comparing the cost of building a small free-weight
323	    70	area (barbells, plates, a rack, a platform) against an equivalent machine circuit covering
324	    71	the same major lift patterns should expect, per this section's estimates, the free-weight
325	    72	option to require far fewer total pieces of equipment and far lower combined cost.
326	    73	
327	    74	**Related** — [[framework--functional-vs-nonfunctional-resistance-machines]],
328	    75	[[heuristic--nfr-machine-limitations-safety-and-appropriate-use]],
329	    76	[[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]] (Ch1, the related point that free-weight
330	    77	resistance already varies via the lifter's own acceleration).

345	    14	# Chasing Perfect Bilateral Symmetry Is Ill-Advised: Sprinters' Push-Off and Swing Legs Are Naturally Asymmetric
346	    15	
347	    16	**What it is** — This entry fulfils the forward reference in this library's Ch3.3.4.4 entry
348	    17	(see
349	    18	[[claim--natural-asymmetry-caution-against-isokinetic-symmetry-correction]]), which deferred
350	    19	"The Concept of Symmetric Training" to this section. Asymmetry in leg length, muscle
351	    20	strength, stride length and other structural/functional features has been blamed for
352	    21	inefficient movement and injury, and imbalances in agonist/antagonist and left/right strength
353	    22	(including isokinetically-measured muscular endurance imbalances) have been singled out as
354	    23	leading causes of muscle injury. However, research the authors do not cite ("Research,
355	    24	however, has revealed", PDF p. 251, printed p. 240) found that isokinetically-measured left/right
356	    25	leg-strength or agonist/antagonist discrepancies as large as 10% do not statistically
357	    26	correlate with a major increase in muscular injuries. Because the body, its muscles, tendons
358	    27	and bones are characteristically asymmetric, attempts to force greater anthropomorphic and
359	    28	kinesiological symmetry "could exacerbate the existing problem or cause new injuries";
360	    29	assessing asymmetry properly requires both static structural measurement (leg length, spinal
361	    30	curvature) and dynamic biomechanical analysis (force distribution, movement patterns, ground
362	    31	reaction force, postural/phasic muscle EMG, movement-phase timing). Structural differences
363	    32	in muscle/tendon length, tendon and ligament attachment sites, and bone size/mass are
364	    33	"quite natural in all humans"; surgical or orthotic correction is warranted only when such
365	    34	structural differences cause serious functional movement imbalances, and even then only
366	    35	after confirming the asymmetry is primarily structural rather than a centrally-stored
367	    36	neuromuscular pattern (in which case the answer is modifying the motor skill itself, not
368	    37	correcting the body). There is "no perfect way" to execute any movement; style is the
369	    38	individualised expression of a motor skill and should be developed by observing and
370	    39	experimenting against an "ideal" model until the athlete's own central nervous programme
371	    40	fits their body, rather than enforcing one rigid technique standard. Yushkevich (1989)
372	    41	analysed leg-strength symmetry in sprinters and concluded striving for full leg symmetry is
373	    42	inappropriate: extensors of all joints of the push-off leg were generally significantly
374	    43	stronger than the swing leg's, with no consistent flexor-strength difference between legs.
375	    44	Asymmetry patterns differed by qualification level: novices showed stronger push-off-leg hip
376	    45	flexors than swing-leg; novice, Class 3 and Class 2 athletes showed stronger swing-leg knee
377	    46	flexors, while Class 1, Master and higher-qualified athletes showed stronger push-off-leg
378	    47	knee flexors; dorsiflexion was stronger in the push-off leg for all athletes except novices.
379	    48	Leg-strength asymmetry increased with sprint proficiency, peaking among Class 2 athletes,
380	    49	then diminishing again with further mastery. Good sprint times correlated more closely with
381	    50	swing-leg strength than push-off-leg strength. Yushkevich's conclusion: not only is
382	    51	symmetrical muscle strength a misguided target, but deliberately asymmetric exercise
383	    52	(running or jumping on sloping/inclined tracks, running curves in both directions, running or
384	    53	jumping in shoes with soles of different thickness, or running with unevenly-weighted legs)
385	    54	can be beneficial, since "asymmetric exercises destabilise the space-time characteristics of
386	    55	motor acts, thereby helping athletes break speed barriers." The authors close with an analogy
387	    56	to the tradition that Eastern-carpet weavers deliberately include at least one flaw, since
388	    57	"perfection is reserved for the Divine," implying similar asymmetry or imperfection may be
389	    58	desirable in human physical performance and training generally. (PDF pp. 251-252, printed pp.
390	    59	240-241, "4.2.8 The Concept of Symmetric Training.")
391	    60	
392	    61	**Why it works** — No cellular or biomechanical mechanism is given for why swing-leg strength
393	    62	predicts sprint time better than push-off-leg strength, or for why asymmetry peaks at Class 2
394	    63	then declines with further mastery; the authors report these as empirical findings from
395	    64	Yushkevich (1989) without deriving them from a stated causal model. For the general "why
396	    65	symmetry-forcing backfires" claim, the authors give no mechanism beyond the risk that forcing
397	    66	symmetry "could exacerbate the existing problem or cause new injuries" (PDF p. 251, printed
398	    67	p. 240). Inference: natural asymmetry may reflect functional specialisation (dominant-limb
399	    68	skill, individualised structure).
400	    69	
401	    70	**When to apply** — Use this claim, together with the Ch3.3.4.4 entry it completes (see
402	    71	Related), as the book's full position on symmetry testing and correction: a numeric L/R or
403	    72	agonist/antagonist discrepancy up to about 10% (isokinetically measured) is not itself
404	    73	evidence of elevated injury risk, and deliberately asymmetric training elements (uneven
405	    74	surfaces, directional bias, unevenly weighted limbs) may have a specific rationale for sprint
406	    75	athletes rather than being technique flaws to eliminate.
407	    76	
408	    77	Eric's baseline: the department's force-plate metric framework includes "optional symmetry
409	    78	metrics (L/R differences)" (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular
410	    79	monitoring," tagged "Adopted practice, framework not Eric's own", origin Hawkin Dynamics).
411	    80	
412	    81	Inference: this entry supports treating symmetry as descriptive/monitoring information
413	    82	rather than an automatic correction target.
414	    83	
415	    84	**When NOT to apply** — In Yushkevich's data asymmetry peaked at Class 2 and declined with
416	    85	higher mastery (PDF p. 251, printed p. 240), so the data do not show that more asymmetry is
417	    86	better. The Yushkevich (1989) sprinter data are single-study, era-specific findings on
418	    87	sprinters graded by sports classification (novice, Class 3 to Class 1, Master), with no
419	    88	sample size given in this passage; the specific qualification-level patterns (novice through Master) and the
420	    89	Class-2 asymmetry peak should not be assumed to generalise to other sports or populations
421	    90	without separate verification. The 10%-discrepancy-does-not-correlate-with-injury finding
422	    91	does not mean no discrepancy threshold matters; it means this specific threshold, measured
423	    92	isokinetically, was not found to correlate in the cited research. Do not read the
424	    93	"deliberately asymmetric training" recommendation as license to ignore genuine
425	    94	functional/structural imbalances that are causing injury or performance-limiting compensation
426	    95	(the authors' own scoping condition above); the recommendation applies specifically to
427	    96	sprint-specific push-off/swing-leg asymmetry, not to every kind of asymmetry.
428	    97	
429	    98	**Example** — The book's own example is the Yushkevich (1989) sprinter data described above;
430	    99	no further invented example is added here.
431	   100	
432	   101	**Related** — [[claim--natural-asymmetry-caution-against-isokinetic-symmetry-correction]]
433	   102	(Ch3.3.4.4, the entry that deferred this section to Ch4.2.8; this entry fulfils that
434	   103	cross-reference and both should carry a reciprocal link),
435	   104	[[heuristic--isokinetic-strength-ratios-vary-by-angle-and-velocity]],
436	   105	[[research-papers/bishop-2016-asymmetries-of-the-lower-limb-the-calculation-conundrum-in-strength-training-and-condition]],
437	   106	[[research-papers/callaway-2026-group-normative-data-and-arbitrary-asymmetry-thresholds-fail-to-represent-individual-playe]]
438	   107	(modern papers the Ch3 sibling links on how asymmetry data should be used).

440	     1	---
441	     2	type: library-entry
442	     3	kind: claim
443	     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
444	     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
445	     6	chapter: "4.2.9"

450	    11	created: 2026-09-27
451	    12	---
452	    13	
453	    14	# "Muscle Isolation" Is Possible Only for Small Muscle Groups at Low Intensity; Heavy or Prolonged Resistance Recruits Stabilisers Until Isolation Is Essentially Impossible
454	    15	
455	    16	**What it is** — Generations of bodybuilding-magazine authors have advocated specific
456	    17	machines, joint-fixation methods, precise limb placement and other techniques claimed to
457	    18	maximally recruit one muscle group while others stay "largely dormant." "EMG studies reveal
458	    19	that isolation of minute muscle groups is indeed possible under low intensities of loading
459	    20	(e.g. Basmajian, 1978)": low-intensity actions like eye-blinking, piano-playing or relaxed speech
460	    21	rely on precise, isolated action of specific small muscle groups. However, once a large load
461	    22	is imposed on a target muscle group by intense resistance, isolation becomes "virtually
462	    23	impossible": as soon as the load is applied, stabilising muscles engage to keep the body or
463	    24	specific joints stable while prime movers cope with the load, and if the nervous system
464	    25	signals the prime movers are inadequate, assistant movers, shunt muscles, emergency muscles
465	    26	and neutralisers may all be recruited to help. Physiotherapists using PNF sometimes impose
466	    27	maximal loading on a joint deliberately to elicit compensatory or overflow activity of
467	    28	muscles other than the prime movers. "The higher the intensity or the greater the duration
468	    29	of the exercise, the less likely is isolation of the prime mover, even if certain joints are
469	    30	restrained as on an isokinetic test machine," and "in many cases the tension developed in
470	    31	the stabilisers or assistant stabilisers will equal or exceed that of the prime movers." The
471	    32	authors' worked example: during heavy
472	    33	standing triceps push-downs on a cable machine, the abdominals, latissimus dorsi and erector
473	    34	spinae "may be as strongly contracted as the triceps," despite this being nominally a
474	    35	triceps-isolation exercise; analysis of many seated or reclining "isolation" machine
475	    36	exercises shows isolation simply does not occur with heavy loads. This is the same load-dependent
476	    37	proximal/distal recruitment shift already noted earlier in the chapter (see
477	    38	[[claim--muscle-recruitment-consistency-and-proximal-distal-shift-with-load]]), where the
478	    39	authors explicitly forward-referenced this section. This does not negate the value of
479	    40	isolation-style exercises: they can be useful in early injury rehabilitation, and the
480	    41	overflow to other muscle groups at higher loads can itself be desirable (if performed
481	    42	safely), since it simultaneously offers isometric and dynamic training to those other muscle
482	    43	groups. The authors' stated purpose for this section is to correct the "misleading concept
483	    44	of muscle isolation" still promoted by many instructors and training texts. (PDF p. 252,
484	    45	printed p. 241, "4.2.9 The Concept of Muscle Isolation.")
485	    46	
486	    47	**Why it works** — The mechanism given is neuromuscular: as load intensity or duration rises, the central
487	    48	nervous system recruits whatever additional muscle groups (stabilisers, assistant movers,
488	    49	emergency muscles, neutralisers) are needed to keep the targeted joint and the body stable
489	    50	and to complete the movement, since a single "isolated" muscle group's own capacity is
490	    51	insufficient against a heavy load; at low intensities, EMG shows isolation of minute muscle
491	    52	groups (PDF p. 252, printed p. 241).
492	    53	
493	    54	**When to apply** — Use this claim to correctly interpret what a "muscle isolation" exercise
494	    55	is actually training at a given load and duration. EMG shows isolation of minute muscle
495	    56	groups at low intensity (PDF p. 252, printed p. 241); the authors separately say isolation
496	    57	exercises can help in the early stages of injury rehabilitation. Inference: low-load rehab
497	    58	isolation work may approach isolation, but the book does not show it for limb muscles.
498	    59	Inference: this fits [[claim--irradiation-effect-raises-prime-mover-force-and-endurance]]'s
499	    60	finding that effort and tension spread between muscle groups. At hypertrophy- or
500	    61	strength-level heavy or prolonged loading, expect and potentially embrace the overflow to stabilisers and
501	    62	assistant movers as additional, simultaneous isometric/dynamic training for those muscle
502	    63	groups rather than treating it as a programming failure.
503	    64	
504	    65	**When NOT to apply** — Do not describe a heavy-load exercise (a heavy cable push-down, a
505	    66	heavy leg-extension set) as "isolating" the target muscle group in marketing, coaching cues,
506	    67	or programme design; per this claim and its EMG evidence, isolation is shown only for minute muscle
507	    68	groups at low training intensities. Do not assume the specific triceps push-down example
508	    69	generalises identically to every "isolation" exercise; the authors give it as one worked
509	    70	illustration, not a universally quantified finding across exercises.
510	    71	
511	    72	**Example** — The book's own example is the heavy triceps push-down engaging abdominals,
512	    73	latissimus dorsi and erector spinae described above; no further invented example is added
513	    74	here.
514	    75	
515	    76	**Related** — [[claim--muscle-recruitment-consistency-and-proximal-distal-shift-with-load]]
516	    77	(this chapter's own forward reference to this entry, 4.2.2),
517	    78	[[claim--irradiation-effect-raises-prime-mover-force-and-endurance]] (Ch3, a related finding
518	    79	on how tension in one muscle group affects others).

    13	
    14	# No Single Training Regime Is "Most Effective": The Authors Judge Combining Regimes the Most Rational Approach
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Asked which of the chapter's several muscular-work regimes (concentric,
    17	eccentric, isometric, isokinetic, static-dynamic, and combinations) is most effective, the
    18	authors argue a categorical answer is not possible, for three reasons: (1) comprehensive
    19	research comparing all regimes has not been conducted; one study comparing eccentric,
    20	concentric, isometric and combined regimes found some advantage of concentric over eccentric
    21	and isometric methods individually, but the combined-regime method showed "a clear
    22	advantage" over all of them (Pletnev, 1975); (2) comparative research is inherently difficult
    23	because training loads are hard to equate across different regimes; (3) it is
    24	"inappropriate to raise the question of the absolute effectiveness of any specific regime,"
    25	since each regime can be the most effective depending on the training situation, stage of
    26	the annual cycle, athlete level, the primary regime of muscular work demanded by the specific
    27	sport exercise, and the specific strength quality being trained. The authors' overall
    28	conclusion, stated with "reasonable certainty": the most rational way to enhance special
    29	strength preparation is to combine the various regimes of muscular work, a conclusion
    30	corroborated by multiple studies (Vorobyev, 1966; Andrianov & Vorobyev, 1969; Kuznetsov,
    31	1970; Verkhoshansky, 1970, 1972; Slobodyan, 1972; Tatyan, 1974; Pletnev, 1975; Khodykin,
    32	1975; Savin, 1974). Such a combination should be selected by considering its cumulative
    33	effect (see [[framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy]]) and
    34	its correspondence to the specific conditions of the sport. (PDF pp. 247-248, printed pp.
    35	236-237, "4.2.6.4 Choice of Muscle Training Regimes.") The authors earlier call any
    36	definitive statement about regimes "or combination of regimes" premature, because the
    37	comparative studies "are not very numerous," are "carried out with athletes of low
    38	qualification," and show "a tendency to deliberately favour that method which is
    39	fashionable" (PDF p. 242, printed p. 231); the "reasonable certainty" conclusion (PDF p.
    40	248, printed p. 237) is not reconciled with that. Only Pletnev (1975) is reported as a
    41	direct comparison ("a clear advantage"); the other citations are said to corroborate that
    42	combination is "the most rational means."
    43	
    44	**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for why combining regimes should be more
    45	effective than any one regime alone; Inference: a plausible explanation, not stated in the text, is that different
    46	regimes stress different components of the strength system (contractile tissue,
    47	elastic/connective tissue, neural drive, fibre-type-specific adaptation) somewhat
    48	independently, so combining them addresses more of the system than repeatedly stressing only
    49	one component.
    50	
    51	**When to apply** — Use this heuristic to resist single-method dogma ("isokinetics is best,"
    52	"only free weights work," "eccentric training is superior") when programming special
    53	strength training; per this section, the authors' own multi-study conclusion favours
    54	deliberately combining regimes (concentric, eccentric, isometric, static-dynamic,
    55	resistance, kinetic-energy) rather than committing to one, selected for cumulative effect
    56	and sport-specific correspondence.
    57	
    58	**When NOT to apply** — Contested because the authors call any definitive statement about
    59	"any regime or combination of regimes" premature (PDF p. 242, printed p. 231), citing
    60	low-qualification samples and fashion bias, then state the combination conclusion with
    61	"reasonable certainty" (PDF p. 248, printed p. 237). The corroborating citations (Vorobyev
    62	1966 through Savin 1974) give no individual effect sizes or protocols in this passage; treat "combining regimes is
    63	most rational" as the authors' summary conclusion across a body of era-specific Soviet sport
    64	science, not a single quantified finding. This heuristic does not specify which combination,
    65	in what proportion, or in what sequence to use for a given sport or athlete; it establishes
    66	only the authors' general principle that combining regimes is the most rational means,
    67	leaving the specific combination as a separate programming decision guided by cumulative-effect and
    68	dynamic-correspondence principles (see 4.3).
    69	
    70	**Example** — Inference: a strength block that mixes free-weight concentric-emphasis lifts,
    71	occasional isometric holds at sticking points, and periodic eccentric-emphasis work (rather
    72	than committing the whole block to one regime) is applying this heuristic directly; the
    73	specific mixture and sequencing would still need to be chosen using the cumulative-effect and
    74	sport-specificity criteria the authors name.
    75	
    76	**Related** — [[claim--static-dynamic-combined-isometric-concentric-method]],
    77	[[framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy]],
    78	[[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]] (Ch4.1, the related point that
    79	order and combination, not just choice of regime, change training outcomes).

    13	
    14	# Two Classes of Training Machine: Functional Resistance (Sport-Specific Pattern) vs Non-Functional Resistance (General Pattern)
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors distinguish two classes of strength machine: functional
    17	resistance (FR) machines, whose purpose is offering resistance in sport-specific movement
    18	patterns, and non-functional resistance (NFR) machines, whose sole purpose is offering
    19	general resistance in non-sport-specific patterns. They call this distinction vital, because
    20	Western "state-of-the-art" fitness centres are usually equipped almost entirely with NFR
    21	machines, so much so that adequate free weights or FR machines can be hard to find in them.
    22	"While the use of NFR machines may be adequate for the casual fitness client, it can be
    23	profoundly counterproductive for sport specific trainees if used in place of FR machines or
    24	free weights" (PDF p. 248, printed p. 237). They quote Zatsiorsky (1995) directly: "the important limitation of many strength training
    25	machines is that they are designed to train muscles, not movement. Because of this, they are
    26	not the most important training tool for athletes." FR devices are "supposed to imitate or
    27	train certain elements of an athletic exercise in order to provide the necessary specific
    28	loads in the different regimes of muscular work (Ratov, 1976)," and are reported effective for aspects of special strength training across many athlete types
    29	(Semenov, 1970; Petrova & Gorbunov, 1970; Verkhoshansky, 1970; Deniskin & Kuznetsov, 1972;
    30	Dobrovolski, 1972, 1973; Kuznetsov & Aiunts, 1974; Savin, 1974), because they permit strict
    31	regulation of load and the movement's spatial characteristics, letting a coach use the
    32	appropriate regime of muscular work and programme force-over-time characteristics while
    33	reproducing stereotypical training movements economically. The authors' example of a
    34	simple, cheap, versatile FR device is the "hi-lo" pulley machine, whose rope-attached
    35	handles (unlike fixed bars and pivots on most NFR machines) allow sport-specific movement
    36	patterns of great complexity; they estimate a circuit of just four pulley machines can
    37	provide training capacity that would otherwise need more than 40 "state of the art" NFR
    38	machines, and that a circuit of 10 pulley machines plus a few benches, jumping boards, bars,
    39	mats and wall-bars can serve more clients with a larger range of exercises than 100
    40	specialised machines, at under 15% of the cost. "Even then, the NFR machine-only facility
    41	would provide inferior multi-dimensional conditioning of the body" (PDF p. 249, printed p.
    42	238). A major FR advantage is visual/computerised feedback on movement
    43	quality and quantity for controlling training. The authors caution that simulating a sport
    44	movement against heavy machine loads can still significantly alter the movement's
    45	force-time characteristics and disrupt its neuromuscular programme; functionality is not
    46	automatic from an exercise merely resembling a sport action, but depends on the functional
    47	objective for which the exercise is used and how it is integrated into the long-term
    48	conditioning programme. (PDF pp. 248-249, printed pp. 237-238, "4.2.7 The Use of Training
    49	Machines," "4.2.7.1 Functional Resistance Machines.")
    50	
    51	**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is specificity: FR machines let a coach control load
    52	and the spatial/temporal pattern of the movement together, closer to the actual sport
    53	action, while still gaining measurement feedback; NFR machines use "fixed bars and pivots"
    54	(PDF p. 248, printed p. 237) in patterns that need not resemble any sport movement, training
    55	"muscles, not movement" per the quoted Zatsiorsky line.
    56	
    57	**When to apply** — Use this framework to audit a training facility or programme for FR
    58	versus NFR balance, per the authors' concern that Western commercial gyms over-provide NFR
    59	equipment. Prefer FR devices (pulley systems, cable machines with free movement paths,
    60	purpose-built sport-simulation devices) when the training goal requires reproducing a
    61	sport-specific spatial/temporal pattern with measurable load control.
    62	
    63	**When NOT to apply** — The authors' own caution applies: using any machine, FR or NFR, to
    64	simulate a sporting movement against heavy load can still disrupt the movement's natural
    65	force-time characteristics and neuromuscular programming; resemblance to a sport action does
    66	not automatically make an exercise "functional." See
    67	[[heuristic--nfr-machine-limitations-safety-and-appropriate-use]] for when NFR machines
    68	remain appropriate despite this section's general preference for FR devices and free
    69	weights.
    70	
    71	**Example** — The book's own example is the "hi-lo" pulley machine and the four-pulley
    72	versus forty-NFR-machine cost/capacity comparison described above; no further invented
    73	example is added here.
    74	
    75	**Related** — [[heuristic--nfr-machine-limitations-safety-and-appropriate-use]],
    76	[[claim--nfr-machine-marketing-claims-examined]].

    12	---
    13	
    14	# NFR Machines: Real Limitations on Proprioception and Joint Loading, but Not Actually Safer Than Free Weights
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Non-functional resistance (NFR) machines can play a useful supplementary
    17	role but generally cannot match free weights and FR machines for multi-dimensional,
    18	full-range neuromuscular and musculoskeletal training. Many NFR machines force the user to
    19	sit or lie, minimising training effect on major stabilising muscles and involving fewer
    20	joints through fewer degrees of freedom; while potentially valuable early in rehabilitation,
    21	this is an incomplete way of training the body for functional development, since machines
    22	that stabilise major body regions and limit the number of moving joints diminish the
    23	capacity to train balance, coordination and proprioception. The authors give a worked
    24	example: a free-standing squat involves three joints (hip, knee, ankle), while a seated knee
    25	extension machine constrains the body to one joint (knee) to exercise the quadriceps, so for
    26	a comparable exercise intensity over the same range of motion, the machine increases
    27	shearing force across the knee; the squat additionally exercises the thigh adductors, spinal
    28	erectors and other stabilisers, and enhances balance and (via longitudinal compressive
    29	loading) bone density. Seated exercise also always imposes a greater lumbar-disc load than
    30	equivalent standing exercise: maintaining a neutral spinal curve while seated raises lumbar
    31	disc pressure by about 40% (Chaffin & Andersson, 1984); allowing the back to flex forward can
    32	raise this by as much as 90%; a well-designed lumbar-supporting backrest lowers the stress
    33	but lumbar disc pressure can still run about 75% higher than standing; stress increases
    34	further against resistance, especially with jerky movements, and seated positions cannot
    35	absorb shock loading via knee/hip/ankle flexion the way standing can. On safety
    36	specifically, the authors reject the common claim that NFR machines are much safer than free
    37	weights, citing no source for the comparison: injuries to the back and knees (leg press, hack-squat, hip-sled), shoulders and
    38	chest (bench press, pec-deck), elbow (bicep curl machines) and back (back-extension
    39	machines) are "just as common with machines as with free weights," and many machines (pec
    40	deck, bench press, leg press, calf raise, seated press) force the movement to start from the
    41	biomechanically least efficient, most harmful position for the relevant joint; spotters are
    42	just as necessary for machines as for free weights, and faulty technique is equally dangerous
    43	with either. Some machines (leg extension, lat pulley, seated bicep curl) genuinely are safer
    44	for someone with back weakness or injury, and can help in early rehabilitation, but
    45	"continual avoidance of stress to the regions involved eventually leads to their progressive
    46	weakening" if relied on long-term. NFR machines remain useful for isolating specific muscle
    47	groups (bodybuilding-style supplementary training) or for the primary stages of injury
    48	rehabilitation, but not as an all-round conditioning replacement for free weights and FR
    49	devices; one exception noted is the lat-pulley machine, generally more suitable and safer
    50	than the free-weight equivalent (bent-over rowing) for training latissimus dorsi. (PDF pp.
    51	249-250, printed pp. 238-239, "4.2.7.2 Non-Functional Resistance Machines," "4.2.7.4 The
    52	Training Safety of Machines.")
    53	
    54	**Why it works** — The proprioception/stability mechanism is that fixing more joints and
    55	supporting more of the body's weight through the machine itself removes the balance,
    56	coordination and multi-joint stabilisation demand that free, standing exercise imposes. The
    57	single-joint-versus-multi-joint mechanism is straightforward: constraining a comparable
    58	training stimulus to fewer joints concentrates the same relative stress onto those joints'
    59	structures (illustrated by the squat-versus-knee-extension shearing-force example). The
    60	lumbar-disc mechanism is postural: seated positions load the discs differently than standing,
    61	and cannot use lower-body joint flexion to absorb shock the way standing positions can.
    62	
    63	**When to apply** — Use NFR machines for early-stage rehabilitation of a specific injured
    64	joint or muscle group, for supplementary bodybuilding-style isolation work, or when back
    65	weakness/injury makes a machine (leg extension, lat pulley, seated bicep curl) genuinely
    66	safer than the free-weight equivalent.
    67	
    68	Eric's baseline: per the protocol documents (tagged Inferred in `method-baseline.md`, "Force
    69	plate and neuromuscular monitoring"), the department runs "the standard CMJ family" on
    70	ForceDecks, and "the isometric seated calf raise is run on the ForceDecks 'Mid-Thigh Pull'
    71	setting: 90-degree ankle/knee position."
    72	
    73	Inference: the seated calf raise is a fixed-angle isometric test, not NFR machine training,
    74	so this section's critique of seated machines does not bear on it directly.
    75	
    76	**When NOT to apply** — Do not rely on NFR machines long-term as a substitute for free
    77	weights or FR devices in a healthy, competitive athlete's programme, since progressive
    78	avoidance of stress to a region "eventually leads to... progressive weakening." Do not
    79	assume NFR machines are inherently safer than free weights; per the authors' uncited
    80	comparison (PDF p. 250, printed p. 239), injuries are "just as common with machines as with
    81	free weights," and spotting and technique matter with both. The lumbar-disc figures (40%,
    82	90%, 75%) come from one cited source, Chaffin & Andersson (1984), for the claim that seated
    83	exercise "always" loads the discs more than standing (PDF pp. 249-250, printed pp.
    84	238-239); the text cites only this one source, and this library holds no modern source on
    85	the point, so treat "always" as the authors' claim, not a checked finding.
    86	
    87	**Example** — Inference: using a seated knee-extension machine during the first two weeks
    88	after a knee injury (early rehabilitation, single-joint control) while progressing toward a
    89	free-standing squat as tolerance improves applies this heuristic's appropriate-use window; continuing
    90	to rely on the knee-extension machine as the primary quadriceps exercise once the athlete
    91	returns to full training would not, per the "progressive weakening" caution above.
    92	
    93	**Related** — [[framework--functional-vs-nonfunctional-resistance-machines]],
    94	[[claim--nfr-machine-marketing-claims-examined]].

     6	chapter: "4.2.7.3, 4.2.7.5"

     9	confidence: supported

    12	---
    13	
    14	# The Authors Argue Variable-Resistance Machines' Core Marketing Premise Is a Physics Error, and That NFR Machines Need Many More Units to Match Free Weights
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Many machine manufacturers design variable-resistance machines to match a
    17	joint's natural torque curve, claiming superiority over free weights and other resistance
    18	devices on this basis. The authors identify a flawed premise behind this claim: manufacturers
    19	imply a free weight's resistance stays constant throughout a lift (e.g. a 50 kg biceps curl
    20	is presented as exerting a constant 50 kg / about 490 Newton force from start to finish). A
    21	simple application of Newton's Second Law (force proportional to acceleration) shows this is
    22	false: the resistance a free weight offers changes with acceleration from rest and at any
    23	point the trainee speeds up or slows down, "as can easily be demonstrated by force plate,
    24	cable tensiometer or high speed video analysis"; a skilled trainee already uses proprioception
    25	to perceive these changes and adjust resistance and direction more efficiently, the authors
    26	argue, than current machines can. Separately, on training efficiency, the authors give
    27	several specific machine-count comparisons: it takes at least 12 NFR machines to
    28	approximately equal the training effect of the clean-and-push-press, at least 4 to rival the
    29	free-standing squat, more than 3 to equal the standing dumbbell curl, and at least 5 to
    30	rival the flexed-knee deadlift; in total, more than 24 NFR machines are required to match the
    31	combined training effect of just four free-weight exercises (clean-and-push-press, squat,
    32	deadlift, biceps curl), at roughly 40 times the combined cost of the equivalent free weights
    33	and racks, with NFR machines also carrying higher maintenance costs and more frequent
    34	breakdowns in a well-used gymnasium than "virtually indestructible" free weights. (PDF pp.
    35	250-251, printed pp. 239-240, "4.2.7.3 Machines and the Variable Resistance Philosophy,"
    36	"4.2.7.5 The Efficiency of Machine Training.")
    37	
    38	**Why it works** — For the variable-resistance critique, the mechanism is Newtonian: force
    39	equals mass times acceleration, so any free weight's true resistance already varies with the
    40	trainee's own acceleration/deceleration throughout the lift, contradicting the marketing
    41	premise that free weights offer constant resistance needing a machine's correction. The
    42	authors give no mechanism for the machine counts. Inference: a compound free-weight exercise
    43	recruits and trains many more muscle groups, movement patterns and stabilising demands
    44	simultaneously than any single-joint NFR machine, so many NFR machines are needed in
    45	combination to approach the same total training stimulus.
    46	
    47	**When to apply** — Use the Newtonian-mechanics point to counter the specific marketing claim
    48	that free weights offer "constant" resistance (see When NOT to apply for its limit); per the
    49	authors, a skilled lifter's own proprioceptive control of bar speed already varies the true
    50	resistance throughout the lift (see also
    51	[[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]], Ch1). Use the machine-count/cost
    52	comparison when evaluating equipment-purchase decisions for a training facility: a small set
    53	of free-weight stations and racks may replicate the combined training effect of a much
    54	larger, more expensive NFR machine circuit, per this section's specific figures.
    55	
    56	**When NOT to apply** — The specific machine-count figures (12, 4, 3+, 5, 24+, roughly 40x
    57	cost) are the authors' own estimates for approximating specific free-weight exercises' total
    58	training effect with combinations of NFR machines; they do not cite a controlled study
    59	establishing these exact ratios, so treat them as illustrative rather than precisely
    60	measured. Inference: the Newtonian point shows free-weight resistance is not constant, but it
    61	does not show that free-weight resistance matches the joint's strength curve; the
    62	manufacturers' torque-angle argument (resistance varying with joint angle, which exists even
    63	at constant velocity) is not directly rebutted in this passage (PDF p. 250, printed p. 239).
    64	The authors do not argue that variable-resistance machines have zero value in this passage,
    65	only that their core "free weights are constant resistance" premise is incorrect. Inference:
    66	some variable-resistance designs may still offer useful features (feedback display, joint
    67	isolation for rehabilitation) independent of that specific flawed premise.
    68	
    69	**Example** — Inference: a facility manager comparing the cost of building a small free-weight
    70	area (barbells, plates, a rack, a platform) against an equivalent machine circuit covering
    71	the same major lift patterns should expect, per this section's estimates, the free-weight
    72	option to require far fewer total pieces of equipment and far lower combined cost.
    73	
    74	**Related** — [[framework--functional-vs-nonfunctional-resistance-machines]],
    75	[[heuristic--nfr-machine-limitations-safety-and-appropriate-use]],
    76	[[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]] (Ch1, the related point that free-weight
    77	resistance already varies via the lifter's own acceleration).

    13	
    14	# Chasing Perfect Bilateral Symmetry Is Ill-Advised: Sprinters' Push-Off and Swing Legs Are Naturally Asymmetric
    15	
    16	**What it is** — This entry fulfils the forward reference in this library's Ch3.3.4.4 entry
    17	(see
    18	[[claim--natural-asymmetry-caution-against-isokinetic-symmetry-correction]]), which deferred
    19	"The Concept of Symmetric Training" to this section. Asymmetry in leg length, muscle
    20	strength, stride length and other structural/functional features has been blamed for
    21	inefficient movement and injury, and imbalances in agonist/antagonist and left/right strength
    22	(including isokinetically-measured muscular endurance imbalances) have been singled out as
    23	leading causes of muscle injury. However, research the authors do not cite ("Research,
    24	however, has revealed", PDF p. 251, printed p. 240) found that isokinetically-measured left/right
    25	leg-strength or agonist/antagonist discrepancies as large as 10% do not statistically
    26	correlate with a major increase in muscular injuries. Because the body, its muscles, tendons
    27	and bones are characteristically asymmetric, attempts to force greater anthropomorphic and
    28	kinesiological symmetry "could exacerbate the existing problem or cause new injuries";
    29	assessing asymmetry properly requires both static structural measurement (leg length, spinal
    30	curvature) and dynamic biomechanical analysis (force distribution, movement patterns, ground
    31	reaction force, postural/phasic muscle EMG, movement-phase timing). Structural differences
    32	in muscle/tendon length, tendon and ligament attachment sites, and bone size/mass are
    33	"quite natural in all humans"; surgical or orthotic correction is warranted only when such
    34	structural differences cause serious functional movement imbalances, and even then only
    35	after confirming the asymmetry is primarily structural rather than a centrally-stored
    36	neuromuscular pattern (in which case the answer is modifying the motor skill itself, not
    37	correcting the body). There is "no perfect way" to execute any movement; style is the
    38	individualised expression of a motor skill and should be developed by observing and
    39	experimenting against an "ideal" model until the athlete's own central nervous programme
    40	fits their body, rather than enforcing one rigid technique standard. Yushkevich (1989)
    41	analysed leg-strength symmetry in sprinters and concluded striving for full leg symmetry is
    42	inappropriate: extensors of all joints of the push-off leg were generally significantly
    43	stronger than the swing leg's, with no consistent flexor-strength difference between legs.
    44	Asymmetry patterns differed by qualification level: novices showed stronger push-off-leg hip
    45	flexors than swing-leg; novice, Class 3 and Class 2 athletes showed stronger swing-leg knee
    46	flexors, while Class 1, Master and higher-qualified athletes showed stronger push-off-leg
    47	knee flexors; dorsiflexion was stronger in the push-off leg for all athletes except novices.
    48	Leg-strength asymmetry increased with sprint proficiency, peaking among Class 2 athletes,
    49	then diminishing again with further mastery. Good sprint times correlated more closely with
    50	swing-leg strength than push-off-leg strength. Yushkevich's conclusion: not only is
    51	symmetrical muscle strength a misguided target, but deliberately asymmetric exercise
    52	(running or jumping on sloping/inclined tracks, running curves in both directions, running or
    53	jumping in shoes with soles of different thickness, or running with unevenly-weighted legs)
    54	can be beneficial, since "asymmetric exercises destabilise the space-time characteristics of
    55	motor acts, thereby helping athletes break speed barriers." The authors close with an analogy
    56	to the tradition that Eastern-carpet weavers deliberately include at least one flaw, since
    57	"perfection is reserved for the Divine," implying similar asymmetry or imperfection may be
    58	desirable in human physical performance and training generally. (PDF pp. 251-252, printed pp.
    59	240-241, "4.2.8 The Concept of Symmetric Training.")
    60	
    61	**Why it works** — No cellular or biomechanical mechanism is given for why swing-leg strength
    62	predicts sprint time better than push-off-leg strength, or for why asymmetry peaks at Class 2
    63	then declines with further mastery; the authors report these as empirical findings from
    64	Yushkevich (1989) without deriving them from a stated causal model. For the general "why
    65	symmetry-forcing backfires" claim, the authors give no mechanism beyond the risk that forcing
    66	symmetry "could exacerbate the existing problem or cause new injuries" (PDF p. 251, printed
    67	p. 240). Inference: natural asymmetry may reflect functional specialisation (dominant-limb
    68	skill, individualised structure).
    69	
    70	**When to apply** — Use this claim, together with the Ch3.3.4.4 entry it completes (see
    71	Related), as the book's full position on symmetry testing and correction: a numeric L/R or
    72	agonist/antagonist discrepancy up to about 10% (isokinetically measured) is not itself
    73	evidence of elevated injury risk, and deliberately asymmetric training elements (uneven
    74	surfaces, directional bias, unevenly weighted limbs) may have a specific rationale for sprint
    75	athletes rather than being technique flaws to eliminate.
    76	
    77	Eric's baseline: the department's force-plate metric framework includes "optional symmetry
    78	metrics (L/R differences)" (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular
    79	monitoring," tagged "Adopted practice, framework not Eric's own", origin Hawkin Dynamics).
    80	
    81	Inference: this entry supports treating symmetry as descriptive/monitoring information
    82	rather than an automatic correction target.
    83	
    84	**When NOT to apply** — In Yushkevich's data asymmetry peaked at Class 2 and declined with
    85	higher mastery (PDF p. 251, printed p. 240), so the data do not show that more asymmetry is
    86	better. The Yushkevich (1989) sprinter data are single-study, era-specific findings on
    87	sprinters graded by sports classification (novice, Class 3 to Class 1, Master), with no
    88	sample size given in this passage; the specific qualification-level patterns (novice through Master) and the
    89	Class-2 asymmetry peak should not be assumed to generalise to other sports or populations
    90	without separate verification. The 10%-discrepancy-does-not-correlate-with-injury finding
    91	does not mean no discrepancy threshold matters; it means this specific threshold, measured
    92	isokinetically, was not found to correlate in the cited research. Do not read the
    93	"deliberately asymmetric training" recommendation as license to ignore genuine
    94	functional/structural imbalances that are causing injury or performance-limiting compensation
    95	(the authors' own scoping condition above); the recommendation applies specifically to
    96	sprint-specific push-off/swing-leg asymmetry, not to every kind of asymmetry.
    97	
    98	**Example** — The book's own example is the Yushkevich (1989) sprinter data described above;
    99	no further invented example is added here.
   100	
   101	**Related** — [[claim--natural-asymmetry-caution-against-isokinetic-symmetry-correction]]
   102	(Ch3.3.4.4, the entry that deferred this section to Ch4.2.8; this entry fulfils that
   103	cross-reference and both should carry a reciprocal link),
   104	[[heuristic--isokinetic-strength-ratios-vary-by-angle-and-velocity]],
   105	[[research-papers/bishop-2016-asymmetries-of-the-lower-limb-the-calculation-conundrum-in-strength-training-and-condition]],
   106	[[research-papers/callaway-2026-group-normative-data-and-arbitrary-asymmetry-thresholds-fail-to-represent-individual-playe]]
   107	(modern papers the Ch3 sibling links on how asymmetry data should be used).
=================== claim--muscle-isolation-is-load-dependent-mostly-illusory-under-heavy-load.md

     2	type: library-entry
     3	kind: claim
     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
     6	chapter: "4.2.9"
     7	topic: load-dependence of muscle isolation
     8	category: [exercise-selection, biomechanics, terminology]
     9	confidence: supported
    10	ingest-tier: full-text
    11	created: 2026-09-27
    12	---
    13	
    14	# "Muscle Isolation" Is Possible Only for Small Muscle Groups at Low Intensity; Heavy or Prolonged Resistance Recruits Stabilisers Until Isolation Is Essentially Impossible
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Generations of bodybuilding-magazine authors have advocated specific
    17	machines, joint-fixation methods, precise limb placement and other techniques claimed to
    18	maximally recruit one muscle group while others stay "largely dormant." "EMG studies reveal
    19	that isolation of minute muscle groups is indeed possible under low intensities of loading
    20	(e.g. Basmajian, 1978)": low-intensity actions like eye-blinking, piano-playing or relaxed speech
    21	rely on precise, isolated action of specific small muscle groups. However, once a large load
    22	is imposed on a target muscle group by intense resistance, isolation becomes "virtually
    23	impossible": as soon as the load is applied, stabilising muscles engage to keep the body or
    24	specific joints stable while prime movers cope with the load, and if the nervous system
    25	signals the prime movers are inadequate, assistant movers, shunt muscles, emergency muscles
    26	and neutralisers may all be recruited to help. Physiotherapists using PNF sometimes impose
    27	maximal loading on a joint deliberately to elicit compensatory or overflow activity of
    28	muscles other than the prime movers. "The higher the intensity or the greater the duration
    29	of the exercise, the less likely is isolation of the prime mover, even if certain joints are
    30	restrained as on an isokinetic test machine," and "in many cases the tension developed in
    31	the stabilisers or assistant stabilisers will equal or exceed that of the prime movers." The
    32	authors' worked example: during heavy
    33	standing triceps push-downs on a cable machine, the abdominals, latissimus dorsi and erector
    34	spinae "may be as strongly contracted as the triceps," despite this being nominally a
    35	triceps-isolation exercise; analysis of many seated or reclining "isolation" machine
    36	exercises shows isolation simply does not occur with heavy loads. This is the same load-dependent
    37	proximal/distal recruitment shift already noted earlier in the chapter (see
    38	[[claim--muscle-recruitment-consistency-and-proximal-distal-shift-with-load]]), where the
    39	authors explicitly forward-referenced this section. This does not negate the value of
    40	isolation-style exercises: they can be useful in early injury rehabilitation, and the
    41	overflow to other muscle groups at higher loads can itself be desirable (if performed
    42	safely), since it simultaneously offers isometric and dynamic training to those other muscle
    43	groups. The authors' stated purpose for this section is to correct the "misleading concept
    44	of muscle isolation" still promoted by many instructors and training texts. (PDF p. 252,
    45	printed p. 241, "4.2.9 The Concept of Muscle Isolation.")
    46	
    47	**Why it works** — The mechanism given is neuromuscular: as load intensity or duration rises, the central
    48	nervous system recruits whatever additional muscle groups (stabilisers, assistant movers,
    49	emergency muscles, neutralisers) are needed to keep the targeted joint and the body stable
    50	and to complete the movement, since a single "isolated" muscle group's own capacity is
    51	insufficient against a heavy load; at low intensities, EMG shows isolation of minute muscle
    52	groups (PDF p. 252, printed p. 241).
    53	
    54	**When to apply** — Use this claim to correctly interpret what a "muscle isolation" exercise
    55	is actually training at a given load and duration. EMG shows isolation of minute muscle
    56	groups at low intensity (PDF p. 252, printed p. 241); the authors separately say isolation
    57	exercises can help in the early stages of injury rehabilitation. Inference: low-load rehab
    58	isolation work may approach isolation, but the book does not show it for limb muscles.
    59	Inference: this fits [[claim--irradiation-effect-raises-prime-mover-force-and-endurance]]'s
    60	finding that effort and tension spread between muscle groups. At hypertrophy- or
    61	strength-level heavy or prolonged loading, expect and potentially embrace the overflow to stabilisers and
    62	assistant movers as additional, simultaneous isometric/dynamic training for those muscle
    63	groups rather than treating it as a programming failure.
    64	
    65	**When NOT to apply** — Do not describe a heavy-load exercise (a heavy cable push-down, a
    66	heavy leg-extension set) as "isolating" the target muscle group in marketing, coaching cues,
    67	or programme design; per this claim and its EMG evidence, isolation is shown only for minute muscle
    68	groups at low training intensities. Do not assume the specific triceps push-down example
    69	generalises identically to every "isolation" exercise; the authors give it as one worked
    70	illustration, not a universally quantified finding across exercises.
    71	
    72	**Example** — The book's own example is the heavy triceps push-down engaging abdominals,
    73	latissimus dorsi and erector spinae described above; no further invented example is added
    74	here.
    75	
    76	**Related** — [[claim--muscle-recruitment-consistency-and-proximal-distal-shift-with-load]]
    77	(this chapter's own forward reference to this entry, 4.2.2),
    78	[[claim--irradiation-effect-raises-prime-mover-force-and-endurance]] (Ch3, a related finding
    79	on how tension in one muscle group affects others).
